documents.title: Early Breast Cancer Diagnosis Treatment Follow-up

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Breast cancer (BC) is the most frequent oncological diagnosis in women, corresponding to approximately 15% of all new cancer diagnoses and 7% of all cancer deaths [ ]. A wide array of strategies, such as early tumour detection and better treatment options, have been accessible, improving patients’ life expectancy and leading to a 5-year survival rate of over 90% in non-metastatic breast cancer. Nevertheless, there are more than 50,000 BC-related deaths every year in North America [ ]. BC is a heterogeneous disease comprising different morphological subtypes and with varying genomic drivers of signaling pathways, yielding distinct prognoses [ ]. Approximately 75% of breast tumours are encoded with luminal differentiation involving endocrine receptor (ER) positivity [ ]. Between 15% and 20% of all BC diagnoses feature the overexpression of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) phenotype, and 10–15% represent triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) [ ]. Whereas the luminal BC subtype, ER+ HER2-negative, is typically responsive to endocrine therapy (ET), chemotherapy has an enhanced efficacy with both the HER2+ and basal-like TNBC [ , , ]. While luminal tumours with a high expression of ER have the most indolent course and most favorable prognosis, the TNBC subtype has the poorest outcomes, likely due to the absence of suitable options for targeted treatments inhibiting specific molecular pathways [ , , ]. Pathological features associated with a higher likelihood of distant metastasis and worse BC prognosis are linked to increased tumour size, poorly differentiated histology and axillary lymph node involvement (LN+) [ , ]. The latter is strongly correlated with a high-risk of mortality [ ]. For example, in ER+ breast cancer, the absolute risk of cumulative breast cancer death at 20 years from the time of diagnosis increases by 13% and 34% in patients with LN+ 1–3 and LN+ ≥ 4, respectively, when compared to patients with unaffected LN [ ]. In those lacking ER expression, the TNBC population has the highest rate of distant metastasis and breast cancer mortality, at 5 years [ , ]. Understanding the tumour morphology, e.g., invasive ductal, lobular or mucinous, ER and HER2 expressions, as well as the pathology features and BC stage, are critical to classifying tumours and guiding the clinician’s decision towards the most appropriate treatment for each case [ , , ]. The role of postoperative systemic therapy is to eliminate latent microscopic malignant cells unidentified in the surgical specimen [ ]. When there are clinical or pathological high-risk features and high recurrence risk scores on genomic expression assays, adjuvant chemotherapy is the treatment of choice for improving overall survival (OS) and lowering the risk of local and distant cancer recurrence [ , , ]. Nonetheless, regardless of BC subtype and which treatment route is taken, relapse events steadily continue beyond the time of chemotherapy completion [ , ]. Conversely, an early treatment start, and adequate adherence, are highly associated with better outcomes [ ]. The addition of anthracycline to taxane chemotherapy is the gold standard in the treatment for breast cancer with high risk for cancer relapse. However, the potential short- and long-term side effects have made the choice of anthracycline questionable. Along with the high emetogenic and immunosuppressive characteristics, they can cause irreversible and life-threatening conditions, such as congestive heart failure (CHF) and leukemia [ , ]. Unfortunately, the risk of CHF induced by anthracycline persists after the treatment is completed, leading to an increased absolute risk of 1.72% at 1 year and 3.62% at 10 years post-treatment ( p < 0.001) [ ]. Almost all of the RCTs comparing anthracycline versus non-anthracycline chemotherapy were conducted before the establishment of the 2022 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines, where it was determined that the evidence of reduced cardiac function is not sufficient to rule out a Cancer Therapy-related Cardiac Dysfunction (CTRCD). Instead, analyzing CHF symptoms is indispensable, since its presentation is often sub-clinical. Thus, it is likely that cardiotoxicity events had been underestimated in many of the RCTs that used anthracycline-based or anti-HER2 therapies, emphasizing the importance of investigating the impact of CHF in retrospective population-based studies [ ]. A suitable taxane-based chemotherapy sparing the anthracycline component is the docetaxel and cyclophosphamide (TC) regimen, which has a remarkably safe profile and attains survival outcomes comparable to the anthracyclines in select breast cancer populations [ , ]. For example, in patients who were previously treated with anthracycline or have underlying cardiac predispositions, TC is a reasonable chemotherapy choice [ , ]. Thus, there continues to be debate around the optimal chemotherapeutic option, and in which breast cancer populations may anthracyclines be omitted. Here, we describe the real-world experience of BC patients treated with adjuvant chemotherapy in Ontario, Canada. We aim to compare the clinical outcomes in patients treated with the TC regimen, versus those receiving the most

For example, in patients who were previously treated with anthracycline or have underlying cardiac predispositions, TC is a reasonable chemotherapy choice [ , ]. Thus, there continues to be debate around the optimal chemotherapeutic option, and in which breast cancer populations may anthracyclines be omitted. Here, we describe the real-world experience of BC patients treated with adjuvant chemotherapy in Ontario, Canada. We aim to compare the clinical outcomes in patients treated with the TC regimen, versus those receiving the most conventional standardized anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy options. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design We conducted an observational, retrospective population-based cohort study of adult women diagnosed with stage I-III breast cancer (ICD-10 C50^) between January 2009 and December 2017. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines in the preparation of this manuscript [ ]. 2.2. Patient Population All patients underwent breast surgery for tumour resection and had a histological diagnosis of invasive breast carcinoma. Patients received adjuvant chemotherapy with TC or anthracycline–taxane-based chemotherapy. Patients were included if their chemotherapy start date was no longer than 120 days from their BC surgery. A minimum of 6 months of follow-up data based on the last registry within the health care databases was required. The end of the follow-up was on 31 March 2018. The exclusion criteria included bilateral BC, previous diagnosis of malignancy, leukemia or CHF, and missing data around demographic information and BC characteristics. Patients were also excluded if they were HER2+ or had an unknown HER2 status but received trastuzumab. 2.3. Exposure Adjuvant chemotherapy was defined as cytotoxic systemic treatments administered intravenously, initiated after the breast surgery was performed. The exposure of interest consisted of the administration of the non-anthracycline TC chemotherapy versus anthracycline–taxane containing regimens. The TC regimen comprised docetaxel and cyclophosphamide administered every 3 weeks for a total of four cycles. The anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy regimens are as follows: fluoracil, epirubicin and cyclophosphamide administered every 3 weeks for 3 cycles, followed by docetaxel every 3 weeks for 3 cycles (FEC-D); doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide were administered every 2 or 3 weeks for a total of four cycles, followed by 12 administrations of paclitaxel, on a weekly schedule, or 4 administrations on a 2-week schedule (ACT). Docetaxel was considered as a substitute for paclitaxel chemotherapy, which was administered every 3 weeks for a total of 4 cycles. Patients treated with paclitaxel on a 3-week schedule were not included because of the inferior outcomes when compared to the standard treatment schedules [ ]. The usage of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) injections was allowed. 2.4. Data Sources Our study data were obtained from ICES (formerly known as the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences); ICES is an independent, non-profit research institute whose legal status, under Ontario’s health information privacy law, allows it to collect and analyze health care and demographic data, without consent, for health system evaluation and improvement. The ICES maintains the health administrative data of more than 14 million Ontario residents [ ]. Encrypted identifiers containing anonymous data were used to access patient information and to link them with other health datasets as follows: The Cancer Activity Level Reporting (ALR) and Ontario Cancer Registry (OCR) databases, as well as the registry elements of data of Ontario’s cancer system and the New Drug Funding Program (NDFP), were accessed to verify all Ontario residents diagnosed with BC (ICD-10 C50^) in a patient-level activity focused on postoperative systemic treatment, such as dates, dose, and type of chemotherapy administrations. The Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP), Canadian Institutes of Health Information Discharge Abstract Database (CIHI-DAD), and CIHI National Ambulatory Care Reporting System (CIHI-NACRS) were used to obtain the diagnostic code information of medical procedures, hospital admissions, emergency room visits and discharge diagnosis. It also provided data about the preceding diagnoses of patient comorbidities based on the Charlson–Deyo index. Breast cancer characteristics, including staging, tumour grade, lymph node status, ER and HER2 status, were extracted from the OCR. These datasets were linked using unique encoded identifiers and analyzed at ICES. Surgical pathology information was used to classify the BC stage. In the case of an unknown HER2 status, patients were classified as HER2 negative if they did not receive trastuzumab. Breast surgery (mastectomy versus lumpectomy and lymph node (LN) surgical assessments (none, sentinel LN biopsy or axillary LN dissection) were identified using procedure codes in the CIHI and Same Day Surgery databases. Radiotherapy was identified from the ALR and OHIP databases. Adjuvant breast radiotherapy was defined as radiation treatment started within 90 days after chemotherapy was completed. The Registered Persons Database (RPDB) provided the demographic information, cause of death and the socioeconomic status, from which the latest median household income quintile by the Canadian

Breast surgery (mastectomy versus lumpectomy and lymph node (LN) surgical assessments (none, sentinel LN biopsy or axillary LN dissection) were identified using procedure codes in the CIHI and Same Day Surgery databases. Radiotherapy was identified from the ALR and OHIP databases. Adjuvant breast radiotherapy was defined as radiation treatment started within 90 days after chemotherapy was completed. The Registered Persons Database (RPDB) provided the demographic information, cause of death and the socioeconomic status, from which the latest median household income quintile by the Canadian postal code were acquired. This research was approval by the Research Ethics Board of Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre. Under the legislation of the Ontario Health’s privacy information program, the patients’ written informed consent was waived. 2.5. Outcomes The primary outcome of interest is overall survival (OS). The survival time was defined in months, from the start of adjuvant chemotherapy (index date) to death from any cause. Patients were right-censored at the end of the study follow-up, if no individual death records were encountered. Secondary outcomes are OS data stratified by the chemotherapy regimens of interest and ER status. A subgroup analysis was used to evaluate OS in ER-positive BC and ER-negative BC, stratified by the chemotherapy regimens, and by the number of axillary LNs. Amongst the chemotherapy options, we compared any diagnosis of congestive heart failure (CHF) from the chemotherapy start date for the rest of patients’ lifetime. We investigated the incidence of febrile neutropenia diagnosis, the most common causes for emergency room visits and hospitalizations, from the chemotherapy starting date to 30 days after its completion. For the respective conditions, we searched for the corresponding International Code Diagnosis (ICD-9 and ICD-10) and acute care visits. To evaluate febrile neutropenia, since there is no specific ICD for this condition, we searched in the administrative database for billing codes associated with acute care visits in women with a diagnosis of early BC, and who were on chemotherapy, postoperatively. For each acute care visit, we used the most responsible diagnosis (MRD). We selected neutropenia as the MRD, plus any diagnosis of fever corresponding to that visit, and created a variable called febrile neutropenia MRD. 2.6. Statistical Analysis We used Kaplan–Meyer methods to analyze the survival curves, based on the adjusted analysis. For the secondary endpoints, we used hazard ratio (HR) estimates in a stratified Cox proportional-hazard regression model (time to event data) for death. For this endeavor, the analysis carried out adjusted the data by all covariates, patient and tumour baseline characteristics, as shown in . The data were analyzed using the software R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) version 4.1. All statistical test analyses were two-sided. A p -value of ≤0.05 was considered statistically significant. The adjusted analyses were generated. A sensitivity analysis was performed to analyze the potential confounding factor among the independent variables. Multiple imputation was applied to adjust for missing data, using the SAS default single Markov chain Monte Carlo method. Assuming a normal multivariate distribution sample, ten complete datasets were generated for statistical inferences [ ]. 3. Results 3.1. Patient Characteristics We identified a total of 74,852 patients diagnosed with stage I-III BC between 2009 and 2017 in Ontario. From those, there were 37,281 patients treated with adjuvant chemotherapy, plus/minus trastuzumab. A total of 26,633 patients were excluded due to the delayed start of adjuvant chemotherapy beyond 90 days, because they received less than 50% of the planned chemotherapy cycles or treatment doses, or because they had HER2 + BC or an unknown status of HER2, but treated were with trastuzumab. Hence, a total of 10,634 women were included in this study ( ). The patients’ baseline characteristics are shown in . A total of 4222 (39.7%) women were between 18 and 50 years old. There were 4970 (46.7%) and 1442 (13.6%) patients between 51 and 65 and older than 65 years of age, respectively. Approximately 33.3% of patients were similarly treated between each of the following intervals: 2009–2011, 2012–2014 and 2015–2017. The most common underlying comorbidities were hypertension, with 2902 (27.3%) cases reported, followed by diabetes and dyslipidemia, with 1255 (11.9%) and 1016 (9.6%) cases reported. The number of patients on the extreme edges of the income quintile categories, Q1 (lowest) and Q5 (highest), were 1565 (14.7%) and 2564 (24.1%), respectively. A total of 6290 (85.3%) women had an income quintile categorized between Q2–Q4. Patients living in rural areas comprised 1158 (10.9%) of the total number of patients. Stratifying by BC stage, there were 2087 (19.6%) women with stage I, 6497 (61.1%) with stage II and 2050 (19.3%) with stage III. From the final cohort of 10,634 patients, there were 2387 (23.5%) patients treated with TC, 2981 (28.0%) patients who received ACT and 5166 (48.5%) treated with FEC-D chemotherapy regimens. The number of patients who had adjuvant radiation that was started within 90 days from the completion of chemotherapy amounted to a total of 7043 (66.2%). 3.2. Overall Survival Analysis The median follow-up was 5.5 (3.5–7.8) years for the overall study population and 4.6 (3.0–7.2) years for patients treated with TC, 4.5 (2.8–6.5) years for those treated with ACT and 6.7 (4.4–8.6) years for those treated with FEC-D. The median OS of the entire cohort was 8.0 years. After adjusting the analysis by the confounders (age, year of BC diagnosis, Charlson comorbidity index, income quintile, urban/rural residence status, ER, HER2 and LN status, histological grade, type of surgery and radiation treatment), the 5-year OS was 93.8% for those treated with TC, 92.7% for those treated with ACT and 90.7% for those treated with FEC-D, ( p = 0.052). The risk of death was higher or not different between those treated with ACT and FEC-D [HR of 1.11 (95% CI, 0.94–1.30), p = 0.21], and lower or not different between those treated with TC and FEC-D [HR of 0.86 (95% CI, 0.71–1.03)], p = 0.102]. Nevertheless, there was a significantly increased OS, or reduced risk of death, favoring TC vs. ACT [HR of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.63–0.95), p = 0.015], ( ). 3.2.1. Overall Survival Analysis by ER Status A total of 7130 (67.0%) women were ER+ BC, and at the 5-year post-treatment mark, the OS was 95.6% for those treated with TC, 94.4% for those treated with ACT and 92.1% for those treated with FEC-D, p = 0.018. The risk of death was significantly lower in patients treated with TC, when compared to those treated with anthracycline–taxane: TC vs. ACT [HR of 0.70 (95% CI, 0.521–0.949), p = 0.0218], TC vs. FEC-D [HR of 0.716 (95% CI, 0.56–0.912), p = 0.007], ( A) ( ). A total of 2379 (22.4%) women were ER− BC, and at the 5-year post-treatment mark, the OS was 88.9% for those treated with TC, 91.0% for those treated with ACT and 86.7% for those treated with FEC-D, p = 0.321. The risk of death was not different in patients treated with TC chemotherapy, when compared to those treated with the anthracycline–taxane regimens: TC vs. ACT [HR of 1.25 (95% CI, 0.88–1.78), p = 0.207]. From the sensitivity analysis, comparing the analyses with versus without multiple imputation for the independent covariates, there was no significant difference in OS in the ER-positive BC population. 3.2.3. In patients with LN+ 1–3, TC vs. ACT, OS HR was 2.26, (95% CI, 0.84–6.11), p = 0.11 and TC vs. FEC-D, OS HR was 1.88 (95% CI, 0.68–5.15) p = 0.22. In patients with LN ≥ 4, TC vs. ACT, OS HR was 2.25 (95% CI, 0.79–6.40) p = 0.13 and TC vs. FEC-D, OS HR was 2.20 (95% CI, 0.79–6.11) p = 0.13 ( ). Similarly to the ER+ group, regardless of the chemotherapy regimen received, a significant increased risk of death, by at least four fold, was observed in those who had LN ≥ 4, compared to those who had LN 0; TC [HR of 4.41 (95% CI, 1.33–14.59), p = 0.015]; ACT [HR of 6.70 (95% CI, 3.96–11.35), p < 0.001]; FEC-D [HR of 8.48 (95% CI, 4.77–15.05), p < 0.001]. In addition, an increased mortality rate was noticed in women with LN 1–3 vs. LN 0, who received ACT [HR of 2.75 (1.71–4.43), p < 0.001] and FEC-D [HR of 4.01 (2.43–6.60), p < 0.001] ( ). In the multivariate regression model, BC features such as tumour size > 2 to 5 cm [HR of 2.37 (95% CI, 1.11–5.06), p = 0.02] and LN ≥ 4 [HR of 4.4 (95% CI, 1.3–14.6), p = 0.015)], and the comorbidities CHF [HR of 3.39 (95% CI, 0.98–11.6), p = 0.05] and renal disease [HR of 4.26 (95% CI, 1.49–12.2), p = 0.006] were all associated with the increased risk of death in the ER– group ( ). From the sensitivity analysis, comparing the analyses with versus without multiple imputation for the independent covariates, there was no significant difference in OS in the ER-negative cohort. 3.3. Cardiotoxicity For this analysis, we evaluated cardiotoxicity when a diagnosis of CHF occurred, from the chemotherapy start day for the rest of the patient’s lifetime. Those who had CHF at baseline (n = 99) were excluded from the analysis ( ). A total of 97 patients were diagnosed with CHF during the time this study was conducted. Cardiotoxicity events were found in 25 (1.0%) out of the 2434 patients treated with TC, in 19 (0.6%) out of the 2957 who received ACT, and in 53 (1.0%) out of the 5113 women who were treated with FEC-D. A comparison between TC vs. ACT, revealed a HR of 1.40 (95% CI, 0.77–2.56), p = 0.27, and TC vs. FEC-D, showed a HR of 1.28 (95% CI, 0.79–2.55), p = 0.32 ( ). 3.4. Emergency Department Visits and Hospitalization From 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2017, there were a total of 3600 visits to the emergency department (ED) for BC patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy. The highest number of ED visits were by those treated with FEC-D (n = 2024; 56.2%), followed by 988 (27.44%) of those treated with TC, and 588 (16.33%) of those treated with ACT, p < 0.0001. Overall, fever (n = 720; 20%), followed by neutropenia (n = 602; 16.7%) and urinary tract infection (n = 149; 4.14%) were the most frequent diagnosis of those visiting the ED ( ). A total of 1308 hospital admissions were registered during that time frame. The most frequent hospitalizations were for those treated with FEC-D (n = 698; 53.36%), followed by those treated with TC (n = 344; 26.3%) and those treated with ACT (n = 266; 20.3%), p < 0.0001. For every 100 breast cancer patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy, 14 hospitalizations would be expected from those treated with FEC-D, 14 from patients treated with ACT, and 9 from the ones treated with TC [RR of 0.61 (95% CI, 0.25–1.48) p = 0.27]. Overall, neutropenia (n = 558; 45%), fever (n = 95; 7.26%) and pneumonia (n = 33; 2.52%) were the most frequent hospitalization diagnosis ( ). 4. Discussion Through a retrospective cohort design, we conducted a population-based real-world study using the administrative data of 10,634 breast cancer patients treated in Ontario, Canada. All patients received chemotherapy after having undergone BC surgery for tumour resection. We compared the treatment efficacy between the TC, ACT and FEC-D chemotherapy regimens. With a median follow-up of 5.5 years, the analysis of the entire population showed a significantly shorter OS in patients treated with ACT compared to those treated with TC [HR of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.63–0.95), p = 0.015]. No substantial differences were seen in OS between those treated with ACT vs. FEC-D. Among patients with ER+ BC, there was a reduced OS in patients treated with ACT or FEC-D, compared to those treated with TC. In the analysis comparing TC vs. ACT or FEC-D treatments, no OS differences were found in the subgroup of patients with LN0, LN 1–3 and LN ≥ 4. In the ER-BC group, no significant survival differences were seen between the TC and any of the anthracycline-based treatments. Although TC was associated with an increased mortality risk in all LN groups, when compared to ACT and FEC-D, a statistically significant reduction in OS was only observed in those treated with TC who had LN 0. The reason for this is not clear. In the ER-BC population, amid the 2379 women and 247 events of deaths registered in that group, there were 1626 (68.3%) patients and 88 (5.4%) deaths in the LN 0 cohort. In the LN 1–3 group, there were 85 (15.6%) deaths among the 542 patients, and in those with LN ≥ 4, there were 74 (37%) deaths among the total of 200 patients. Three patients had missing data in the ER-BC cohort. These findings lead to the assumption that the sample size of the studied population was less likely statistically powered for a time-to-event analysis in the LN 0, and more likely statistically powered in the LN 1–3 and LN ≥ 4 groups. The predicting risk factors associated with the poorest outcomes in ER+ were a histological grade of 3 and LN ≥ 4, and those in the ER− group were tumour size (≥2–5 cm), LN ≥ 4, and underlying CHF and renal disease. Exploring the potential reasons for the finding of an increased risk of death related to anthracycline–taxane treatments, we found that this could be associated with their use in a large majority of patients with high risk features for BC recurrence, including a younger age, LN+, and tumours larger than 2 cm. Among all the treatments compared, the higher mortality associated with ACT could be associated with the group possessing a more unfavorable BC morphology, as 60.2% of patients had a histological grade of 3 and 41.8% had TNBC. In summary, the population selected to receive anthracycline–taxane treatments were mostly at a higher risk for relapse or had a high burden of disease. Regarding CHF diagnosis, our study did not find significant cardiotoxicity events in the comparison between TC and any of the anthracycline–taxane regimens. In our study, a total of 48.6% of patients were treated with FEC-D chemotherapy. Thus, this group had significantly more ED visits (56.22%) and hospitalizations (53.36%), compared to those treated with TC or ACT. However, these absolute numbers do not reflect the real proportion when analyzed by treatment received/event (ED visit or hospital admission). Thus, using this parameter, patients who were treated with ACT had significantly less ED visits, when compared to TC and FEC-D. No substantial relative

Regarding CHF diagnosis, our study did not find significant cardiotoxicity events in the comparison between TC and any of the anthracycline–taxane regimens. In our study, a total of 48.6% of patients were treated with FEC-D chemotherapy. Thus, this group had significantly more ED visits (56.22%) and hospitalizations (53.36%), compared to those treated with TC or ACT. However, these absolute numbers do not reflect the real proportion when analyzed by treatment received/event (ED visit or hospital admission). Thus, using this parameter, patients who were treated with ACT had significantly less ED visits, when compared to TC and FEC-D. No substantial relative risk difference was identified between the last two chemotherapy comparisons. There was no statistically significant increased risk of hospitalization between any of the chemotherapy options. As the main causes for ER visits and hospitalizations were fever/neutropenia, and the specific proportion of patients who were given G-CSF prophylaxis in our study is undetermined, it is hypothesized that the absence of prophylaxis with G-CSF in women receiving FEC-D treatment could, to some extent, justify those high rates. During the timeframe of this study, the G-CSF was covered for the dose-dense ACT regimen. However, only after 2012 did the G-CSF turned out to be publicly funded, at a provincial level, for all chemotherapy regimens that could lead to at least 20% of febrile neutropenia events, and this included the FEC-D regimen. 4.1. Comparison with Other Studies Our study showed similar results that have been demonstrated by the combined analysis of PLANB and SUCCESS C trials, which recruited 5924 patients with HER2-negative BC with pathological intermediate and high-risk factors for recurrence. Regardless of the breast cancer ER status, these studies did not show a 5-year OS benefit for adjuvant anthracycline–taxane over TC chemotherapy, with a HR of 1.00 (95% CI, 0.79–1.25, p = 0.99) [ ]. A recent joint efficacy analysis by the Anthracyclines in Early Breast Cancer (ABC) trials included 4242 women with HER2-negative BC, from the USOR 06-090, NSABP B-46-I/USOR 07132, and NSABP B-49 controlled trials. These study results did not demonstrate any OS difference between TC and anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy, with a HR of 1.05 (95% CI, 0.87–1.26; p = 0.64) at 5-year [ ]. A recently systematic-review and meta-analysis included seven RCTs and 11,803 women with early HER2-negative BC. This study showed a high quality of evidence that there is no OS advantage between TC vs. anthracycline–taxane, with a HR of 1.02 (95% CI, 0.89–1.16, p = 0.83) [ ]. An observational study of women with ER+ HER2-negative breast cancer, with a high-risk score on MammaPrint ® , aimed to predict the anthracycline sensitivity, by analyzing the pathologic complete response (pCR), after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Patients were treated with TC or anthracycline–taxane. In patients classified into the MammaPrint ® High-1 risk category, a similar chemotherapy effectiveness was seen between the two chemotherapy regimens, revealing no difference in pCR rates. Nevertheless, in the group where the risk of recurrences was higher, the High-2 category, anthracycline–taxane was substantially more efficacious than TC (pCR rate 32% vs. 0%, p < 0.001). Through the lens of genomic expression assays (GEAs), it is unknown whether the chemotherapy efficacy outcomes could translate into OS and DFS differences between TC and anthracycline–taxane, in neoadjuvant or adjuvant settings, in patients with high-risk scores on GEAs [ ]. It is imperative to underscore that there have not been any RCTs comparing the effectiveness between TC chemotherapy, delivered in four cycles (TCx4) versus six cycles (TCx6), or the comparison between TCx4 (rather than TCx6) versus anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy. Another retrospective real-world cohort study has examined the comparison between TCx4 and TCx6, finding no disparity in the relapse and mortality rates between the two regimens, and noting fewer treatment toxicities among those treated with TCx4 [ ]. The US Oncology 9735 randomized trial also showed that TCx4 was more effective than the combination of anthracycline and cyclophosphamide (AC), yielding improvements in DFS and OS [ ]. As a result, many oncology guidelines recommend the use of TCx4 for adjuvant BC treatment [ ]. In our study, in the ACT group, we included patients treated with paclitaxel delivered on a dose-dense schedule and paclitaxel administered weekly, since both are comparable treatment strategies [ ]. Regarding cardiotoxicity events, our cohort study showed similar results, compared to a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs. Their study analyzed 9732 women with HER2-negative BC, and they found high-quality evidence to indicate that there is no significant difference in CHF diagnosis between patients treated with adjuvant TC vs. anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy [ ]. Previous reports indicated that 6% of the patients who had been administered with anthracyclines demonstrate clinically evident cardiotoxicity, with as many as 18% developing subclinical congestive heart failure [ ]. Their study analyzed 9732 women with HER2-negative BC, and they found high-quality evidence to indicate that there is no significant difference in CHF diagnosis between patients treated with adjuvant TC vs. anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy [ ]. Previous reports indicated that 6% of the patients who had been administered with anthracyclines demonstrate clinically evident cardiotoxicity, with as many as 18% developing subclinical congestive heart failure [ ]. The factors that increase the risk of developing cardiotoxicity include the cumulative dose of anthracycline, radiation therapy to the left chest, African American ethnicity, diabetes, hypertension, and severe underlying health conditions. The addition of trastuzumab plus/minus pertuzumab in HER2 + BC significantly raises the likelihood of cardiac dysfunction in patients previously exposed to anthracyclines [ , ]. Numerous studies examining anthracycline-induced CHF included cancer patients who received monoclonal antibodies targeting the HER2 domain, potentially leading to an overestimation of anthracycline’s cardiotoxicity risk [ , ]. An observational study of cancer patients treated with chemotherapy in Ontario, Canada, showed that the most frequent ED visits were related to fever or infection [ ]. Two retrospective cohort studies of women with early breast cancer treated with adjuvant chemotherapy, in Canada, evaluated similar endpoints. Pittman et al. showed that the most frequent cause of ED visits were fever without neutropenia (23.3%), pain (12.8%), and febrile neutropenia (9%) [ ]. In the study by Torres et al., the most common ED visit and hospitalization diagnosis were fever and neutropenia, respectively [ ]. Moreover, in the latter study, there was a significant increase in acute care visits and hospital admission in patients who received FEC-D chemotherapy [ ]. 4.2. Strengths and Limitations To our knowledge, there has not yet been a published paper about the BC population in Ontario, Canada, comparing the survival-related endpoints between TC and anthracycline–taxane based chemotherapy in HER2-negative BC treated in adjuvant settings. Through a descriptive and observational cohort study, we conducted a comprehensive real-world evidence-based analysis of women with early HER2-negative BC treatedwith TC versus anthracycline–taxane chemotherapy. We utilized solid and reliable individual-level administrative data of individuals registered in our Health Care System in Ontario, Canada. To achieve this endeavor, we succinctly refined the study population by excluding those with missing data of treatment doses and schedule, patients’ baseline characteristics and BC surgical information. We aimed to maximize the accuracy of chemotherapy efficacy, and we excluded patients who received less than 50% of the planned chemotherapy administration doses and schedule. Thus, these attempts reduced the eligible population. To reduce confounding and selection bias, the final analysis was adjusted by relevant patients’ prognostic and BC characteristics, and we conducted a sensitivity analysis and multiple imputation. Patients with an advanced age are commonly underrepresented in RCTs, with a potentially inaccurate replication of a genuine clinical environment of BC patients due to the clinical trial setting. Our retrospective cohort study had a satisfactory number of patients who were 65 years or older. Our study carried out a reasonably prolonged median follow-up duration of 5.5 years, satisfactory to observe death events to accomplish the study endpoints. The administrative health database utilized for this work is susceptible to limitations. For example, there is a risk of the misclassification of the diagnostic code used to evaluate the cause of ED visits, hospitalizations, and febrile neutropenia diagnosis. Our database is also susceptible to underreporting. For example, women’s menopausal status, compliance with endocrine therapy, and chemotherapy adverse events were not reported. As a result, we could not investigate the usage of endocrine therapy in patients with ER+ BC, or to compare the safety profile between treatments. With regards to the use of propensity score matching (PSM) to balance patients’ baseline characteristics, there were limitations about this method that could be applicable to our study. From our perspective, implementing a PSM might have actually led to an increased imbalance, rather than a reduction, particularly in terms of increasing post-matching covariate imbalance. Therefore, we decided against using PSM. Prior to the era of genomic medicine, the clinician’s decision about which ER+ HER − BC patient would benefit from receiving adjuvant chemotherapy was based on increased risk features from the surgical specimen. GEAs, such as OncotypeDX ® or MammaPrint ® , indicate that, many times, chemotherapy is not advantageous for patients with a high risk of cancer relapse, and overtreatment should be avoided [ , ]. It is important to highlight that, according to the time frame of this study from which patients were treated with chemotherapy, it is likely that most of the ER+ HER2-negative patients did not have GEA, and perhaps not all patients included in this study would have derived a substantial benefit from chemotherapy. It is important to highlight that, according to the time frame of this study from which patients were treated with chemotherapy, it is likely that most of the ER+ HER2-negative patients did not have GEA, and perhaps not all patients included in this study would have derived a substantial benefit from chemotherapy. Moreover, at the time this study was conducted, the advantage of immune checkpoint inhibitors on the treatment of TNBC was unknown. To date, the addition of pembrolizumab to chemotherapy, preoperatively, has shown to be efficacious in improving the rates of pCR, and in reducing BC relapse events, when added to the adjuvant setting [ , ]. 5. Conclusions Our study shows that anthracycline-containing regimens were the most largely prescribed adjuvant chemotherapy option for women with early HER2-negative BC. Among the treatment comparisons, ACT had the lowest OS. These patients were mostly at a higher risk for relapse, as they were predominantly young, and had large and poorly differentiated tumours. Similarly, women who had ER+ BC, and received ACT or FEC-D, had the poorest OS, when compared to TC, likely due to their unfavorable BC features.

chunks.content: In the United States, ~​​​​​​60% of patients diagnosed with breast cancer undergo breast-conserving surgery (BCS) for nonpalpable tumors, necessitating tumor localization. – Wire localization (WL), where a thin metal wire is placed into the tumor immediately before surgery, has been the most common approach for the localization of nonpalpable breast tumors, even though there are several disadvantages to the technique. WL relies on the immediate availability of a radiologist and radiology suite, ideally located within the surgery facility, so that patient transport does not compromise wire placement. WL can also be uncomfortable for the patient since multiple wires may protrude from the breast. Therefore, WL has to be performed as close to the surgery as possible to avoid wire migration as well as minimize patient discomfort. In addition, the surgeon must understand the 3-dimensional wire location for optimal incision placement. Localization of specific lymph nodes in the axilla is difficult with a wire due to the anatomic location. Due in part to these challenges, other technologies have been developed, including intraoperative ultrasound, radioactive intraoperative occult lesion localization, hematoma localization, radar localization, magnetic seed localization such as Magseed, SAVI Scout, and radioactive seed localization (RSL). RSL entails inserting a single standard I-125 titanium seed into a nonpalpable breast lesion using mammographic or sonographic guidance. The patient is exposed to minimal radiation, similar to a 2-view mammogram, ~2 cGy. , A gamma probe is then used to guide excision. Due to its long half-life (59 d), the seed can be placed several days before surgery, improving scheduling flexibility and dissociating the surgeon from the radiologist. Also, the seed is embedded in the breast tissue, like the marking clip, and therefore causes less patient discomfort. Known drawbacks of RSL include seed migration, inability to reposition, and bracketing difficulty. Concerns regarding radioactive contamination have been addressed by traps that buffer the seed from vacuum suction systems. Most studies comparing RSL and WL have been retrospective or nonrandomized in nature. In the United States, only 2 small, single-center, randomized controlled trials have been conducted, which demonstrated comparable rates of positive margins, re-excision rates, and excised tissue volumes for RSL and WL. , Three other randomized controlled trials conducted outside the United States used surgical volume, specimen margins, surgical duration, and need for reoperation to compare the 2 methods. – RSL was deemed an acceptable alternative to WL in all 5 of these randomized controlled trials, particularly due to similar negative margin and re-excision rates. In 2 of the trials, RSL also demonstrated better satisfaction scores, with patients reporting less pain and better convenience and surgeons reporting less difficulty. , As the patient journey during their breast cancer diagnosis and treatment is often distressing, it is important to focus on aspects of care such as patient satisfaction. With health care costs increasing in the United States, especially in cancer care, localization procedure costs should be considered. Four studies have looked at cost, but only one was conducted in the United States. There are mixed data on the cost efficiency between RSL and WL. – However, some data suggest that overall complication and re-excision rates are lower with RSL, which may decrease total cost. Our study is the largest randomized, controlled trial in the United States comparing RSL and WL in patients with breast cancer. The aim of this randomized controlled trial was to compare RSL and WL in patients with nonpalpable, unifocal breast cancer. We focused not only on surgical margins but also on time efficiency, health care costs, complication rates, and patient, surgeon, pathologist, and radiologist satisfaction. METHODS Study Design This study was a single-center, unblinded, randomized, prospective clinical trial conducted between July 2015 and January 2021. The primary objective was to compare negative margin rates following initial resection between patients randomized to RSL or WL for the treatment of breast cancer. Secondary objectives included time from consultation to operation, time in radiology, surgery, and pathology, tissue weight, satisfaction, cost, adverse events, and complications. The institutional review board approved this consent-based study. Enrollment pauses occurred in August 2015 for 5.8 months due to a personnel shortage and in March 2020 for 4.5 months due to COVID-19. Participants were recruited from and received care at 4 hospitals. Eligibility Criteria Female patients aged 29 to 99 years with a biopsy-proven malignant unifocal breast lesion requiring image-guided localization for excision by BCS were eligible. Patients with multifocal, multicentric, locally advanced disease, prior ipsilateral breast cancer, treated with neoadjuvant therapy, and currently pregnant were excluded. Eligible patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive RSL or WL in an unblinded fashion and were stratified by the surgeon and invasive status at clinical staging to reflect differing definitions of negative margins between invasive cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and potential differences between surgeons. The randomization schedule was provided by

hospitals. Eligibility Criteria Female patients aged 29 to 99 years with a biopsy-proven malignant unifocal breast lesion requiring image-guided localization for excision by BCS were eligible. Patients with multifocal, multicentric, locally advanced disease, prior ipsilateral breast cancer, treated with neoadjuvant therapy, and currently pregnant were excluded. Eligible patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive RSL or WL in an unblinded fashion and were stratified by the surgeon and invasive status at clinical staging to reflect differing definitions of negative margins between invasive cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and potential differences between surgeons. The randomization schedule was provided by an independent statistician who was not directly involved in the study before the study opening. Before activation, the randomization schedule was made available directly in the enterprise clinical trial management system. Study participation was discussed during the initial surgical consult. Consent was obtained by the clinical trials team subsequent to this visit. Localization Procedures Wire placement was performed by 17 trained radiologists. For seed placement, one designated radiologist trained in I-125 seed technology trained all other radiologists. Two supervised cases by the designated radiologist were required before independent placement. Surgical Procedure Seven breast surgeons participated in the trial. The surgical technique was similar to the 2 localization techniques. A designated surgeon trained in I-125 seed technology trained all other surgeons. Three supervised cases by the designated surgeon were required before independent surgical use. At our institution, surgical margins are assessed by intraoperative radiography. The specimen radiograph is examined by the surgeon and radiologist to evaluate any margins of concern. Any close margins are taken as an additional margin at the time of the initial operation. End Points The primary end point was negative margin status after initial surgical resection, defined as no ink on the tumor for invasive disease and ≥2 mm from the inked margin for DCIS on pathology. – A close margin (DCIS and papillary carcinoma) was defined as <2 mm from ink on pathology. Secondary end points concerning intervals of time were defined as follows: time from initial consult to operating room for initial surgery (days), time in radiology from start to end of the localization procedure (minutes), operating room time from first incision to closure (minutes) (for patients undergoing sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy, the sum of time for lumpectomy and SLN biopsy), and pathology time as start to end time of specimen dissection (WL, clip identification; RSL, seed removal and clip identification). Patient, radiologist, surgeon, and pathologist/pathology assistant satisfaction was captured using a 5-point Likert-type scale, ranging from extremely negative (mapped to a numerical score of 1) to extremely positive (mapped to a numerical score of 5). Radiologists, surgeons, and pathologists/pathology assistants each completed 1 paper survey within 5 days of the procedure rating aspects of the case (procedure ease, satisfaction, and convenience). Patients completed 2 paper surveys, the first after the localization procedure (assessing pain, anxiety, ease of scheduling, and satisfaction) and the second at their postoperative visit (assessing pain, anxiety, cosmetic outcome, and satisfaction). Some dissections were performed by a pathology assistant, and some by pathologists. Adverse events were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.0; reportable adverse events (grades 1–5) deemed related to the localization and/or surgery that required treatment or intervention were documented, alongside reported complications from the treating clinicians. Adverse event data collection concluded 30 (±5) days after the final surgery. Total charge amounts were collected for each patient’s localization and, if applicable, adverse events requiring treatment. Statistical Analysis As informed by Jakub et al, an 80% negative margin rate was expected in the WL arm. Based on a 2-sided alpha=0.05 level test, 200 randomized subjects per arm (400 total) would provide at least 80% power to declare superiority for the RSL arm, assuming the true negative margin rate in the RSL arm was 90%. All efficacy analyses included all randomized patients and were informed by the intent-to-treat principle—participants were analyzed according to the localization group they were originally assigned, regardless of the localization procedure received. All randomized patients were included in analyses of complications and adverse events, and participants were analyzed according to the localization procedure received. Negative margin rates were calculated, and the corresponding 95% CI was estimated using the Clopper–Pearson method for binomial CIs. Rates were compared between the arms based on a logistic regression model, incorporating the surface area of the excised specimen, the stratification variables of the surgeon, and presence of invasive disease component as covariates. The surgical specimen surface area was calculated as the product of skin-to-deep, medial-to-lateral, and cranial-to-caudal measurements. Time intervals, tissue weights, and surface areas were analyzed quantitatively using analysis of variance techniques. Satisfaction scores were analyzed as ordered categorical responses; cumulative logit models, including stratification variables, were estimated. All analyses of radiology

The surgical specimen surface area was calculated as the product of skin-to-deep, medial-to-lateral, and cranial-to-caudal measurements. Time intervals, tissue weights, and surface areas were analyzed quantitatively using analysis of variance techniques. Satisfaction scores were analyzed as ordered categorical responses; cumulative logit models, including stratification variables, were estimated. All analyses of radiology outcomes included covariates for invasive status and radiologist. All secondary analyses of surgery outcomes included covariates for invasive status and surgeon, while all analyses of pathology outcomes included covariates for invasive status, surgeon, and pathologist. Incident rates for adverse events and complications were evaluated using Fisher exact test. A learning period for RSL was defined as the surgeon’s first 6 surgeries. All surgeons completed their learning periods after the first enrollment pause. One surgeon who performed only 4 RSL procedures was excluded from the learning curve analysis. Data were compared between the periods using generalized linear models with adjustments for surgeon and histology (and specimen surface area for negative margin rates). Cost Analysis An institution’s total costs are proprietary and reimbursement is dependent on insurance stakeholder; thus, standard health economics reporting methods were used to “transform cost” by applying year-specific and institution-specific cost-to-charge ratios to the total charge amount. Costs were reported from the perspective of the hospital system and inflated from year of service to 2020 US dollars using the Medical Component of Consumer Price Index. Cost analyses utilized a decision analytic model of estimated transformed costs associated with RSL or WL. The model was stratified by type of localization, SLN biopsy, subsequent re-excision, and adverse events. Exclusions included patients who had additional procedures unrelated to localization, missing billing data, a mastectomy after BCS, off study before subsequent re-excision, and surgery performed in 2021. Hypothetical scenario analysis was used to test the robustness of the cost data, which included assumed equal proportions regardless of having an SLN biopsy, subsequent re-excision, or an adverse event. RESULTS Patient Characteristics Overall, 400 patients were randomized to receive RSL (N=200) or WL (N=200) for malignant breast disease (Fig. ). Most women identified as White [333 of 400 (83%)] and non-Hispanic/Latino [376 of 400 (94%)], with a median age of 62 years [interquartile range (IQR), 54–68 y)] (Table ). Seventy-eight percent of patients (312 of 400) had cT1 disease, 85% (338 of 400) had an invasive disease component at presentation, 89% (356 of 400) were estrogen receptor positive, and 75% (300 of 400) were HER2 nonamplified. Imbalances in patient or disease characteristics between the arms were not detected. Eleven patients were taken off study before localization due to being found ineligible per protocol after screening (N=6), being withdrawn per investigator discretion (N=2), or withdrawing consent (N=3) (Fig. ). The remaining 389 patients (97%) underwent localization before BCS and completed protocol-defined procedures. One hundred percent of patients (200 of 200) randomized to WL received the WL intervention. Ninety-four percent of patients (188 of 200) randomized to RSL received the RSL intervention. One patient randomized to RSL received WL. Localization Outcomes Overall, 17 radiologists performed 389 localizations. The median number of localizations per radiologist was 14 (IQR, 3–43). Median time in radiology for all subjects was 11 minutes (IQR, 7–15 min). Mean time in radiology was not significantly different between arms (RSL 12.8 ± 9.5 min vs WL 11.4 ± 6.0 min) ( P =0.18). Radiologists completed surveys for 387 of 389 (>99%) cases. The 2 incomplete surveys (1 RSL case and 1 WL case) were not distributed. For radiologists, there were no detectable differences in ease ( P =0.31) or satisfaction ( P =0.50) between the arms in multivariable analysis (Fig. ); however, radiologists rated RSL more favorably for convenience (OR 3.32; 95% CI: 1.65–6.69; P <0.01) as compared with WL. At the time of localization, 387 of 389 (>99%) patients completed surveys. The 2 incomplete surveys (1 RSL case and 1 WL case) were not distributed. Patients in the RSL arm were more likely to report less pain (OR 2.50; 95% CI: 1.69–3.71; P <0.01), less anxiety (OR 2.62; 95% CI: 1.79–3.84; P <0.01), and greater overall satisfaction with the localization procedure (OR 3.24; 95% CI: 1.70–6.22; P <0.01) as compared with patients in the WL arm. Surgical Outcomes Negative margins were obtained in 80% (95% CI: 75%–86%) of patients randomized to RSL and 85% (95% CI: 80%–89%) of patients randomized to WL after the first resection (Table ). There was no significant difference in these negative margin rates ( P =0.29) between the RSL and WL arms, independent of the operating surgeon, presence

Surgical Outcomes Negative margins were obtained in 80% (95% CI: 75%–86%) of patients randomized to RSL and 85% (95% CI: 80%–89%) of patients randomized to WL after the first resection (Table ). There was no significant difference in these negative margin rates ( P =0.29) between the RSL and WL arms, independent of the operating surgeon, presence of invasive disease, and specimen surface area. Considering the study was designed to evaluate the differences between the arms, this indicates that the result for the primary objective was negative—the evidence did not suggest that RSL was superior to WL in achieving negative margins after initial surgical resection. Further multivariable analysis comparing RSL to WL showed the 95% CI for the difference (RSL – WL) between the arms’ negative margin rates was −0.12 to 0.02 and included zero. Negative margin rates by disease histology (invasive, DCIS, papillary carcinoma) were also similar between arms (Table ). No I-125 seeds were lost. The median time from the initial consult to the operating room for surgery was 26 days (IQR, 17–33) for RSL and 27 days (IQR, 17.5–34) for WL ( P =0.62). Median specimen surface area was 100.3 cm 3 (IQR, 66.7–138.9 cm 3 ) for RSL, and 102.1 cm 3 (IQR, 67.9–142.7 cm 3 ) for WL, with no significant difference between the arms (P =0.58). The median time in surgery for all patients was 89 minutes (IQR, 67–109 min). RSL was associated with increased surgical time in 78% of patients (302 of 389) who required an SLN biopsy (RSL median time, 102 min [IQR, 84.5–119 min] vs WL median time, 93 min [IQR, 74–109 min]; P =0.002). There was no difference in operating room time for patients undergoing BCS without an SLN biopsy [RSL median time, 58 min (IQR, 53–72 min) vs WL median time, 54.5 min (IQR, 47-67 min); P =0.19]. Surgeons completed surveys for 381 of 389 (98%) cases. The 8 incomplete surveys (4 RSL cases and 4 WL cases) were either not distributed or not completed by the surgeons. The RSL procedure was more likely to receive greater overall satisfaction ratings from the surgeons as compared with the WL procedure (OR 1.67; 95% CI: 1.09–2.58; P =0.02) (Fig. ). Patients completed 386 of 389 (>99%) postoperative surveys. The 3 incomplete surveys (1 RSL case and 2 WL cases) were inadvertently missed at the postoperative visits. Patients who underwent the RSL procedure were less likely to report anxiety as compared with patients who underwent WL (OR 1.45; 95% CI: 1.01–2.06; P =0.04). Surgical Outcomes by Study Period Excised specimen surface areas and negative margin rates were calculated during and after the RSL learning period (first 6 cases per surgeon). The median specimen surface area was 102.9 cm 3 (IQR, 84.6–125.0 cm 3 ) during the learning period and 96.6 cm 3 (IQR, 61.5–138.9 cm 3 ) after the learning period. Negative margin rates were 0.86 and 0.78 during and after the learning period, respectively. Independent of operating surgeon and histology, surface area of the excised specimens ( P =0.29) and negative margin rates (P =0.70) did not differ based on the study period. Pathology Outcomes RSL was associated with increased dissection time [RSL median time, 30 min (IQR, 25–34 min) vs. WL median time, 28 min (IQR, 24–33 min); P =0.047] (Table ) in multivariable analysis. There was no detectable difference in specimen weights between the arms [RSL median weight, 46.5 g (IQR, 33–65 g) vs WL median weight, 44 g (IQR, 30–61 g); P =0.11]. Pathologists completed surveys for 379 of 389 (97%) cases; surveys were inadvertently missed in 3 RSL cases and 7 WL cases. There was no significant difference in pathologist-reported ease for RSL as compared with WL ( P =0.23) (Fig. ). Adverse Events and Complications Sixty-five subjects (17%) experienced 92 adverse events (Table ). The frequency of patients with adverse events was similar between the localization procedures [RSL 17.6% (33 of 188) vs WL 15.9% (32 of 201); P =0.69]. The most common adverse events were procedural complications and infections, which were numerically similar between the arms [seromas requiring treatment, RSL n=19 vs WL n=13 ( P =0.20); breast infection, RSL n=6 vs WL n=2 ( P =0.16); wound infection, RSL n=2 vs WL n=5 ( P =0.45)]. One patient (0.3%) experienced a serious adverse event attributed to surgery, which was a grade 3 infection of the axilla following RSL and BCS. The patient was treated, and the infection was resolved. Complications were reported by radiologists in 13 of 387 patients (3.4%) with

WL 15.9% (32 of 201); P =0.69]. The most common adverse events were procedural complications and infections, which were numerically similar between the arms [seromas requiring treatment, RSL n=19 vs WL n=13 ( P =0.20); breast infection, RSL n=6 vs WL n=2 ( P =0.16); wound infection, RSL n=2 vs WL n=5 ( P =0.45)]. One patient (0.3%) experienced a serious adverse event attributed to surgery, which was a grade 3 infection of the axilla following RSL and BCS. The patient was treated, and the infection was resolved. Complications were reported by radiologists in 13 of 387 patients (3.4%) with completed surveys. Localization complication rates were similar between the arms [RSL 4.3% (8 of 187) vs WL 2.5% (5 of 200); P =0.40] (Table ). Complications attributed to the wire included the need for an additional wire and placement difficulty. Five patients received an additional wire, and no patient received an additional seed. One patient randomized to RSL required a wire, which was difficult to place. Complications specific to RSL included issues with seed deployment and migration. Complications were reported by surgeons in 14 of 381 patient cases (3.7%) with completed surveys. Surgery complication rates were similar between the arms [RSL 3.8% (7 of 184) vs WL 3.6% (7 of 197); P >0.99] (Table ). The most commonly reported surgery complication (n=5) was the utilization of an additional wire [RSL 1.6% (3 of 184) vs WL 1.0% (2 of 197)]. Seed [RSL 1.6% (3 of 184)] and wire migration [WL 1.0% (2 of 197)] were also reported by surgeons. Cost Results For base case analysis, which incorporated adverse events, the estimated cost of RSL was $18,500, whereas the estimated cost for WL was $17,900, a $600 difference in cost with RSL incurring a higher cost (Table ). This difference decreased to $400 when adjusted for equal probability of sentinel lymph node biopsy, re-excision, and adverse events. DISCUSSION While several randomized controlled trials in the United States have compared breast preoperative localization, , , , our study is the largest conducted to date within a high-volume center that focused on the most commonly used technologies, the wire and radioactive seed. Our study also focused on patient and physician satisfaction as well as overall cost, which has not been evaluated previously. We determined that RSL is an acceptable alternative to WL for obtaining similar negative margins. There was no difference in operating room time between the localization techniques when limiting surgery time to lumpectomy alone, and no difference in surface area of excised specimens. Furthermore, there was no significant difference in the number of adverse effects or complications. Our results are similar to those by Lovrics et al and Langhans and colleagues, which demonstrated that RSL has similar rates of positive margins, re-excision rates, and volume of tissue excised as compared with WL. , Importantly, both patient and surgeon satisfaction were higher with RSL. There was no difference in pathologist or radiologist satisfaction by localization technique; however, radiologists noted that RSL was more convenient. This was likely due, in part, because patients reported decreased pain and anxiety with the RSL procedure. A procedure is likely more convenient to a radiologist when the scheduling is more flexible, and the patient is more comfortable. Prioritizing the patient experience and exploring avenues for improvement are important during this very distressing time in a patient’s life. We found a $600 cost difference between localization techniques, with the seed being more expensive. The extra cost for RSL was due to slight increases in localization, surgery, and dissection times. The higher cost for RSL would likely be acceptable given that it is associated with decreased pain and anxiety for the patient, high surgeon satisfaction scores, and may improve operating room utilization. The cost difference decreased to $400 when switching from the base case to an equal probability scenario of sentinel lymph node biopsy, re-excision, and adverse events. Two studies conducted in Canada and the Netherlands found that RSL was more expensive than WL (98 CAD and €217, respectively), , while another study at an institution that utilized a bundled payment system found that total health care costs were on average $115 lower with RSL compared with WL. Given that costs are proprietary, it is difficult to report on specific cost findings. Therefore, our cost analyses served as estimates to determine whether a large cost difference might deter the use of either technology, which was not found to be true. Given a clear preference for the RSL technology by patients and providers, we should continue to advocate for affordable new localization technologies. Furthermore, there may be other unseen cost savings, such as decoupling the seed localization procedure from the date of operation, which may ease scheduling and improve utilization of the operating room.
