This approach has demonstrated significant anticancer efficacy against multidrug-resistant human ovarian cancer cells. BsEVs enhance drug sensitivity by inhibiting adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, utilizing nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), and inducing mitochondrial dysfunction. This disruption impairs the function of efflux pumps that typically contribute to drug resistance. In vivo studies have shown that treatment with BsEVs significantly inhibits the growth of OVCAR-8/MDR and OVCAR-8 tumors. Furthermore, evidence suggests that OVCAR-8/MDR tumors are more responsive to BsEV treatment compared to OVCAR-8 tumors. These findings highlight the promising potential of BsEVs in cancer therapy, particularly in overcoming multidrug resistance in ovarian cancer cells [ ] ( ). 6.2 Exosomes improve delivery targeting Researchers have explored the therapeutic potential of DDP loaded exosomes derived from M1 macrophages obtained from umbilical cord blood, particularly in the context of ovarian cancer and platinum resistance. Monocytes from umbilical cord blood can be differentiated into M1 or M2 macrophages through cytokine stimulation, and these macrophages can release exosomes encapsulating cisplatin. The use of M1-derived exosomes containing cisplatin (M1exoCIS) has been shown to significantly enhance the cytotoxic effects of the drug, restoring the sensitivity of ovarian cancer cells to cisplatin compared to traditional cisplatin formulations. The increased targeting and binding efficacy of M1exoCIS in ovarian cancer cells are largely due to its interaction with overexpressed integrin receptors. Exosomes from M1 macrophages contain lncH19, which leads to increased PTEN protein expression and heightened apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells upon treatment with M1exoCIS. Additionally, M1exoCIS suppresses the expression of miR-130a and Pgp genes in ovarian cancer cells, effectively overcoming cisplatin resistance [ ]. To enhance the targeted delivery of exosomes to specific tissues or organs, exosome surface proteins can be modified, allowing for precise delivery to targeted lesions and enhancing therapeutic effects. In an in vivo xenograft model, researchers demonstrated that administering Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD)-modified exosomes loaded with miR-484 facilitated vascular normalization, thereby increasing the susceptibility of cancer cells to chemotherapy-induced apoptosis. Mechanistically, miR-484 suppressed the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) and its receptors in endothelial cells. The targeted delivery of miR-484 via RGD-modified exosomes not only normalized vasculature but also enhanced the tumor’s sensitivity to chemotherapy [ ]. Further research has examined the use of exosomes loaded with the Chuanxiong-derived alkaloid monomer, tetramethylpyrazine (TMP), known for its anti-tumor properties, including inhibition of tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and drug resistance. Exosomes carrying TMP (EXO-TMP) have shown promising anti-ovarian cancer effects, especially when combined with PTX. EXO-TMP was effective in overcoming cellular drug resistance by suppressing the expression of multidrug resistance protein 1 (MDR1), multidrug resistance-associated protein 1 (MRP1), and glutathione S-transferase Pi 1 (GSTP1). Moreover, EXO-TMP demonstrated specific targeting capabilities toward A2780T cells, effectively mitigating their drug resistance. These findings suggest that EXO-TMP could be a promising drug delivery strategy for reversing drug resistance in ovarian cancer [ ]. 6.3 Enhancing drug delivery with exosomes Triptolide, a bioactive compound derived from the Chinese herbal remedy Tripterygium wilfordii , exhibits potent anti-tumor, immunomodulatory, and anti-inflammatory properties. However, its clinical use is limited by significant adverse effects. To address these limitations, researchers have developed exosome-encapsulated formulations of triptolide (TP-Exos). This innovative delivery system has demonstrated a marked improvement in the anti-cancer efficacy of triptolide against ovarian cancer while reducing its toxicity to vital organs compared to the unencapsulated drug. According to Guo et al. [ ], TP-Exos induced apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells, modulated tumor immunity by activating the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway, and selectively suppressed M2-type tumor-associated macrophages and their pro-tumor factors in the tumor microenvironment. These findings suggest that TP-Exos could be a promising therapeutic option for ovarian cancer. The efficacy of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) as a genome-editing tool depends on efficient intracellular delivery systems. Recent studies have demonstrated that tumor cell-derived exosomes can effectively transport CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids to cancer tissues. Specifically, these exosomes exhibit superior delivery capabilities in vivo compared to those derived from epithelial cells, as they selectively accumulate in ovarian cancer tumors in SKOV3 xenograft mice, likely due to their cell-specific tropism. Exosomes carrying CRISPR/Cas9 have been shown to suppress poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) expression, inducing apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inhibition of PARP-1 enhances the sensitivity

The efficacy of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) as a genome-editing tool depends on efficient intracellular delivery systems. Recent studies have demonstrated that tumor cell-derived exosomes can effectively transport CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids to cancer tissues. Specifically, these exosomes exhibit superior delivery capabilities in vivo compared to those derived from epithelial cells, as they selectively accumulate in ovarian cancer tumors in SKOV3 xenograft mice, likely due to their cell-specific tropism. Exosomes carrying CRISPR/Cas9 have been shown to suppress poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) expression, inducing apoptosis in ovarian cancer cells. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inhibition of PARP-1 enhances the sensitivity of these cells to cisplatin, leading to a synergistic cytotoxic effect [ ] ( ). N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulators play crucial roles in the fate of m6A-modified transcripts, cancer progression, and drug resistance. Gene therapy using siRNA shows potential for correcting aberrant expression of m6A regulators, though challenges with specificity and systemic toxicity necessitate the use of targeted delivery vectors. Researchers have developed a dual-purpose nanomedicine platform combining regulation of m6A-related epigenetics with chemotherapy for ovarian cancer treatment. This system involves encapsulating siRNAs targeting YT521-B homology (YTH) N6-methyladenosine RNA-binding protein 1 (YTHDF1) and the chemotherapy docetaxel (DTX) within small extracellular vesicles derived from mesenchymal stem cells. This approach effectively targets tumors, depleting YTHDF1 and suppressing eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 subunit C (EIF3C) translation in an m6A-dependent manner. The synergistic interaction between YTHDF1 targeting and epigenetic regulation significantly enhances the antitumor efficacy of DTX, suppressing ovarian cancer progression without notable systemic toxicity [ ]. Biomimetic hybrid nanoparticles, termed miR497/triptolide-loaded hybrid exosome-lipose nanoparticles (TP-HENPs), have been developed to co-deliver miR497 and triptolide. In vitro studies show that these nanoparticles are efficiently taken up by tumor cells, resulting in increased apoptosis. Moreover, they effectively accumulate at the tumor site and exhibit strong anti-cancer efficacy in vivo without adverse effects. Mechanistically, these nanoparticles facilitate the dephosphorylation of the hyperactivated PI3K/AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway, enhance the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and promote the shift of macrophages from the M2 to M1 phenotype. The co-delivery of TP and miR497 using exosome-liposome hybrid nanoparticles has proven especially effective in overcoming chemoresistance in ovarian cancer, presenting a promising strategy for cancer therapy [ ] ( ). 7 Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) detection of ovarian cancer exosomes EVs, including exosomes, hold significant potential in cancer therapy due to their unique molecular characteristics [ ]. However, the heterogeneity and complexity of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) pose substantial challenges for accurate molecular profiling. Traditional methods such as Western blotting, ELISA, and flow cytometry, while useful, often fall short in terms of sensitivity, specificity, multiplexing capability, and the need for large sample volumes. Over the past few decades, various technologies have been developed to enhance the accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity of sEV detection, including chemiluminescence, electrochemistry, and notably, SERS. SERS has emerged as a highly sensitive and rapid method for analyzing multiple proteins on the surface of sEVs. Compared to other sEV detection technologies, SERS offers advantages such as low noise [ , ], resistance to photobleaching, robustness, and high sensitivity. As an optical technique, SERS enhances Raman scattering signals when molecules are in close proximity to metal nanoparticles. Since its discovery in the 1970s, SERS has been applied across various fields, including drug development and food quality control, and has shown particular promise in the detection of sEVs for cancer diagnosis. In sEV analysis, SERS-based immunoassays commonly utilize a “sandwich” format. In this setup, sEVs are captured using probes like antibody-coupled magnetic beads, and detection is achieved using SERS nanotags, which consist of Raman-active molecules encapsulated with metal nanoparticles. The resulting “sandwich” immunocomplex provides a platform for detecting sEVs [ ]. There are three main strategies for assembling these immunocomplexes: labeling sEVs with SERS nanotags followed by enrichment with capture probes, simultaneous incubation of all components, or enrichment with capture probes prior to labeling with SERS nanotags. However, comprehensive studies comparing the efficacy of these different assembly strategies in SERS detection of sEVs are lacking. Such studies are essential for developing standardized protocols for using SERS in sEV detection. The membrane of sEVs typically contains common biomarkers such as CD9, CD63, and CD81, which are part of the tetraspanin family. These biomarkers are frequently used to capture sEVs and form the “sandwich” immunocomplex for detection. However, tetraspanins are not uniformly distributed on the surface of sEVs, and their expression levels may vary across different types of cancer-derived sEVs. Most studies have relied on anti-CD63 antibodies to capture sEVs from various cancer types, potentially missing a significant portion of sEVs due to the variable expression of this protein. Identifying a more abundant tetraspanin protein specific to ovarian cancer-derived sEVs (OVC-derived sEVs) could significantly improve the capture efficiency and sensitivity of the assay. This advancement would enhance the

of the tetraspanin family. These biomarkers are frequently used to capture sEVs and form the “sandwich” immunocomplex for detection. However, tetraspanins are not uniformly distributed on the surface of sEVs, and their expression levels may vary across different types of cancer-derived sEVs. Most studies have relied on anti-CD63 antibodies to capture sEVs from various cancer types, potentially missing a significant portion of sEVs due to the variable expression of this protein. Identifying a more abundant tetraspanin protein specific to ovarian cancer-derived sEVs (OVC-derived sEVs) could significantly improve the capture efficiency and sensitivity of the assay. This advancement would enhance the overall accuracy of sEV-based diagnostics and facilitate the detection of ovarian cancer [ , ]. Recent research has focused on identifying specific surface proteins to classify and characterize sEV phenotypes, particularly for detecting ovarian cancer. Surface markers such as cancer antigen 125 (CA125), EpCAM, and CD24 have been selected from various cell lines for this purpose [ ]. A notable approach involves using gold nanopore arrays to capture ovarian cancer-derived EVs, which are then characterized using SERS. This method, combined with principal component analysis (PCA), allows for the identification of distinct component differences among the EVs. A logistic regression-based machine learning model was subsequently applied, achieving approximately 99% accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in classifying the EVs [ ]. This method is not only quick and easy but also non-invasive, making it a highly practical diagnostic tool. In another study, a simple platform utilizing plasma brackets embedded with microscale biological silicate substrates and silver nanoparticles was developed for SERS analysis of EVs from ovarian and endometrial carcinomas. The sensitivity of detecting these cancers was found to decrease significantly after enzymatic digestion of the EVs, highlighting the critical role of intact EVs in diagnostic accuracy. This platform underscores the importance of using SERS as a tool for evaluating the heterogeneity of EVs from clinical samples in a cost-effective, rapid, and label-free manner [ ]. Further advancements in SERS technology, combined with mass spectrometry (MS), have been used to analyze EVs isolated from plasma samples of healthy donors (HD), umbilical cord blood, and patients with early-stage high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC). Plasma EVs were purified using size exclusion chromatography and subsequently analyzed with SERS, MS, and atomic force microscopy. After identifying the fraction with the highest EV purity, the study characterized EVs from HDs, donors with non-cancerous gynecological conditions, and early-stage HGSC patients. These advanced analytical techniques allow for detailed profiling and comparison of EVs, providing valuable insights into the molecular composition and potential biomarkers associated with different stages of ovarian cancer. This comprehensive approach using SERS and complementary techniques demonstrates the potential for developing highly sensitive and specific diagnostic tools for ovarian cancer. The integration of SERS with machine learning and other analytical technologies offers a powerful means to enhance the accuracy of cancer diagnostics, particularly in the context of EV characterization [ ]. 8 Challenges and prospects Exosomes have shown significant potential in tumor biology, particularly as carriers of tumor-specific antigens and nucleic acids. These features enable exosomes to serve as valuable diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for noninvasive cancer assessment. Moreover, exosomes can help identify individuals at risk of metastatic disease, and manipulating their production may present novel therapeutic targets. The use of exosomes as vehicles for delivering cellular information offers a promising approach for targeted cancer therapy, with functional exosome mimetics potentially enhancing drug efficacy [ ]. However, while various synthetic drug delivery systems have been developed, their clinical application has often been limited by challenges such as inefficiency, cytotoxicity, and immunogenicity [ ]. The negative charge on the surface of exosomes contributes to their stability in the bloodstream and facilitates the efficient delivery of biomolecules to target cells, making them effective drug carriers [ ]. Despite the growing interest in exosome research, several unresolved questions remain. Most exosome-based treatments are still in the experimental phase and lack extensive clinical trials. One major challenge is the isolation of exosomes, which involves addressing issues related to standardization of isolation methods, exosome heterogeneity, potential toxicity of therapeutic exosomes, and detailed investigation into their molecular components [ ]. The complexity of exosome heterogeneity stems from factors such as size, molecular diversity, and varying cellular origins [ ]. In ovarian cancer patients, circulating exosomes are a mixture of vesicles released from different regions of the female reproductive system. To effectively tackle these complexities, a unified approach to exosome analysis, encompassing both isolation and characterization, has been suggested. Techniques like microfluidic devices, magnetic bead-based methodologies, and aptamer-based separation can be employed for precise exosome isolation [ , , , ]. For the molecular analysis of exosomal cargo, a range of advanced techniques are available. These include nanopore-based detection of individual molecular signals, CRISPR-based sensors for analyzing surface proteins specific to cancer, and plasma sensors for categorizing

origins [ ]. In ovarian cancer patients, circulating exosomes are a mixture of vesicles released from different regions of the female reproductive system. To effectively tackle these complexities, a unified approach to exosome analysis, encompassing both isolation and characterization, has been suggested. Techniques like microfluidic devices, magnetic bead-based methodologies, and aptamer-based separation can be employed for precise exosome isolation [ , , , ]. For the molecular analysis of exosomal cargo, a range of advanced techniques are available. These include nanopore-based detection of individual molecular signals, CRISPR-based sensors for analyzing surface proteins specific to cancer, and plasma sensors for categorizing distinct exosome subsets. Additionally, electrochemical sensors can provide valuable insights. The integration of multi-omics approaches—genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics—coupled with machine learning, enables the identification of specific cancer biomarkers at the final stage of individual exosome analysis. Such comprehensive analysis is critical for advancing precision and personalized medicine in cancer treatment. A crucial aspect of exosome research involves the toxicological evaluation of exosomes, as the secretion patterns and molecular cargo of exosomes can influence the behavior of recipient cells, particularly when exposed to various substances, including drugs and chemicals [ ]. Recent studies have highlighted the non-toxic nature of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived exosomes. However, it is also important to explore the therapeutic potential of exosomes from other sources, such as plant-derived exosomes and dendritic cell-derived exosomes. Comprehensive toxicological analyses of these alternative exosome sources are necessary to fully understand their implications and safety profiles. Further research in this area will help clarify the potential risks and benefits, paving the way for the safe and effective use of exosomes in clinical applications [ , ]. Emerging evidence underscores the pivotal role of exosomes in mediating communication between cancer cells and the immune system. Targeting tumor-derived exosomes offers a promising avenue for reducing immunosuppression and enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapy [ ]. However, before exosomes can be utilized in clinical immunotherapy for ovarian cancer, it is essential to thoroughly evaluate their potential side effects to optimize their therapeutic effectiveness. Overcoming these challenges could usher in a new era of exosome-based cancer vaccines, while exosome research continues to advance the realization of precision medicine. The reproducibility, reliability, and sensitivity of SERS-based biosensing technology depend on the rational design of SERS substrates, proper handling of biological samples, precise control of detection conditions, and thorough analysis of spectral data. Efforts should be made to control potential influencing factors in the future. SERS substrates with high uniformity, strong enhancement effects, and clean surfaces should be fabricated and appropriately modified. Choosing suitable Raman probe molecules can also enhance biocompatibility and avoid non-specific adsorption during testing. Additionally, biological samples should be stored and pretreated as closely as possible to normal physiological conditions to prevent irreversible changes. Selecting appropriate SERS detection conditions is vital for obtaining reliable detection information. Moreover, it is essential to establish a standardized biomolecule SERS database for accurate spectral information identification. If necessary, calibration of the probe responses in the detection system should be performed, or suitable data processing and statistical analysis methods should be employed. The future of early detection of tumor biomarkers lies in the development of ultra-sensitive, highly specific, high-throughput, and universal detection platforms to meet the needs of life sciences and clinical diagnosis. While the application of SERS technology has made significant strides, numerous challenges remain in accelerating the translation of SERS technology. Collaborative approaches involving nanotechnology, materials science, plasmonics, and optics will continuously enhance exosome research. Modifying the surface molecules of exosomes to achieve cell and tissue targeting specificity represents a potent strategy for precise delivery of therapeutic agents. By loading proteins, small molecules, or functional genetic material into exosomes, it is possible to direct therapeutic effects specifically to diseased areas or target cells. Exosomes have the potential to function as nanocapsules for the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, particularly in tackling drug-resistant tumors. However, thorough investigation, validation, and standardized clinical trials are crucial to confirm the safety and efficacy of exosome-based therapies before their widespread clinical use. While exosomes offer numerous advantages as drug carriers, such as biocompatibility and ability to bypass certain drug resistance mechanisms, they also face challenges including limited drug-loading capacity, production and purification difficulties, and vulnerability to degradation during storage and transportation. Successfully incorporating nucleic acid drugs into exosomes, identifying suitable host cells for their production, and ensuring stable ligand-receptor interactions for targeted delivery remain critical hurdles for clinical applications. Optimizing the combination of producer and target cells is essential for efficient therapeutic exosome production. This field, characterized by its potential for innovation, continues to evolve rapidly. With ongoing research and technological advancements, new strategies are likely to emerge, enhancing the use of exosomes in cancer diagnosis and treatment, thus significantly impacting patient care. 9 Conclusions The significant role of exosomes in tumor drug resistance and

With ongoing research and technological advancements, new strategies are likely to emerge, enhancing the use of exosomes in cancer diagnosis and treatment, thus significantly impacting patient care. 9 Conclusions The significant role of exosomes in tumor drug resistance and their potential as efficient carriers are increasingly recognized. By harnessing the unique properties and intercellular communication capabilities of exosomes, researchers have gained critical insights into the complex mechanisms underlying cancer progression, metastasis, and drug resistance. Although challenges persist regarding exosome heterogeneity, isolation techniques, potential toxicity, and comprehensive molecular analysis, ongoing advancements in knowledge and technology are steadily overcoming these obstacles. Current research is exploring the utility of exosomes as a valuable tool in combating ovarian cancer, particularly in enhancing drug delivery systems, overcoming drug resistance, and ultimately improving survival outcomes. This exploration is anticipated to lead to significant advancements in precision and personalized medicine for ovarian cancer treatment. Additionally, the application of SERS technology in studying exosomes presents a promising approach for understanding drug resistance in ovarian cancer. As this field evolves, it is poised to revolutionize diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, ushering in a new era of tailored cancer care. chunks.content: Introduction Palliative care programs improve quality of life [ ], and guidelines recommend integration of palliative care upon diagnosis of advanced cancer [ ]. Yet, palliative care remains significantly underutilized among historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups [ – ]. Black, Hispanic/Latino, Asian, and Indigenous patients receive significantly fewer palliative care consultations than non-Hispanic White patients [ – ]. Furthermore, these individuals are more likely to receive aggressive end-of-life care, experience less participatory decision-making and receive poorer communication about prognosis, advance care planning, and goals of care [ , – ]. Despite these well-documented disparities, historically marginalized communities are often underrepresented in palliative care research. Most palliative care studies utilize samples that significantly over-represent non-Hispanic White participants [ ]. The reasons for this are multifactorial; barriers to research participation among marginalized racial and ethnic groups include mistrust, lack of information, limited opportunities, competing demands, fear of unintended outcomes, stigma, and issues related to health insurance coverage and legal status [ , ]. More inclusive research is necessary in order to effectively address disparities and achieve equity in palliative care [ ]. Although there has been increasing attention on improving diversity in health research broadly, most research in this area has been on identifying and addressing inequities in biomedical clinical trials [ , ], rather than focusing on palliative care studies [ ]. Examining inclusive research strategies is particularly important in palliative care research, since openness to palliative care is influenced by culture and thus requires increased cultural sensitivity and community engagement [ – ]. The goals of the present study were twofold. First, we sought to establish the feasibility and acceptability of study procedures for assessing symptoms and shared decision-making (SDM) among Black patients with advanced lung cancer. Second, we elicited participants’ suggestions for improving these study procedures specifically, and for ensuring inclusivity of research procedures in general. To achieve these goals, we leveraged a study of SDM about palliative care among Black patients with advanced lung cancer [ ], a population that experiences significant disparities in palliative care [ – ]. The parent study aimed to assess the impact of patient-reported and observed SDM on symptom burden, satisfaction with care, and palliative care receipt. Thus, this study provided an ideal opportunity to assess Black patients’ perspectives on procedures that are commonly applied in palliative care research. We hypothesized that the study procedures would be feasible and acceptable, and that qualitative interviews would identify opportunities for improvement. Methods Participants & Procedures This mixed-methods study used a convergent parallel design [ , ]. Upon completion of data collection, qualitative and quantitative data were integrated using a merging approach [ ]. Study procedures were reviewed and approved by the Georgetown-MedStar Joint Oncology Institutional Review Board (Protocol #00004381). Guided by principles of community-based participatory research (CBPR) [ ], a community advisory board (CAB) composed of patient advocates with advanced lung cancer gave input on the study design, procedures, and materials. CAB members were paid an annual stipend of $500, reviewed study materials, then discussed their feedback in virtual meetings. Key changes based on CAB feedback included: (1) clarifying and highlighting the study’s overall purpose; (2) adjusting wording to increase cultural sensitivity; (3) improving accessibility/usability; and (4) sharing aggregate study results with participants. Participants were recruited from thoracic oncology clinics in three cancer centers between August 2022 and January 2023. Eligibility criteria included: age ≥18; diagnosed with advanced (stage III-IV or extensive) lung cancer; Black or African-American; English-speaking; and scheduled for a routine follow-up oncology appointment. We excluded patients with severe cognitive impairment or who were receiving hospice care. Previous experience with palliative care was not an inclusion or exclusion criterion; we included both individuals who had previously seen a palliative care provider and those who were naïve to palliative care. After providing written informed consent, participants completed a baseline assessment (T0; approximately 15 minutes). Participants then attended a routine oncology outpatient appointment, and were given the option of audio-recording it. Regardless of their audio-recording decision, participants completed follow-up assessments within one week after the appointment (T1; approximately 5 minutes) and one month after T1 (T2; approximately 5 minutes). Assessments were completed on paper, by telephone with a research team member, or online, as preferred by the participant. The measures included in each assessment are detailed in . Upon completing the follow-up assessments, participants completed an optional qualitative, semi-structured exit interview (see ) in-person (in a private room in the thoracic oncology clinic or in the infusion suite), by telephone, or via a web-based video platform. Interviews ( M =34 minutes, range: 15-77 minutes), were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Participants were compensated up to $60 for completing study activities. Interviews ( M =34 minutes, range: 15-77 minutes), were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Participants were compensated up to $60 for completing study activities. Measures Demographic and clinical characteristics. Participants self-reported their age, gender identity, education, annual household income, and insurance status. Participants’ clinical characteristics (cancer type/stage, time since diagnosis, treatment regimen, ECOG performance status [ ]) were extracted from the electronic medical record (EMR). Feasibility of study procedures. We tracked rates of patient eligibility, enrollment, and retention over the course of the study. A priori , we defined a minimum criterion for feasibility of ≥70% enrollment of eligible patients and ≥70% retention through T2. Acceptability of study procedures. The 4-item Treatment Acceptability and Preferences Questionnaire (TAPQ) assessed acceptability of study procedures [ ]. Participants rated each item on a 4-point Likert scale (1=“not at all” to 4=“very much”). Item scores were averaged to create scale scores ranging from 1-4 (higher=more acceptable). A priori , we defined TAPQ scores ≥3 as indicating adequate acceptability, with ≥70% of participants meeting this threshold indicating study procedure acceptability. Acceptability was assessed at T0, T1, and T2 in order to examine acceptability of study procedures over time. Quantitative Data Analysis Analyses were conducted with IBM SPSS (v29). We calculated frequencies to determine feasibility and acceptability of study procedures, and determined whether they met ≥70% benchmarks as described above. Qualitative Data Analysis We utilized an inductive qualitative data analysis approach, including open coding, axial coding, and selective coding [ – ]. Members of the study team (CCC, AA, OMB, JS, AK, HDV) reviewed a randomly selected subset of transcripts and collaboratively developed a detailed codebook consisting of data-driven codes from the raw data [ ]. Next, all transcripts were independently coded in Dedoose by two of three raters (AA, OMB, JS). Coding disagreements were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. Final Integration of Qualitative and Quantitative Data Following data analysis, study team members (CCC, HDV) integrated data through joint displays to evaluate congruence between the quantitative and qualitative findings Results Feasibility We approached 69 patients; of them, 40 (58%) completed the eligibility screener ( ). Five (12%) of the 40 screened individuals were not eligible. Thus, 35 patients met eligibility criteria and 30 of these eligible patients (86%) consented to participate, exceeding our a priori threshold for feasibility (≥70% enrollment of eligible patients). Demographic and clinical characteristics for enrolled patients are provided in . Of the 30 enrolled patients, 22 (73%) agreed to the appointment audio-recording, 20 (67%) completed the appointment audio-recording, 29 (97%) completed the T1 survey, and 27 (90%) completed the T2 survey. This exceeded our a priori threshold for feasibility of ≥70% retention through T2. Acceptability There was little change over time in average acceptability scores ( ). Across time points, participants rated the study procedures as acceptable (TAPQ ≥3) in 88% of observations. This exceeded our a priori threshold for acceptability (≥70%). Qualitative Themes Qualitative analysis identified three main categories of themes: participants’ motivation for participating, their overall experiences in the study, and recommendations for future research. provides exemplar participant quotes for each theme. Motivation for Participation Theme 1. Participants primarily decided to enroll in the study out of a desire to help others. Participants felt that by participating in this study they could improve care and/or communication for “the next person” (Participant #12) or “somebody else just coming behind me” (Participant #1). This altruistic motivation was summarized by one participant who said: “[Upon hearing about the study] I was inquisitive, thinking, ‘How could this benefit me?’ But then I thought, ‘If it doesnť benefit me, maybe the participation may benefit someone else.’ ” (Participant #6) Participants conceptualized the potential benefits to others very broadly, often extending beyond their immediate communities. For example, one participant stated, “I really hope that my input with the participation of this survey is beneficial to society in some way” (Participant #6). Theme 2. Participants appreciated the study’s focus on the Black community. A research study that specifically focused on the experiences and needs of Black individuals was a novel concept for many; as one participant stated, “I really didn’t know that they studied African Americans and cancer” (Participant #22). Participants were interested in identifying and addressing possible racial disparities in healthcare: “What piqued my interest is how does [cancer] affect minorities as opposed to other people. So, I want to know, is there any type of disparity between the two and if we’re getting the same amount of quality care as any other

Participants appreciated the study’s focus on the Black community. A research study that specifically focused on the experiences and needs of Black individuals was a novel concept for many; as one participant stated, “I really didn’t know that they studied African Americans and cancer” (Participant #22). Participants were interested in identifying and addressing possible racial disparities in healthcare: “What piqued my interest is how does [cancer] affect minorities as opposed to other people. So, I want to know, is there any type of disparity between the two and if we’re getting the same amount of quality care as any other race. Yeah. Just making sure there’s no disparity between the two, treatment wise and the offering of medication or just the overall quality of care.” (Participant #19) Participants particularly appreciated the focus on Black patients’ symptom experiences, given the difficulty that some members of the Black community experience in openly discussing their symptoms. One participant mentioned: “We’re so used to not going to the doctor because there’s nothing really wrong and that’s fine. I would do my check-ups and stuff. But we’re so used to, ‘Oh we’ll be okay. Just put a Band-Aid on it.’ Not knowing the Band-Aid is only masking what the real problem is.” (Participant #10) Theme 3. Participants wanted to learn more about themselves, lung cancer, and/or research. Some participants felt that participating in the study was a way to learn more about their condition. Others were interested in the research process itself, and were driven to participate by their desire for personal growth and education. Experiences in the Study Theme 4. Most participants were comfortable with the study procedures. Participants described the surveys as “very easy” (Participant #11) and “user-friendly” (Participant #19). Feeling that questions were tied to the study purpose facilitated survey completion. One participant stated, “I thought that all of the questions was related to my understanding of what this project is about” (Participant #4). While most participants were comfortable with the study procedures, some expressed apprehension about the appointment audio-recording, primarily due to confidentiality concerns. One participant reflected that their comfort level with audio-recording changed over the course of the study. When initially consenting to the study they “just didn’t feel comfortable enough” with audio-recording, but during the exit interview said “at this point, I feel different about it” (Participant #25). This may suggest that participants’ comfort with study procedures changes as they gain familiarity with the study and study team. Theme 5. Participants found the study informative. This was particularly the case for recently diagnosed participants, who reflected that they were “going through something that [they’ve] never experienced before” (Participant #10) or that they “don’t know anything about” (Participant #11). In addition, participants often found the study experience to be a learning opportunity. Several participants noted that they had never been invited to participate in a research study before, and did not know other people who had participated in research. As one participant said: “The survey has opened my eyes to what can happen and how everything has progressed in the medical field by doing surveys now. They never did surveys before, I donť think, because some people in my family had cancer and I never heard of them doing surveys. So I think this is great.” (Participant #3) Theme 6. Participation empowered or reminded patients to ask questions of their oncology clinicians. Answering the survey questions caused participants to reflect on their experiences and identified topics to raise with their care teams. As one participant stated: “When I’m in the room, it makes me sit there and think of things I need to bring up. Before I didn’t think about it at all. I just come, I get my treatment and I leave. Now I’m thinking, ‘Did I ask this? What do I wanna know?’ ” (Participant #24) Theme 7. Participants appreciated study team members’ efforts to build rapport. Participants described the research staff as “personable” (Participant #30), “courteous” (Participant #4), and “caring” (Participant #14), which made it easier to engage with the study procedures. As a result of these positive experiences, participants generally indicated that they would be interested in participating in other similar studies in the future. Theme 8. Supportive friends and family members helped participants to engage in study activities. Some participants felt that they would not have been able to participate in the study without assistance from friends or family members, either because they felt overwhelmed by their cancer diagnosis or because they needed input to answer the survey questions. Thus, engaging support people in the research process was a significant facilitator for study participation. Recommendations for Future Research Theme 9. Shorter surveys would increase engagement. 8. Supportive friends and family members helped participants to engage in study activities. Some participants felt that they would not have been able to participate in the study without assistance from friends or family members, either because they felt overwhelmed by their cancer diagnosis or because they needed input to answer the survey questions. Thus, engaging support people in the research process was a significant facilitator for study participation. Recommendations for Future Research Theme 9. Shorter surveys would increase engagement. One participant warned that lengthy surveys might cause the research team to “lose [their] audience” (Participant #10). Shorter surveys would be particularly important for participants who were older, experiencing significant physical symptoms, or with less formal education. Participants also reflected that some of the questions felt redundant: “It’s almost like you talk to a child, and you ask them one way. They don’t answer, so you ask them a different way. It’s like, ‘Wait a minute.’ So maybe some of those type of questions can come off, and something else can go on.” (Participant #10) In summary, participants expressed a preference for shorter surveys with questions that did not feel repetitive and were clearly and directly related to the study purpose. Theme 10. Participants discussed potential alternative timelines for the study, both compressed and lengthened. Participants’ feedback on the study timeline was mixed. Some felt that the one-month follow-up did not sufficiently capture their experience, and that a longer follow-up period would be preferable. On the other hand, some participants felt that the study timeline was prolonged, and they would have preferred to do all of the study activities at a single time point. This was particularly true for patients who had experienced major life stressors during their study participation. As one participant shared, “I’ve been through a lot since the last time I’ve seen y’all. I’ve been hospitalized, I lost my mother. It’s a lot of things that’s goin’ on in my life” (Participant #25). Theme 11. A private environment is crucial for candid survey responses. In an effort to reduce participant burden, the research team frequently completed study assessments before, during, or after routine clinical encounters. Some participants appreciated “that it was done right there in the hospital” (Participant #27). However, others would have preferred to complete these assessments at home. In the clinic setting, some participants expressed hesitation to share their honest opinions: “you might not want to say certain things in an open environment like this” (Participant #13). Theme 12. Incorporate educational components into observational research protocols. Although participants understood the observational nature of the study, they also noted that “just answering questions” felt “impersonal” (Participant #30). To overcome this, some participants suggested incorporating educational components at the end of the study. They felt that informational pamphlets or videos would help to keep participants engaged and provide them with some potential benefits to participation. Integration of Quantitative and Qualitative Findings depicts each study construct with columns to compare and contrast the results from the surveys and interviews. Recommendations for future research based on these findings are also provided. Discussion Black patients with advanced cancer are frequently under-represented in palliative care research [ ] and there is limited data on their experiences in palliative studies. In this mixed-methods study, we determined feasibility, acceptability, and opportunities for improving study procedures for assessing symptoms and SDM among Black patients with advanced lung cancer. Quantitative data indicated that the study methods were feasible and acceptable. Qualitative themes provided insight into participants’ motivation for enrolling, experiences in the study, and recommendations for future research. Overall, results inform inclusive research practices for future studies of Black patients with advanced lung cancer. Our focus on the experiences of Black patients with advanced lung cancer allowed for an in-depth description of a group typically under-represented in palliative care research. Results address a gap in the literature, which often documents disparities but rarely examines Black patients’ study experiences or what influences their research participation. Our findings also build knowledge of inclusive palliative care research practices. Although guidance and resources exist for enhancing recruitment and enrollment of those from under-represented groups in clinical therapeutic trials [ , ], we are not aware of similar guidance for accrual to non-therapeutic studies of palliative care and clinical communication. As these studies’ methods differ from treatment-focused clinical trials, tailored best practices are needed and may be informed by the experiences described herein. In contrast to some prior studies, our enrollment rate for eligible individuals was high (86%). Although Black patients enroll in clinical trials at similar rates to White patients when offered to participate [ ], some studies have noted challenges enrolling Black participants. For example, in a remote symptom monitoring study, Black patients declined participating more than 3-times as often as White patients, even when approached at similar

accrual to non-therapeutic studies of palliative care and clinical communication. As these studies’ methods differ from treatment-focused clinical trials, tailored best practices are needed and may be informed by the experiences described herein. In contrast to some prior studies, our enrollment rate for eligible individuals was high (86%). Although Black patients enroll in clinical trials at similar rates to White patients when offered to participate [ ], some studies have noted challenges enrolling Black participants. For example, in a remote symptom monitoring study, Black patients declined participating more than 3-times as often as White patients, even when approached at similar rates [ ]. Similarly, Black patients with breast cancer are under-represented in clinical trials of symptom management [ ]. It must be acknowledged that there are many valid reasons for Black patients to decline research participation, such as research procedures that fail to consider cultural factors that are unique to the Black community, higher burden of participation due to systemic inequalities, and lack of trust in scientific communities due to historical injustices [ ]. Patient-centered approaches, like the ones engaged in this study and suggested by participants, may help to overcome these barriers to research participation for Black patients. Participant retention in our study was also high (90%), which aligns with prior literature suggesting that challenges with enrollment do not always translate to challenges with retention. In a recent cancer symptom monitoring trial, rates of adherence to the study procedures and withdrawal were similar for Black and White participants [ ]. In a scoping review, trial retention rates were typically above 70% for Black participants [ ], suggesting that, once enrolled, Black patients with cancer often remain engaged in the study procedures (although there are exceptions) [ ]. There are multiple explanations for why our study did not face similar challenges enrolling Black patients as some prior studies. Participant interviews revealed that our study’s focus on the Black community increased participants’ interest in enrolling in the study. In addition, community advisory board members provided input on the study documents and procedures, ensuring that the materials were appropriate and engaging for Black patients. Finally, appointment audio-recording was optional, allowing us to include participants who did not wish to be audio-recorded (27%). Taken together, these findings suggest actionable recommendations to enhance inclusion of Black patients with advanced cancer in palliative care research. Participant interviews highlighted the importance of shortening surveys, engaging caregivers in the research process, and ensuring data collection occurs in private locations. Consistent with prior research [ ], participants especially appreciated the research staff members’ efforts to build rapport, clearly explain the study procedures, and confirm ongoing consent. Rapport building may be particularly important when research staff are not from the same racial or ethnic background as the participants [ ], as was the case in this study. Furthermore, participants expressed a desire to learn, found participation to be informative, and recommended inclusion of educational materials in future studies. Accordingly, embedding educational opportunities for participants in observational studies may enhance enrollment and the participant experience. While our study has several notable strengths, there are also limitations. This study used convenience sampling. Because we did not collect data from non-participants, we do not know how our enrolled participants differ from the broader population of patients. For self-report surveys and interviews, it is possible that demand characteristics could influence participants’ ratings of the study. To reduce this concern, we reminded participants that their responses were not shared with their care team, and we examined several objective markers of feasibility (such as enrollment rate). Finally, few participants in this study had prior experience with palliative care, which may have affected their interest in or willingness to participate in the study. For these reasons, additional studies are needed to generate conclusive recommendations for enhancing accrual of Black patients with advanced cancer into palliative care research. Conclusion In this mixed-methods study, common research practices in palliative and communication studies were feasible and acceptable for most Black participants with advanced lung cancer. Findings on participants’ motivation for enrollment, experiences in the study, and recommendations for future research can be used to inform inclusive practices among research teams engaging in studies of palliative care and communication. Ultimately, developing and engaging in inclusive practices is expected to be a key step toward addressing disparities in symptom burden and palliative care receipt among Black patients with advanced cancer. chunks.content: Introduction Cancer is one of the leading causes of death worldwide with the World Health Organization reporting 9.6 million deaths and 18.1 million new cases in 2018. , Cancer-cachexia (CC) is a wasting syndrome that occurs in up to 80% of cancer patients. , CC is the primary cause of death for 22%–30% of cancer patients, , with incidence predicted to grow in years to come. Despite CC's widespread implications, it is often poorly diagnosed and often missed completely. Typically, there is an examination of weight loss, body mass index (BMI), and skeletal muscle, and clinically requires greater than 5% loss of body weight over a 6-month period, BMI less than 20 kg/m 2 , and low muscle mass (sarcopenia) to be diagnosed. , However, CC is often irreversible once weight loss begins to occur; therefore, using weight loss as diagnostic criteria is therapeutically inadequate and outlines the need to identify a pre-cachectic signature both for diagnostic and treatment purposes. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to examine the development of CC from bench to bedside in multiple organ systems. To begin we will describe demographics in cancer patients and degenerative mechanisms in the skeletal muscle during CC. Additionally, we will address molecular alterations in other organs in CC. Notably, as much of the existing evidence in CC is from pre-clinical models the bulk of our discussion on mechanisms of CC comes from pre-clinical models and needs further validation in clinical studies. Cancer cachexia patient demographics and clinical progression As previously stated, CC can affect as much as 80% of cancer patients depending on the type of cancer. , However, CC outcomes following cancer diagnosis and treatment are influenced by factors such as age, body composition, biological sex, type of cancer and activity level. , , Herein, we will examine CC occurrence as a function of age, biological sex and type of cancer. CC is of particular importance in the elderly demographic, since sarcopenia, age-related loss of muscle mass and function, commonly occurs alongside CC. In fact, among patients in a specialized geriatric oncology clinic, up to 65% presented with CC. Despite the prevalence of CC in aged populations, older subjects continue to be poorly represented in pre-clinical models of CC and randomized phase II and III CC clinical trials. , , Understanding the development of CC in the aged population is crucial for developing effective therapies as especially when considering other common comorbidities in this population CC onset and progression may differ in young patients when compared to aged patients. In addition, biological sex has been recently reported as an important factor in terms of cancer incidence and mortality. Although both male and female subjects exhibit CC, the development of CC may differ between sexes. A recent study shows cancer incidence is 20% higher in males between sexes and the male-to-female incidence ratio was distinctly different in many primary malignant tumor developments such as liver, bladder, oral cavity, esophageal, and thyroid cancer in the US. Moreover, the mortality rate in malignant cancers is nearly 30% higher in males compared to females in various age groups. , Moreover, cancer-induced cachexia generally occurs in 40%–50% of female patients and 40%–60% of male patients over 60 years of age , and overall prevalence of severe muscle loss criteria among cancer patients was much higher in males (61%) than females (31%). These distinct underlying differences between sexes in cancer incidence and mortality are complicated to delineate, but this phenomenon can be attributed by both external (lifestyle, alcohol consumption, smoking, and delayed diagnosis) and internal factors (hormone levels, and biological sex-based molecular changes). , We will discuss more detailed biological sex-based molecular changes in the skeletal muscle later in this review. All cancers can present with cachexia and common cancers such as those of the pancreas, lung, and liver are responsible for approximately half of all cancer-related deaths worldwide. Cancers that are more commonly associated with cachexia are often diagnosed at an advanced stage and have direct effects on digestion. Furthermore, tumor characteristics such as tumor proliferation rates and inflammatory profiles contribute to CC. , Baseline assessments of pre-cachexia (early stage of CC without marked weight loss; i.e., ≤5%) or mass loss history are critical for predicting CC trajectory at later stages of cancer progression. To predict if CC will occur in patients, there is a need for a defined pre-cachectic signature, which would allow for the development and implementation of preventative treatments to decrease the severity of CC or even prevent CC. Recently, many clinical studies have taken place to identify characteristics of CC across several different types of cancers in humans. Surprisingly, results of clinical studies often show different outcomes than pre-clinical animal models. To predict if CC will occur in patients, there is a need for a defined pre-cachectic signature, which would allow for the development and implementation of preventative treatments to decrease the severity of CC or even prevent CC. Recently, many clinical studies have taken place to identify characteristics of CC across several different types of cancers in humans. Surprisingly, results of clinical studies often show different outcomes than pre-clinical animal models. For example, in pre-clinical animal models there is consistent data showing that muscle proteolysis is occurring with CC; however, the results from clinical studies are much more variable. Our group recently reviewed common pre-clinical models of CC, notably current efforts are ongoing to develop pre-clinical models of CC to more accurately recapitulate human CC. One excellent example of these efforts is the recent development of the KPP mouse model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA). Notably, the KPP mouse exhibits similar gene ontology to human patients and a more protracted time course of development than common allografted tumor models. One source of variation could be that in pre-clinical animal models’ experimental conditions such as tumor size are tightly controlled for, while in clinical studies the progression of cancer is often not controlled for. More data from clinical models is needed in order to fully understand the development of CC in humans. For example, mitochondrial dysfunction is a common finding in pre-clinical animal models that is understudied in clinical models. Dolly et al. recently published a more in-depth review of recent clinical studies. Below are some common findings detailing the progression of CC in pre-clinical animal models. Considering the varying impacts of CC across age groups, biological sex, types of cancer and others, there is a strong need to identify novel biomarkers associated with the progression of CC that could be useful for diagnostic purposes prior to marked weight loss. In fact, identification of biomarkers is among a series of identified priorities in cancer cachexia and critical initiatives in this effort have been recently established. Recent studies have identified different types of potential bloodborne biomarkers in various cancer models. For instance, Talbert and coworkers found elevated circulating levels of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) in cachectic pancreatic cancer patients which was absent in their weight stable counterparts, providing a potential biomarker for CC. A similar finding has been reported that higher plasma C18-ceramide to C24-ceramide (C18:C24) levels were found in cachectic pancreatic cancer patients compared to non-cachectic patients. In addition, bloodborne biomarkers to identify pre-cachexia could include inflammatory cytokines, microRNA's, and lipolysis markers. Specifically, interleukin (IL)-6 is elevated in blood in pre-clinical models of CC. Downstream of IL-6, signaling transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) 3 signaling is linked to phenotypes of cancer-cachexia including skeletal muscle wasting, cardiac dysfunction and hypothalamic inflammation. , , , Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK/ERK) is another downstream target of IL-6 that contributes to increased mitochondrial fission factors in tumor-bearing mice. , Intriguingly, the induction of cancer-cachexia is IL-6 independent in female mice. Furthermore, our recent data show plasma-derived proteins such as Serum Amyloid A1 (SAA1) content was exclusively higher in mice with LLC-induced cachexia even when compared to models of disuse-induced muscle atrophy. However, it should be noted that biomarkers may differ depending on the type of cancer. More recently, clinical trials have been conducted to identify novel biomarkers for CC in humans. Some common biomarkers observed in clinical trials include c-reactive protein, albumin, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), free fatty acids, IL-6, and IL-10 28 . One issue with looking at biomarkers in humans is that the biomarkers are screened for in all stages of cancer, which makes it difficult to identify a potential biomarker for early detection of CC. Hence, studies using pre-clinical models that are looking for these bloodborne biomarkers during different stages and types of cancer are needed to identify novel biomarkers that can be utilized to effectively diagnose and prevent it. Role of chemotherapy and radiation therapy in cancer cachexia development Common classes of chemotherapeutics such as taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel or taxol) or vinka alkaloids (e.g., vinblastine) are used to treat multiple cancers including breast cancer, lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, and gastrointestinal cancer. , Chemo- or radiation therapy reduces the physical fitness of cancer patients, which has negative impacts on CC outcomes. Early muscle loss during chemotherapy is associated with poor treatment response and reduced survival. Pre-clinical models and clinical studies show that chemotherapies such as taxanes or vinka alkaloids induce severe muscle weakness, impaired neuronal activities, and mitochondrial dysfunctions. , , , While some data suggest common mechanisms may exist between cancer-induced and chemotherapy-induced cachexia, unfortunately to date few pre-clinical studies have attempted to investigate the combinatory effects of cancer and cancer treatment on cachexia outcomes.
