Transcriptomic profiling identifies FoxO1 as a potential key effector mediating the synergistic response to linperlisib and chiglitazar To uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying the synergistic effects of linperlisib and chiglitazar, we performed transcriptomic profiling of FL cells treated with the combination regimen. Volcano plot analysis revealed a broad spectrum of differentially expressed genes, including substantial upregulation and downregulation events (Fig. ). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis identified multiple key pathways, notably those related to cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, and the FoxO signaling pathway (Fig. ). GSEA further confirmed significant enrichment of FoxO1-associated transcriptional programs (NES = 1.39812, p = 0.00244; Fig. ). Within the PI3K signaling network, genes including CDKN1A , CDKN1B , FoxO1 , FoxO3 , and FoxO4 were prominently altered (Fig. ). Western blotting analysis showed that combination treatment downregulated upstream PI3K/AKT components (p110δ, pan-AKT, and phosphorylated AKT) and upregulated PPARα and FoxO1, whereas FoxO3 and FoxO4 levels changed only modestly (Fig. ), suggesting selective activation of FoxO1 in response to PI3K/PPARα modulation. Subcellular fractionation assays revealed a pronounced nuclear accumulation of FoxO1 protein upon combination treatment (Fig. ), with densitometric analysis confirming a significant increase in its nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (Fig. ). Accordingly, qPCR showed strong induction of FoxO1 mRNA, exceeding that of FoxO3 or FoxO4 (Fig. ). Immunofluorescence imaging corroborated both increased FoxO1 expression and its enhanced nuclear localization following combination group (Fig. ). Collectively, these data suggest that FoxO1 acts as a key transcriptional effector downstream of PI3K/PPARα signaling, mediating the enhanced apoptotic and anti-proliferative responses elicited by linperlisib and chiglitazar co-treatment. Metabolomic analysis reveals that chiglitazar activates FoxO1 through metabolic reprogramming and glycolysis inhibition Untargeted metabolomic profiling was performed in RL FL cells to characterize the effects of chiglitazar on FoxO1 activity. Volcano plot analysis revealed extensive metabolic remodeling, with a large number of significantly altered metabolites observed compared to that in the control (Fig. ). KEGG enrichment analysis of these differential metabolites highlighted the FoxO signaling pathway, carbon metabolism, and central carbon metabolism in cancer as among the most affected pathways (Fig. ). An integrated KEGG analysis of combined metabolomic and transcriptomic datasets further identified the FoxO signaling pathway as a top-enriched node (Fig. ), suggesting a direct link between metabolic rewiring and transcriptional regulation. Functionally, chiglitazar significantly suppressed glycolytic flux, as evidenced by reduced glucose uptake (Fig. ), lactate production (Fig. ), and intracellular pyruvate leves (Fig. ). Consistent with these metabolic changes, western blotting demonstrated decreased expression of key glycolytic regulators, including HIF1α, Glut1, and PGK1, along with reduced AKT phosphorylation. Notably, phosphorylation of FoxO1 at T24 and S256 was also suppressed, suggesting enhanced nuclear localization and transcriptional activity (Fig. ). In addition to these post-translational changes, FoxO1 mRNA was upregulated by chiglitazar (Fig. ). To determine whether this transcriptional activation was directly mediated by PPARα. we performed dual-luciferase reporter assays, which confirmed that PPARα activation robustly enhanced FoxO1 promoter activity (Fig. ). Bioinformatic analysis predicted a PPARα response element (PPRE) at –402/–378 bp within the promoter (Fig. ). Mutation of this motif abolished chiglitazar-induced promoter activation in the luciferase assay (Fig. ), confirming its functional importance. ChIP-qPCR further demonstrated increased PPARα binding to the FoxO1 promoter upon chiglitazar treatment (Fig. ). Together, these results indicate that chiglitazar activates FoxO1 transcriptionally via direct PPARα promoter engagement and post-translationally via glycolysis inhibition, thus contributing to its synergistic therapeutic effects with linperlisib. Linperlisib and chiglitazar synergistically suppress tumor growth and activate FoxO1 signaling in an FL PDX model We established a PDX model of FL to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of linperlisib combined with chiglitazar in a clinically relevant setting. Compared with the control and monotherapy groups, the combination group exhibited markedly reduced tumor volumes and weights, as confirmed by tumor resection images and measurements (Fig. ). Tumor growth curves further demonstrated that the combination treatment yielded the most significant inhibition of tumor progression (Fig. ). Mice in the linperlisib group showed mild body weight loss; however, this effect was not exacerbated by combination treatment (Fig. ). Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a significant reduction in tumor cell proliferation in the combination group, as shown by Ki67 staining and quantification (Fig. ). Furthermore, p-AKT expression was the lowest in the combination group, indicating more effective inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling (Fig. ). In contrast, FoxO1 nuclear localization was the highest in the combination group, suggesting that PI3K inhibition and metabolic reprogramming synergistically restore FoxO1 activity in vivo (Fig. ). Taken together, these results establish the AKT–FoxO1 signaling pathway as a critical downstream target of the combination treatment in FL. Discussion This study establishes that combined targeting of PI3Kδ and PPARα with linperlisib and chiglitazar produces synergistic antitumor activity in FL. We identify the reactivation of the transcription factor FoxO1 as the central integrator through which this combination concurrently suppresses oncogenic PI3K/AKT signaling and reprograms tumor metabolim, thereby overcoming the adaptive resistance that frequently limits PI3Kδ inhibitor monotherapy. Although PI3Kδ inhibition has demonstrated clinical activity in relapsed/refractory FL, treatment responses are often incomplete and curtailed by adaptive resistance [ – ]. Our work expands this understanding by revealing a previously unrecognized regulatory axis in which PPARα‑driven metabolic modulation reactivates FoxO1 tumor‑suppressive function through both transcriptional and post‑translational mechanisms. This highlights the mechanistic novelty and therapeutic potential of targeting metabolic-signaling convergence in lymphoid malignancies. Specifically, our results demonstrate that chiglitazar markedly suppresses glycolysis, as evidenced by decreased glucose uptake and reductions in lactate and pyruvate production. These metabolic alterations are consistent with previous research indicating chiglitazar’s role in modulating glucose and lipid metabolism through PPAR activation [ – ]. Importantly, these changes were accompanied by increased nuclear localization and transcriptional activity of FoxO1, driven by PPARα-mediated upregulation and AKT-dependent phosphorylation attenuation [ ]. To delineate the transcriptional mechanism more precisely, we identified a predicted PPARα response element (PPRE) at −402/–378 bp within the FoxO1 promoter, confirmed direct PPARα binding via ChIP‑qPCR, and demonstrated that mutating this element abolishes chiglitazar‑induced promoter activation (Fig. ). These findings establish a direct PPARα–FoxO1 transcriptional regulatory axis, demonstrating that chiglitazar activates FoxO1 not only through metabolic rewiring but also through direct promoter engagement [ ]. Functional validation using FoxO1 knockdown confirmed FoxO1’s central role in mediating the effects of the combination therapy. Knockdown of FoxO1 significantly reduced drug-induced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest while restoring cell proliferation. Concurrently, the expression levels of key downstream targets, including Bim, Bax, p21, and p27, were markedly decreased. These results not only confirm the mechanistic indispensability of FoxO1 in driving the therapeutic response but also corroborate its established role as a tumor suppressor in B-cell malignancies, consistent with previous findings [ – ]. Our in vivo results align closely with the in vitro findings, demonstrating significant tumor growth inhibition by the combination therapy in both CDX and PDX FL models. The use of both models strengthens the translational relevance of our findings. In PDX tumors, immunohistochemistry demonstrated a marked increase in FoxO1 expression in the combination group (Fig. ), which accompanied the most pronounced reductions in tumor burden and Ki67 proliferation. Our in vivo results align closely with the in vitro findings, demonstrating significant tumor growth inhibition by the combination therapy in both CDX and PDX FL models. The use of both models strengthens the translational relevance of our findings. In PDX tumors, immunohistochemistry demonstrated a marked increase in FoxO1 expression in the combination group (Fig. ), which accompanied the most pronounced reductions in tumor burden and Ki67 proliferation. Although nuclear localization was not directly assessed in vivo, the strong correlation between FoxO1 upregulation and treatment response supports its potential value as a pharmacodynamic biomarker [ ]. These data not only substantiate FoxO1 activation as a mechanistic endpoint but also suggest its potential as a pharmacodynamic biomarker to monitor treatment response in vivo. Notably, the combination therapy did not cause additional adverse effects in comparison with linperlisib monotherapy, such as weight loss, consistent with clinical reports of linperlisib’s tolerability. These findings further support the clinical potential of the combination therapy. The rationale for selecting linperlisib and chiglitazar was based on their distinct yet complementary mechanisms of action. Linperlisib was chosen for its high PI3Kδ selectivity and improved safety relative to earlier PI3K inhibitors such as idelalisib, whereas chiglitazar was selected for its ability to remodel tumor metabolism at clinically relevant concentrations [ , , ]. Together, these agents form a multilayered therapeutic strategy that simultaneously targets oncogenic signaling and metabolic reprogramming. Chiglitazar, a pan-PPAR agonist, has demonstrated anti-tumor effects in multiple contexts; however, its efficacy in FL is limited when used alone [ ]. Our dose selection was guided by prior pharmacologic studies in hematologic models, and we hypothesized that metabolic modulation through PPAR activation could synergize with PI3Kδ inhibition to overcome adaptive resistance. Additionally, linperlisib was selected for its favorable pharmacodynamic properties and clinical safety profile, including its selectivity for PI3Kδ and reduced off-target toxicities compared to earlier agents such as idelalisib. Regarding clinical application, we envision this combination therapy as a promising strategy for relapsed or refractory FL, particularly in patients who exhibit resistance to PI3K monotherapy. Given its favorable tolerability and dual mechanistic action, this regimen could also be explored as a frontline option in biomarker‑defined subgroups, such as FoxO1‑low or glycolysis‑high FL. Incorporating FoxO1 expression into future clinical trial designs may facilitate patient stratification and enhance therapeutic precision [ ]. Despite these promising findings, several limitations exist. First, the number of patient-derived models used is limited; thus, we might not have fully captured the biological heterogeneity observed among FL patients. Expanding the number and diversity of patient-derived models in future studies will be crucial for enhancing the generalizability of these findings. In addition, this study did not explore the long-term safety or potential resistance mechanisms in detail; these aspects should be explored in subsequent research. Furthermore, the comprehensive effects of this combination therapy on the tumor microenvironment and immune system warrant systematic evaluation in future experiments. These limitations notwithstanding, our study lays a solid foundation for the preclinical rationale and clinical translation of this therapeutic approach. This study’s findings have significant implications for cancer research and clinical practice. Given our identification of FoxO1 as a critical mediator linking metabolism and transcriptional regulation, we propose a novel combinational therapeutic strategy using linperlisib and chiglitazar and provide both theoretical and practical insights into overcoming resistance mechanisms in FL treatment. This combination treatment approach could potentially enhance therapeutic outcomes in FL patients and provide a valuable framework for addressing treatment challenges in other B-cell lymphomas. documents.title: Mantle cell lymphoma ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline

chunks.content: Introduction Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is a rare and aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that is characterized by the chromosomal t(11;14) translocation, which leads to an overexpression of cyclin D1. Although MCL typically demonstrates high response rates to induction chemotherapy, it is associated with a significant risk for relapse. Historically, MCL has been considered an incurable disease with poor long-term outcomes and a median overall survival (OS) of 4 to 5 years. , Elderly patients (commonly defined as ≥65 years) or those who are considered unfit typically receive rituximab (R) in combination with chemotherapy regimens such as bendamustine or CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone). , In contrast, fit patients, generally younger than 65 years, are treated with R-CHOP combined with a high-dose cytarabine-containing regimen, with or without the addition of cisplatinum, followed by autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT). , , In clinical trials, R maintenance (RM) after first-line treatment with R-CHOP and a high-dose cytarabine-containing regimen, but not FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab), has demonstrated the potential to prolong survival. , In retrospective cohort studies, RM improved survival after R-bendamustine (BR); however, the analyses of patients who were treated with R-CHOP were limited by small sample sizes. , , , Among patients who were treated with intensive therapy, retrospective studies have indicated that RM after ASCT was associated with improved progression-free survival (PFS) and OS. , In the randomized study by Le Gouille et al , RM after ASCT improved the 4-year OS by 9% when compared with observation only (89% vs 80%; P = .04). At the 7-year follow-up, the PFS benefit remained significant, although the OS difference was no longer statistically significant (83% vs 72%; P = .09). More recently, studies have investigated the addition of ibrutinib to standard chemoimmunotherapy and demonstrated an improvement in PFS but not in OS to date. , Whether the benefit of RM observed in the clinical trials, typically conducted in selected patient populations that meet strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, also applies to the real-world MCL population is largely unknown. This study aimed to characterize the clinical features, treatment modalities, and outcome of patients with MCL in a population-based setting in the Netherlands with a specific focus on the impact of RM over time in different treatment groups. Material and methods The Netherlands Cancer Registry Data were obtained from the nationwide, population-based the Netherlands Cancer Registry (NCR). The population-based NCR is maintained and hosted by the Netherlands Comprehensive Cancer Organization and has, since 1989, nationwide coverage of at least 95% of all malignancies. All newly diagnosed malignancies are reported to the NCR via the Nationwide Network of Histopathology and Cytopathology and the National Registry of Hospital Discharges (eg, in- and outpatient discharges). Information on patient characteristics and treatment is routinely recorded in the NCR by trained registrars of the NCR through retrospective medical record reviews. Information on the last known vital status of all patients (eg, alive, deceased, emigrated) is obtained through annual linkage with the Nationwide Population Registries Network, which holds vital statistics on all residents in the Netherlands. Since 1 January 2014, detailed information on the diagnostic and treatment characteristics of all hematologic malignancies diagnosed in the Netherlands has been recorded in the NCR. The data are entered 1 year after diagnosis. According to the Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects, this type of observational study does not require approval from an ethics committee in the Netherlands. The privacy review board of the NCR approved the use of anonymous data for this study. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Study population Patients, ≥18 years, who were diagnosed with histopathologic MCL in the Netherlands between 1 January 1989 and 31 December 2020 were identified in the NCR using the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (World Health Organization), morphology code 9673/3, based on pathology reports. For the overall cohort (1989-2020), first-line therapy is presented for 3 calendar periods, namely 1989 to 2000, 2001 to 2014, and 2015 to 2020. The calendar periods were based on the introduction of R in the Netherlands as part of routine clinical practice and, more recently, as maintenance. The period 1989 to 2000 represents the pre-R era, the period 2001 to 2014 represents the R era, and the period 2015 to 2020 represents the era of additional RM implementation ( ). Because of the COVID-19 pandemic that started in 2020, patients with histopathologically confirmed MCL beyond 2020 were not included in this study. Survival follow-up was available until 1 February 2025. After this date, all patients who were alive were censored in the survival analyses. In analysis A, the OS and relative survival (RS) for the whole cohort (eg, patients diagnosed between 1989 and 2020), according to age (18-65 years and ≥66 years) and the 3 calendar periods, were calculated. Detailed

2014 represents the R era, and the period 2015 to 2020 represents the era of additional RM implementation ( ). Because of the COVID-19 pandemic that started in 2020, patients with histopathologically confirmed MCL beyond 2020 were not included in this study. Survival follow-up was available until 1 February 2025. After this date, all patients who were alive were censored in the survival analyses. In analysis A, the OS and relative survival (RS) for the whole cohort (eg, patients diagnosed between 1989 and 2020), according to age (18-65 years and ≥66 years) and the 3 calendar periods, were calculated. Detailed information on treatment was available for all patients from 2014. First-line therapy was categorized into 3 groups: (1) R-CHOP; (2) R-CHOP followed by high-dose cytarabine-containing regimens and ASCT (intensive therapy); and (3) other, such as CHOEP (cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin [doxorubicin], oncovin [vincristine], etoposide, and prednisone), CVP (cyclophosphamide, oncovin [vincristine], prednisone), R monotherapy, chlorambucil, BR, ibrutinib, or radiotherapy. Patients participating in clinical studies or treated otherwise were excluded from all analyses. Progression of disease within 12 months (POD12) following diagnosis was evaluated in analysis B, in which progression of disease (POD) was categorized as <6 months after diagnosis and within 6 to 12 months after diagnosis. Because all relapses were recorded 1 year after diagnosis, information on POD12 only was available ( ). The impact of RM, depending on remission status after first-line therapy, on the OS for patients who were treated with R-CHOP or intensive therapy was evaluated in analysis C. Patients with stable disease, primary refractory disease, or unknown remission status were excluded from analysis C because these patients did not qualify for RM ( ). End points The primary end point was OS. For analysis A, RS was a secondary outcome measure. RS was defined as the ratio of the observed OS of the patient cohort to the expected OS of a similar group from the general population, matched for age and sex. RS reflects the excess mortality associated with MCL, independent of other causes of death, and provides an estimate of disease-specific survival when the cause of death information is unavailable. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to present the patient and treatment characteristics. Pearson χ 2 tests were used to compare categorical covariables, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to compare non-normally distributed continuous covariables between the 2 treatment groups. The OS was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. A log-rank test was used to evaluate the differences in survival distributions. The RS and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated as the OS divided by the expected survival of an equivalent population using the Ederer II methodology from Dutch population life tables, stratified by age and the 3 calendar periods (1989-2000, 2001-2014, and 2015-2020). The impact of RM, age at diagnosis (per year increment), sex, Ann Arbor stage (1-2, 3-4, and unknown), response (complete remission [CR] vs partial remission [PR]), and Mantle Cell Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (MIPI) score (low, intermediate, and high risk) as categorical variables on the risk for mortality was evaluated using uni- and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses. The results from the Cox regression analyses produce hazard ratios (HRs) with the associated 95% Cls. All covariables with a significant difference in the univariable regression model were included in the multivariable regression model. Covariables were sequentially removed, starting with the highest P value, until all remaining variables had P values ≤.05. The statistical analyses were performed using Stata/SE 17.0 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX). Results Patient characteristics In total, 4751 patients with MCL were identified for the period of 1989 to 2020 ( ), with a median age of 70 years and a male-to-female ratio of 2.6:1 ( ). From 2014 to 2020, a total of 1396 patients were diagnosed with MCL, of whom 513 (37%) were treated with R-CHOP and 265 (19%) were treated with intensive chemotherapy. The baseline characteristics of these patients are described in and . Patients who were treated with R-CHOP were significantly older than patients who received ASCT (median age: 72 vs 61 years; P < .01). Outcome over time (analysis A) The 5-year OS for the entire cohort was 41% ( ). When evaluating survival for the 3 calendar periods, the 5-year RS improved from 38% in 1989 to 2000 to 47% in 2001 to 2014 and to 60% in the most recent calendar period (2015-2020; P < .01; ). The 5-year RS of patients aged 18 to 65 years was significantly higher than the 5-year RS of patients older than 65 years (66% vs 38%; P < .01; ). Over time, the RS improved in both age groups, with a 32% increase among young patients and a 20% increase among the elderly ( A-B). Outcome among primary refractory patients (analysis B) Among the 778 patients diagnosed between 2014

periods, the 5-year RS improved from 38% in 1989 to 2000 to 47% in 2001 to 2014 and to 60% in the most recent calendar period (2015-2020; P < .01; ). The 5-year RS of patients aged 18 to 65 years was significantly higher than the 5-year RS of patients older than 65 years (66% vs 38%; P < .01; ). Over time, the RS improved in both age groups, with a 32% increase among young patients and a 20% increase among the elderly ( A-B). Outcome among primary refractory patients (analysis B) Among the 778 patients diagnosed between 2014 and 2020, 101 patients (13%) experienced POD within 12 months. The OS of patients with POD within 12 months was poor, with 1-year and 2-year OS rates of only 38% and 25%, respectively. There was no significant difference in OS between patients with primary refractory disease and those with an early relapse ( ). In the multivariable analysis, neither age, sex, RM, MIPI score, nor stage of disease at initial diagnosis was associated with risk for POD within 12 months of diagnosis. Outcome according to treatment and impact of RM (analysis C) Between 2014 and 2020, the use of RM increased ( ), primarily driven by its introduction in patients ≤65 years. Between 2015 and 2017, the proportion of patients who received RM following intensive chemotherapy increased from 0% to 71%. Among patients who were treated with R-CHOP, RM was applied in 40% to 60% of cases. The baseline characteristics of patients who were treated with RM and those who were not were comparable ( and ). Among 513 patients who were treated with R-CHOP, the 5-year OS was 43% ( ). Of the 398 patients who achieved a response (CR or PR), 227 (57%) received RM. The OS was similar between patients who were treated with RM and those who were not ( P = .79). Among the 262 patients with a CR, there was a trend toward an OS benefit among patients who treated with RM when compared with those who were not ( P = .06), with 5-year OS estimates of 50% and 64%, respectively ( ). Among the 140 patients with a PR, the OS was significantly better among those who received RM than among those who did not ( P < .01), with 5-year OS estimates of 44% and 33%, respectively ( ). Among patients who did not receive RM, those with a CR had a superior 5-year OS rate than those with a PR (64% vs 33%; P < .01). Among the 265 patients who were treated with intensive therapy, the 5-year OS was 74% ( ). Of the 230 patients who achieved a CR or PR, 114 (50%) received RM. In this group, the 5-year OS was similar between those who received RM and those who did not. For patients with a CR, the 5-year OS was 83% with RM vs 77% without RM ( P = .46); for those with a PR, the 5-year OS was 55% vs 70%, respectively ( P = .29; ). A multivariable analysis was performed separately for patients who were treated with R-CHOP and those who were treated with intensive therapy. In the R-CHOP group, RM was associated with a reduced risk for mortality (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.53-0.90). Factors associated with an increased risk for mortality in this group included PR after induction (HR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.11-1.85), older age (HR per year increment, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.04-1.08), and a higher MIPI score (intermediate score: HR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.2; high score: HR, 2.08; 95% CI, 1.45-3.0). Among patients treated with intensive therapy, PR was also associated with increased mortality (HR, 2.26; 95% CI, 1.28-4.01), as was older age (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.11; ). In this group, RM was not significantly associated with survival. Discussion In this nationwide, population-based study, we evaluated the long-term survival outcomes among patients with MCL and assessed the impact of RM in routine clinical practice. RS improved by 22% over the past 3 decades, largely reflecting the introduction of R, improvements in supportive care, diagnostics, and the integration of novel agents ( ). Our findings also underscore the importance of RM, particularly in a subgroup of patients with a PR following R-CHOP induction. The survival benefit of R in induction regimens for MCL has been well documented since the early 2000s, with Coiffier et al and others demonstrating significantly improved response rates and time to treatment failure when R was added to CHOP-like regimens. , In younger, fit patients, the outcomes improved further with high-dose cytarabine-based induction and ASCT consolidation, as shown in the European MCL Network trial. More recently, the TRIANGLE trial highlighted the role of ibrutinib in further augmenting frontline treatment. Several clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy

RM, particularly in a subgroup of patients with a PR following R-CHOP induction. The survival benefit of R in induction regimens for MCL has been well documented since the early 2000s, with Coiffier et al and others demonstrating significantly improved response rates and time to treatment failure when R was added to CHOP-like regimens. , In younger, fit patients, the outcomes improved further with high-dose cytarabine-based induction and ASCT consolidation, as shown in the European MCL Network trial. More recently, the TRIANGLE trial highlighted the role of ibrutinib in further augmenting frontline treatment. Several clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy of RM in MCL. The European MCL Elderly trial (Kluin-Nelemans et al ) reported improved PFS and OS with RM following treatment with R-CHOP but not among those who received FCR. Similarly, RM after ASCT was associated with improved survival in the LyMa trial (Le Gouill et al ); however, the OS benefit did not retain significance at long-term follow-up. These trials shaped international guidelines and established RM as a standard approach following first-line treatment. Our real-world data largely validate the findings of clinical trials, particularly in supporting the role of RM after R-CHOP induction therapy. In addition, our study provides insight into the value of response-based analyses after induction therapy. In the multivariable analysis, RM following R-CHOP therapy was independently associated with reduced mortality. Notably, this benefit was most pronounced among patients with a PR, with a trend toward an OS advantage observed in patients with CR ( P = .06), possibly limited by the sample size and duration of follow-up. Next, the difference between patients with CR and those with PR could have been more pronounced if response assessments were uniformly conducted using positron emission tomography/computed tomography imaging (PET/CT). In our cohort, data on the method of response evaluation were available from 2017 to 2020, showing that the method of response assessment was PET/CT in 84% of patients who achieved CR, whereas it was 33% in patients with a PR, suggesting that the uniform use of PET/CT could have led to better differentiation of patients with PR. The effect of treatment response is not well captured in randomized controlled trials, which often lack the granularity or statistical power to assess subgroups based on depth of response. The findings of this study are somewhat similar to previous observational studies. In a large US cohort study, Martin et al reported a statistically significant improvement in time to next treatment with RM following both BR and R-CHOP. However, an OS benefit was observed only after BR and not R-CHOP, potentially because of a limited sample size in the R-CHOP group. Similarly, a second US-based, real-world analysis by Di et al demonstrated improved outcomes with RM after BR or R-CHOP; however, most patients received BR, and the effect of RM was not evaluated independently in the R-CHOP–treated population. Importantly, neither study stratified by remission status, potentially masking important heterogeneity. Our findings did not align with those from Hoster et al, who reported that minimal risidual disease (MRD)-positive patients benefited less from RM. Differences in the first-line induction regimens, cohort size, information on remission, or progression status, follow-up period, and the inclusion of patients treated as early as 2007 likely contributed to the heterogeneity in the outcomes of real-world studies. Collectively, these results suggest that remission status may be a critical determinant of RM efficacy and survival, and its use may be limited in those with CR or molecular remission. Interestingly, in our cohort, RM was not associated with improved OS following intensive chemoimmunotherapy and ASCT. Although retrospective data , and the LYMA trial initially supported RM in this setting, its long-term impact remains debated, especially in the context of evolving frontline strategies that incorporate novel agents. As suggested by Sarkozy et al, RM may not overcome the adverse prognosis of early relapse (POD24), and its benefit may be less apparent in patients who already achieved deep remissions. The poor outcomes observed in patients with early progression (POD < 12 months) are consistent with previous studies and highlight the need for better risk stratification and therapeutic strategies. Emerging treatments, including next-generation Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitors, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, offer hope for this high-risk population. , , , , , , , Our study is strengthened by the large, unselected cohort of patients who were uniformly treated with R-CHOP and who underwent comprehensive follow-up; however, it is limited by the lack of data on toxicity, MRD status, response assessment in routine clinical practice, reasons for (non-)initiation of RM, and information on second-line therapy. Therefore, analyses of the impact of salvage strategies (eg, Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, bendamustine, or chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy) in light of RM on survival could not be performed. Moreover, we acknowledge that

T-cell therapy, offer hope for this high-risk population. , , , , , , , Our study is strengthened by the large, unselected cohort of patients who were uniformly treated with R-CHOP and who underwent comprehensive follow-up; however, it is limited by the lack of data on toxicity, MRD status, response assessment in routine clinical practice, reasons for (non-)initiation of RM, and information on second-line therapy. Therefore, analyses of the impact of salvage strategies (eg, Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, bendamustine, or chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy) in light of RM on survival could not be performed. Moreover, we acknowledge that real-world decision-making, particularly in elderly patients or those with comorbidities, may reflect unmeasured confounders that are difficult to adjust for. In conclusion, our study validates the survival improvement in MCL over recent decades and supports the selective benefit of RM, especially in patients who achieved PR after R-CHOP. These findings emphasize the need for individualized application of RM and support further evaluation of MRD-guided and response-adapted maintenance strategies in prospective studies. documents.title: Marginal zone lymphomas ESMO Clinical Practice

chunks.content: Introduction Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (EMZL) of mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) represents a heterogeneous entity with diverse clinical presentations and management strategies. , The recommended first-line therapy in gastric EMZL is upfront Helicobacter pylori eradication, which has resulted in unprecedented long-term response rates, due to the strong pathophysiological linkage of lymphomagenesis to chronic antigenic stimulation by H pylori . , , Although EMZL is generally regarded as an indolent disease with median survival times >12 years, a subset of patients experience a more aggressive course characterized by early disease progression or relapse. , , The MALT–International Prognostic Index (MALT-IPI) is the most widely applied prognostic tool incorporating age (<70 vs ≥70 years), Ann Arbor stage (I-II vs III-IV), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; above vs below the upper limit of normal) to stratify patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups. Although subsequently validated in 3 independent cohorts, the MALT-IPI was originally derived exclusively from patients enrolled in the International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group (IELSG)-19 trial, who were treated with chlorambucil, rituximab, or their combination. Nevertheless, it is routinely used across nearly all disease settings, regardless of therapeutic approach, stage, or lymphoma localization. , , Its applicability beyond contexts resembling the IELSG-19 population remains debated, and several studies have proposed modifications or the incorporation of additional parameters to improve prognostic precision in EMZL. , Among these, the concomitant presence of autoimmune disease (AD) appears to be particularly interesting. Although successful H pylori eradication eliminates the antigenic drive in gastric EMZL, chronic autoimmune-mediated B-cell stimulation mostly persists despite eradication therapy. , Indeed, patients with concomitant AD have demonstrated inferior response to H pylori eradication compared with those without AD in a previous study, raising the question whether chronic autoimmune stimuli may be added to the prognostic assessment in EMZL. We have therefore conducted a retrospective analysis of a large, real-world cohort of patients with EMZL, with the objectives of assessing the performance of the MALT-IPI across different therapeutic settings, and exploring whether incorporation of concomitant AD could refine prognostic discrimination beyond the established MALT-IPI. Materials and methods Patient characteristics We have retrospectively analyzed patients with newly diagnosed EMZL managed at the Medical University of Vienna between January 1999 and December 2024. Clinical data were retrieved from patient records, and disease staging was performed according to the modified Ann Arbor classification. Histological diagnoses were (re-)evaluated by a reference hematopathologist according to the current World Health Organization classification criteria for EMZL of MALT. The MALT-IPI was calculated based on age ≥70 years, stage III/IV disease, and elevated LDH, as previously published. Subgroup analysis of the predictive and prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI was performed according to primary EMZL localization, EMZL stage, and first-line therapy. Given the speculated impact of autoimmune conditions on the clinical course of patients with EMZL, we aimed to explore whether incorporation of autoimmunity, captured here as the concomitant presence of AD or antinuclear antibody (ANA) seropositivity, could refine predictive or prognostic discrimination of the MALT-IPI. We have therefore exploratorily constructed the “MALT-AD-IPI” and the “MALT-ANA-IPI” by expanding the MALT-IPI by 1 additional point for the presence of AD or ANA seropositivity as a fourth variable (low-risk = 0 points, intermediate-risk = 1 point, high-risk = 2 points, very high-risk ≥3 points). This study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna (EC approval number: 791/2011). Due to the retrospective nature of this study, individual informed consent was waived by the ethics committee. Statistical analysis Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis and compared using the log-rank test. PFS was defined as the time from diagnosis to progression, relapse, or death. OS was defined as the time from diagnosis to death of any cause. Patients without events were censored for OS and PFS analysis at their respective last clinical follow-up. For each risk-scoring tool, subgroup analyses were performed according to primary lymphoma localization (ie, gastric and extragastric EMZL) and by first-line treatment strategy (ie, systemic therapy, H pylori eradication, local therapy, or watchful waiting). A 2-sided P value of <.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Results Patient characteristics In total, 498 patients with EMZL were analyzed ( ). The median age at diagnosis was 62 years (range, 19-90), and 286 of 498 (57.4%) patients were female. Although 172 of 498 (34.5%) patients had primary gastric EMZL, 326 of 498 (65.5%) patients had primary extragastric disease. Among those, EMZL was predominantly located in the ocular adnexa (120/326, 36.81%), the lung (53/326, 16.26%), the parotid gland (51/326, 15.64%), or the intestine (24/326, 7.36%). Most patients had Ann Arbor stage I or II disease (373/487, 76.6%; n = 11 unknown), whereas 114 of 487 (23.4%) were diagnosed with stage III or IV lymphoma. Systemic therapy was the first-line treatment in 189 of 496 (38.1%)

Although 172 of 498 (34.5%) patients had primary gastric EMZL, 326 of 498 (65.5%) patients had primary extragastric disease. Among those, EMZL was predominantly located in the ocular adnexa (120/326, 36.81%), the lung (53/326, 16.26%), the parotid gland (51/326, 15.64%), or the intestine (24/326, 7.36%). Most patients had Ann Arbor stage I or II disease (373/487, 76.6%; n = 11 unknown), whereas 114 of 487 (23.4%) were diagnosed with stage III or IV lymphoma. Systemic therapy was the first-line treatment in 189 of 496 (38.1%) patients (n = 2 unknown), whereas 135 of 496 (27.22%) patients received upfront H pylori eradication and 124 of 496 (25.0%) received local therapy including radiotherapy or surgery. An additional 38 of 496 (7.66%) patients were managed with “watchful waiting.” The median PFS and OS in our cohort were 58.73 months (range, 0-248.28) and 301.74 months (range, 0-367.73), respectively. Prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI in patients with EMZL The MALT-IPI could be calculated for 441 of 498 (90.0%) patients, and was low in 216 of 441 (49.0%), intermediate in 183 of 441 (41.5%), and high in 42 of 441 (9.5%). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated superior PFS among patients with low-risk MALT-IPI (median PFS = 73.64 months [95% confidence interval (CI), 51.39-109.45]) compared with patients in intermediate- (median PFS = 57.90 months [95% CI, 41.00-97.71]) and high-risk groups (22.88 months [95% CI, 16.77-39.12]; P < .001; A). Similarly, OS was significantly longer in patients within the low-risk group ( P < .001; B). The 10-year OS rate in patients in the low-risk group was 84.7% (95% CI, 77.6-92.5) compared with 76.8% (95% CI, 68.0-86.7) for intermediate-risk and 51.7% (95% CI, 29.9-89.6) for high-risk groups ( P < .001). These findings confirm the prognostic utility of the MALT-IPI in primarily unselected real-world patients with EMZL, and suggest a representative patient collective in our analysis. Subgroup analysis of the prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI We next explored the predictive and prognostic power of the MALT-IPI in selected clinical subgroups. Although the score retained prognostic value in the overall cohort, its discriminative capacity was more nuanced when stratified by clinical subgroups. Prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI according to primary EMZL localization Upon stratification of our cohort into patients with primary gastric EMZL and primary extragastric EMZL, the MALT-IPI largely retained predictive and prognostic significance in patients with primary extragastric EMZL ( C-D; ). The median PFS was 81.8 months (95% CI, 72.7-not reached (NR)) in low-risk, 65.5 months (95% CI, 49.5-114.3) in intermediate-risk, and 18.7 months (95% CI, 13.6-39.1) in high-risk extragastric EMZL, with 10-year OS rates of 85.7% (95% CI, 76.5-96.0), 76.3% (95% CI, 65.4-89.0), and 50.9% (95% CI, 28.8-90.0), respectively (log-rank P < .001 each). Upon stratification of our cohort into individual extragastric anatomical primary localizations, the MALT-IPI retained its predictive and prognostic performance in patients with EMZL of the ocular adnexa and the parotid gland (log rank P < .05 each; A-D). In patients with intestinal EMZL, the median PFS was significantly shorter in patients with high-risk EMZL (log-rank P = .013; E), but OS did not show statistically significant differences between MALT-IPI risk groups ( P > .05; F). In patients with primary pulmonary EMZL, neither PFS nor OS differed between MALT-IPI risk groups (log-rank P > .05 each; G-H), although analysis was certainly limited by sample size in individual localizations. In patients with primary gastric EMZL, neither PFS nor OS showed significant differences between risk groups (log-rank P > .05 each; A-B). Prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI according to first-line therapy As for extragastric primary EMZL localization, the MALT-IPI retained its prognostic value in patients receiving upfront systemic therapy ( E-F). In this subgroup, median PFS ranged from 90.8 months (95% CI, 72.7-NR) for patients in the low-risk group to 18.0 months (95% CI, 11.4-63.6) for patients in the high-risk group, and 10-year OS rates were 78.9% (95% CI, 67.2-92.7), 75.2% (95% CI, 62.5-90.4), and 47.9% (95% CI, 26.0-88.5) across the 3 strata (log-rank P < .001 each). However, in patients treated with local therapy (radiotherapy or surgery; C-D), upfront H pylori eradication ( E-F), or watchful waiting ( G-H), neither PFS nor OS showed significant differences between risk groups, with the exception of OS in patients treated with local therapy (log-rank P = .00019). PFS and OS in the remaining groups were largely overlapping across all MALT-IPI strata (log-rank P > .05), underscoring the limited applicability of the score in these clinical settings. Prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI in patients with stage I/II or III/IV EMZL We next analyzed the performance of the MALT-IPI according to EMZL stage. In patients with stage I/II EMZL, no PFS benefit of patients with low-risk MALT-IPI was observed ( A; log-rank P =

neither PFS nor OS showed significant differences between risk groups, with the exception of OS in patients treated with local therapy (log-rank P = .00019). PFS and OS in the remaining groups were largely overlapping across all MALT-IPI strata (log-rank P > .05), underscoring the limited applicability of the score in these clinical settings. Prognostic performance of the MALT-IPI in patients with stage I/II or III/IV EMZL We next analyzed the performance of the MALT-IPI according to EMZL stage. In patients with stage I/II EMZL, no PFS benefit of patients with low-risk MALT-IPI was observed ( A; log-rank P = .67). However, patients with intermediate-risk MALT-IPI had significantly shorter OS than patients with low-risk MALT-IPI ( B; log-rank P = .003). Interestingly, although certainly limited by sample size (n = 6), patients with high-risk stage I/II EMZL had longer OS than patients in low- and high-risk groups. In patients with stage III/IV EMZL, patients in the high-risk group had significantly shorter OS and PFS than patients in the intermediate-risk group (log rank P = .0012 and <.0001; C-D). Given the fact that having stage III/IV EMZL precludes categorization as low-risk in the MALT-IPI, patients in the low-risk group were absent in stage III/IV EMZL ( ). Incorporation of autoimmunity into the MALT-IPI does not significantly improve prognostication of patients with EMZL Information on the presence of concomitant AD was available for 419 of 498 (84.1%) patients. Of those, 141 of 419 (31.1%) had a concomitant AD. The ANA serostatus was assessed in 453 of 498 (91.0%) patients, of whom 72 of 453 (15.9%) were seropositive. Thus, 148 patients were classified as low-risk, 178 as intermediate-risk, 81 as high-risk, and 12 as very high-risk according to the exploratory MALT-AD-IPI. The MALT-AD-IPI could not be calculated in 79 of 498 patients (15.9%) due to missing data. According to the MALT-ANA-IPI, 182 of 419 patients (43.4%) were classified as low-risk, 168 of 419 (40.1%) as intermediate-risk, 60 (14.3%) as high-risk, and 9 of 419 (2.2%) as very high-risk (n = 79 not available (NA); ). In our cohort, no significant difference in the first-line treatment strategy was noted comparing patients with and without either autoimmunological parameter ( P > .05 each). The addition of either AD (MALT-AD-IPI) or ANA seropositivity (MALT-ANA-IPI) resulted in risk group stratifications that were broadly comparable to the classical MALT-IPI ( ). In the MALT-AD-IPI, the median PFS was 18.7 months (95% CI, 15.1-NR) in the very high-risk group, compared with 46.5 months (95% CI, 30.6-NR) in high-risk, 62.9 months (95% CI, 49.5-90.3) in intermediate-risk, and 71.0 months (95% CI, 50.4-121.1) in low-risk groups (log-rank P < .001; A). Although median PFS times suggest promising risk-group separation, Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed no clear separation of low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups. Similarly, the MALT-ANA-IPI identified a very high-risk group with a median PFS of 16.8 months (5.4-NR), compared with 41.8 months (95% CI, 32.3-NR) in high-risk, 57.9 months (95% CI, 37.2-82.8) in intermediate-risk, and 74.0 months (95% CI, 51.1-134.9) in low-risk groups (log-rank P < .001; B). However, Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed no clear separation of patients in the intermediate- and high-risk groups. Comparable results were obtained for OS. In the MALT-AD-IPI, 10-year OS rates were 89.6% (95% CI, 81.6-98.3) in low-risk, 76.7% (95% CI, 67.4-87.2) in intermediate-risk, 80.5% (95% CI, 68.6-94.5) in high-risk, and 34.3% (95% CI, 12.4-94.6) in very high-risk groups (log-rank P < .001; C). The MALT-ANA-IPI showed similar stratification, with 10-year OS rates of 87.2% (95% CI, 79.5-95.7), 78.3% (95% CI, 69.6-88.1), 75.0% (95% CI, 58.3-96.3), and 22.2% (95% CI, 4.2-100.0) for patients in the low-, intermediate-, high-, and very high-risk groups, respectively (log-rank P < .001; D). However, similar to PFS, the apparent stepwise decrease in median OS did not translate into clearly separated survival curves. Discussion The present analysis provides an in-depth evaluation of the prognostic and predictive utility of the MALT-IPI in a large, real-world cohort of patients with EMZL. Although the MALT-IPI remains the most widely applied risk stratification tool in EMZL, its derivation from a single, trial-based population and treatment context has raised concerns about its generalizability. By systematically assessing its performance across clinical subgroups and exploring autoimmune-based modifications, our findings demonstrate both the strengths and the limitations of the score in contemporary practice. In the overall cohort, the MALT-IPI retained significant prognostic discrimination for both PFS and OS, confirming its validity in unselected patients. However, its performance was heterogeneous across clinical contexts. Specifically, the index demonstrated robust predictive and prognostic power among patients with extragastric EMZL, particularly in patients with EMZL of the ocular adnexa or the parotid gland, as well as in patients with primary intestinal EMZL, whereas no consistent separation of risk groups was observed among patients with primary gastric EMZL. With regard to first-line treatment, the MALT-IPI retained predictive

the strengths and the limitations of the score in contemporary practice. In the overall cohort, the MALT-IPI retained significant prognostic discrimination for both PFS and OS, confirming its validity in unselected patients. However, its performance was heterogeneous across clinical contexts. Specifically, the index demonstrated robust predictive and prognostic power among patients with extragastric EMZL, particularly in patients with EMZL of the ocular adnexa or the parotid gland, as well as in patients with primary intestinal EMZL, whereas no consistent separation of risk groups was observed among patients with primary gastric EMZL. With regard to first-line treatment, the MALT-IPI retained predictive and prognostic power in patients treated with systemic therapy, but not in patients treated with upfront H pylori eradication or in patients that were initially managed with watchful waiting. Interestingly, although we did not observe clear risk-group separation in the PFS of patients treated with upfront local therapy, OS was progressively decreasing with increasing MALT-IPI in this cohort. These findings are highly consistent with the clinical and biological context in which the MALT-IPI was originally derived, the IELSG-19 trial, in which patients received chlorambucil, rituximab, or their combination. The retained performance in extragastric and systemically treated cohorts thus likely reflects similarity to the trial’s population and therapeutic setting. By contrast, gastric EMZL, historically the first to be consistently managed with H pylori eradication or localized radiotherapy, represents a biologically distinct and clinically more indolent subgroup. , In these patients, prognosis may be predominantly driven by local response to bacterial eradication (ie, the removal of the antigenic stimulus), and persistent antigenic pressure in cases refractory to eradication that might not be captured by systemic parameters such as elevated LDH or advanced age. Indeed, H pylori eradication alone induces regression in a high proportion of patients with EMZL, whereas failure is associated with deeper invasion, H pylori –negative status, or chromosomal translocations such as t(11;18) that confer antigen independence. , , Consequently, the conventional MALT-IPI, which emphasizes systemic disease burden, failed to capture the major prognostic determinants in patients with primary gastric EMZL in our cohort. The same held true for patients managed with H pylori eradication, in whom PFS and OS curves largely overlapped across MALT-IPI strata. Previous studies proposing adaptations or refinements of the MALT-IPI, including the recently developed Revised MALT-IPI, have aimed to enhance prognostic precision by incorporating disease-specific parameters, such as involvement of multiple mucosal sites, though their applicability in routine clinical practice remains to be defined. , Unfortunately, data on multiple mucosal sites were not consistently available in our cohort, reflecting the retrospective nature of data collection dating back to 1999, which precluded direct comparison of our findings to the Revised MALT-IPI. Given the well-established association between chronic immune stimulation and the pathogenesis of EMZL, we have evaluated whether incorporation of AD or ANA seropositivity could refine prognostic discrimination. Overall, both extended indices generated risk groups broadly comparable to those of the classical MALT-IPI, but identified a small subset of patients with particularly poor outcomes. The median PFS and OS in these patients were shorter than in patients in the high-risk group of the classical index, supporting the notion that chronic autoimmune activation may promote treatment-resistant disease biology. However, outside of this subgroup, neither modification substantially improved the overall prognostic performance. In both the MALT-AD-IPI and MALT-ANA-IPI, outcomes in the low- and intermediate-risk groups were comparable to those of the original index, and patients in the high-risk group often overlapped with patients in the intermediate-risk group of the classical score. Although median PFS and 10-year OS rates suggested some added value of incorporation of autoimmunity into the prognostic assessment, Kaplan-Meier curves did not demonstrate consistent additional separation between risk groups. Of note, the upfront treatment choice between patients with and without concomitant autoimmunity did not differ significantly in our cohort, suggesting that concomitant autoimmunity was largely not considered a treatment-deciding parameter. These results suggest that, although autoimmunity and ANA positivity may identify biologically distinct patients with adverse features, their inclusion alone does not meaningfully enhance population-level risk stratification. From a biological perspective, these findings are intuitive. In H pylori –driven EMZL, eradication of the underlying antigenic trigger often leads to durable remission. In contrast, autoimmune-mediated antigenic stimulation represents a persistent, systemic driver of B-cell proliferation and survival, which cannot be eliminated by local or anti-infective therapy, and may foster refractory or aggressive disease. , The potential prognostic relevance of autoimmunity and ANA seropositivity underscores the interplay between chronic immune stimulation and lymphoma persistence. Indeed, previous studies have shown that patients with autoimmune comorbidities, particularly Sjögren syndrome or Hashimoto thyroiditis, exhibit inferior responses to H pylori eradication and are more likely to require systemic treatment. Although our data suggest that the presence of autoimmune phenomena may identify a small group of particularly vulnerable patients, these parameters alone appear

represents a persistent, systemic driver of B-cell proliferation and survival, which cannot be eliminated by local or anti-infective therapy, and may foster refractory or aggressive disease. , The potential prognostic relevance of autoimmunity and ANA seropositivity underscores the interplay between chronic immune stimulation and lymphoma persistence. Indeed, previous studies have shown that patients with autoimmune comorbidities, particularly Sjögren syndrome or Hashimoto thyroiditis, exhibit inferior responses to H pylori eradication and are more likely to require systemic treatment. Although our data suggest that the presence of autoimmune phenomena may identify a small group of particularly vulnerable patients, these parameters alone appear to be insufficient to refine global prognostic stratification, and interpretation of these findings warrants caution. The number of patients identified as very high-risk was small in both indices (n = 9 and n = 12 in the MALT-AD-IPI and MALT-ANA-IPI, respectively), and the assessment of autoimmunity was not uniformly performed across the entire study period. Future studies using standardized definitions and larger, independent data sets will be required to validate the prognostic impact of autoimmune status, and to determine whether incorporation of composite immunologic markers may provide more robust discrimination. In the future, incorporation of composite immune signatures may better capture the impact of systemic immune activation on EMZL outcomes. In conclusion, this study confirms the validity of the MALT-IPI in contemporary practice, but also delineates its limitations, particularly in patients with gastric EMZL managed with H pylori eradication or localized modalities. Integration of AD or ANA serostatus identifies a small subset of patients with dismal outcomes, but does not consistently improve prognostic accuracy across the broader cohort. These findings warrant further prospective validation and consideration in future trial designs, considering the potential limited prognostic power of the MALT-IPI in patients with primary gastric EMZL and upfront H pylori eradication treatment. documents.title: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia ESMO

chunks.content: 1 Introduction In Western countries, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL; CLL is cancer in the bloodstream; SLL is in the lymph node system [ , , ]) is one of the most common mature B‐cell neoplasms. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (of which 95% of cases are Waldenström macroglobulinaemia [WM]) is a rare type of non‐Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) characterised by bone marrow infiltration and monoclonal immunoglobulin M gammopathy in the blood that mostly affects adults [ ]. Both lymphoid neoplasms are frequently observed in the older population and are considered incurable, albeit with high survival rates. Per current guidelines, patients with asymptomatic CLL/SLL and WM are closely monitored [ , , , ]. For patients who require treatment, therapeutic options include anti‐CD20 monoclonal antibody‐based chemoimmunotherapy and newer agents such as Bruton Tyrosine Kinase inhibitors (BTKi) for both CLL and WM and BCL2 inhibitors for CLL [ , , , , , , ]. As CLL/SLL and WM are indolent cancers [ , ], survival rates can be relatively high. International literature suggests a 5‐year overall survival rate of 81% for WM [ ] and a 10‐year survival rate of > 60% for patients with CLL ≥ 75 years old in both Germany and the United States (US) [ ]. Recent studies using registry data indicated a decreasing trend in the incidence‐based mortality of CLL in Switzerland [ ] and WM in women in the US [ ]. In Australia, a similar trend was seen in the Australian Cancer Registry report for CLL/SLL and WM, with an increase in the 5‐year survival rate, while the mortality rate was reported as decreasing [ ]. For example, the 5‐year observed survival rate of CLL/SLL in Australia increased from 71.4% for the period of 2010–2014 to 74% for the period of 2015–2019 and from 64.4% to 69.5% between the same periods for WM, respectively [ ]. However, there were no estimated mortality and survival rates for CLL/SLL and WM over a longer period. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW), NHL is the sixth most diagnosed cancer in Australia [ ], with a projected increasing trend in age‐standardised incidence rate for all NHLs (e.g., up to 20.4 cases per 100,000 persons projected in 2021) [ ]. To the best of our knowledge, the temporal increasing trend in CLL/SLL and WM incidence rates was reported in an older Australian study using historical lymphoma (lymphoid neoplasms) data from 1982 to 2006 and in the AIHW cancer report using cancer registry data since 2003 [ , ]. Among all NHLs, CLL/SLL ranked as the most common subtype [ ] with an accumulated total age‐standardised incidence rate between 7.6 and 9.6 per 100,000 person‐years for the reported period from 2003 onward. The WM incidence fluctuated between 0.5 and 0.8 per 100,000 persons for the same reporting period [ , ]. However, the future projection for CLL/SLL and WM incidence was limited in Australia (i.e., 3 years). Similarly, although 16,929 prevalent cases for CLL were recorded by the end of 2018 in the Australian cancer registry [ ], no specific rate by sex and age group was reported. Recent data for incidence, prevalence, survival and mortality of less‐aggressive lymphoid neoplasms with high survival rates, such as CLL/SLL and WM, in Australia are limited. It is essential to investigate the epidemiology of these two subtypes of NHL in the Australian context. Therefore, this study aimed to: Quantify the current incidence rate, prevalence, and mortality indicators of CLL/SLL and WM and Examine the incidence, prevalence, and survival trend of CLL/SLL and WM and predict the trend for the next 30 years, where feasible. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design A population study was performed to examine national administrative data from the four cancer registries (Victoria, Australian Capital Territory, Tasmania and Queensland) of the Australian Cancer Database (ACD) which represent half of the Australian population. At the time of analysis, data were not available from New South Wales, Western Australia, South Australia, and Northern Territory's registries. Descriptive and survival analyses were employed to quantify the current incidence rate, survival, and prevalence of CLL/SLL and WM. Linear regression was used to project and/or predict the incidence and prevalence trend for the observed data and project the 30‐year incidence rate where possible. All analyses were stratified by sex and age group when applicable. 2.2 Data Sources and Data Field In Australia, routine reports of newly diagnosed cancer cases to Australian cancer registries and the ACD, managed by the AIHW, are mandatory. The data were extracted and masked by the AIHW using pre‐defined data fields, including sex, year of diagnosis, age group at diagnosis, International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD)‐O‐3.2 topography code, ICD‐O‐3.2 histology code, ICD‐10 disease code, rounded survival time (to the nearest multiple of five), age group at death and cause of death

and project the 30‐year incidence rate where possible. All analyses were stratified by sex and age group when applicable. 2.2 Data Sources and Data Field In Australia, routine reports of newly diagnosed cancer cases to Australian cancer registries and the ACD, managed by the AIHW, are mandatory. The data were extracted and masked by the AIHW using pre‐defined data fields, including sex, year of diagnosis, age group at diagnosis, International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD)‐O‐3.2 topography code, ICD‐O‐3.2 histology code, ICD‐10 disease code, rounded survival time (to the nearest multiple of five), age group at death and cause of death (derived from the National Mortality Database). 2.3 Study Population Patients diagnosed with CLL/SLL and WM and registered in the ACD between 01 January 2009 and 31 December 2018 using the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision, Australian Modification (ICD‐10‐AM) codes were identified. The ICD‐10‐AM codes were C91.1/C83.0 and C88.0 and the ICD‐O‐3.2 histology codes 9823 and 9761 for CLL/SLL and WM, respectively. Due to ACD's data collection methodology, late registration, people with sex recorded as intersex/non‐binary/other, and people whose usual residence at diagnosis was in other territories (Christmas Island, Cocos [Keeling] Islands, Jervis Bay and Norfolk Island) were not included in the dataset. The NSW Cancer Registry granted external ethics approval to conduct this study (ID 2022/ ETH01850 ). In addition, an ethics exemption for this study was approved by the Deakin University Human Ethics Research Committee (DUHERC 2022‐091). 2.4 Outcome Measures Adapting methodologies used in the AIHW reports and previous studies, the incidence rate and prevalence of CLL/SLL and WM were calculated based on the incidence‐based data and the specific Australian mid‐year population size for incidence rate and end‐of‐year population size for prevalence [ ]. The incidence rate and prevalence were expressed in a format meeting ethics requirements (i.e., 10,000,000 [or 10 7 ] person‐years). Subgroup analysis by age group and sex was undertaken when appropriate. The incidence rate trend for the next 30 years was predicted using the coefficient calculated from least‐squares linear regression [ ]. Due to the absence of a cross‐sectional study reporting the point prevalence of CLL/SLL and WM, the 10‐year observed trend of prevalence was examined. 2.5 Statistical Analysis The unit record de‐identified data, aggregated by age group and survival rounded to the nearest multiple of five, were imported into MS Excel, Stata SE17 software (StataCorp., College Station, TX, USA) and Joinpoint Trend Analysis software vs. 5.3.0 [ ] for data cleaning and analysis. Descriptive analyses were performed for the demographic characteristics of the identified cohort. The χ 2 test was used to compare the differences in characteristics by subgroup. A significance level of 0.05 was set as statistically significant. Incidence was defined as the number of new patients registered in the ACD during a given year. 10 years prevalence refers to the total number of patients with the disease who are still alive at the end of the follow‐up period (i.e., 2018). Mortality refers to patients who died due to any cause during the study period while survival is the percentage of patients with cancer who are alive for a specified amount of time post‐diagnosis [ ]. The details of the annual mortality calculation and the calculation algorithm is presented in Table . Given the median survival time of 12.30–13.30 years for patients with CLL/SLL in the literature [ , ], and the absence of mortality cases among patients diagnosed in previous years (i.e., mortality of patients diagnosed 10–15 years ago in this data set), we did not calculate the annual mortality rate or predict the mortality trend for the observed period. Finally, we calculated the male‐to‐female ratios for incidence rate and prevalence. We estimated the annual age‐standardised (ASD) incidence rate and age‐standardised prevalence by sex using the direct age standardisation approach that employed the population distribution derived from the ABS provided 2001 Australian standard population [ ]. The annual prevalence proportion by specific age group, which represents the disease prevalence within a specific age group of the total population, was calculated by using age‐specific disease cases as the numerator and the person‐years at risk within the age interval as the denominator [ ]. Due to the lack of prevalence data in Australia for both CLL/SLL and WM, we employed DisMod II [ ], a popular method used in studying disease burden when the dataset is absent or incomplete. This approach allowed for estimation of the proxy prevalence proportions by sex and specific age group for a specific year (i.e., 2009). Age‐standardised prevalence was calculated using the prevalence proportions by sex and specific age group. A 10‐year prevalence was also calculated using the identified 10 years incidence and corresponding mortality cases. A cross‐sectional analysis approach was adopted, capturing a snapshot of incidence and mortality for a particular year.

This approach allowed for estimation of the proxy prevalence proportions by sex and specific age group for a specific year (i.e., 2009). Age‐standardised prevalence was calculated using the prevalence proportions by sex and specific age group. A 10‐year prevalence was also calculated using the identified 10 years incidence and corresponding mortality cases. A cross‐sectional analysis approach was adopted, capturing a snapshot of incidence and mortality for a particular year. The employed formulae are outlined in the section. Mid‐year population sizes served as the denominator for calculating incidence rates and prevalence proportions by sex and age group. For the calculation of the 10‐year prevalence, end‐of‐year population data were utilised for the year 2018. Specific population figures by sex and age group were derived to calculate the respective incidence rate and prevalence proportion by sex and age group. The mid‐year and end‐of‐year population sizes were extracted from the Australian Bureau of Statistics [ ]. The censoring date was 31 December 2018 in the current dataset. Survival time was defined as the number of days between the diagnosis date and the exit date. Time to death was determined according to the death event documented in the National Death Index. Survival time in days was divided by 365.25 to convert to years. A least‐squares linear regression was used to capture the time trend of best fit through the 2009–2018 incidence rate and prevalence. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. This is the approach used by the AIHW for short‐term incidence prediction [ ]. Plots of actual incidence rate, age‐standardised incidence rate, age‐standardised prevalence and prevalence proportion for a specific age group over the data duration showed a linear relationship; therefore, the 10‐years age group was included in the model as a categorical variable. The following regression equation was used for the linear prediction of incidence rates for the next 30 years: Y = β 0 + β 1 T with β 0 denoting the intercept, β 1 denoting the coefficients and T denoting time (continuous variables) [ ]. Assessment of the coefficient of determination ( R 2 , R squared), a measure to assess the error of the fitted regression model in predicting outcomes, was also estimated. Joinpoint regression limited to a maximum of one joinpoint comprised of two segments model due to the dataset containing only 10 data points [ ] was also conducted to provide additional assessment, addressing uncertainty in projecting future incidence trends (i.e., capturing the decline in rate). The result of the joinpoint linear regression is included in the Data , along with its final selected model (by using BIC criteria that defaulted in the software [ ]) and the associated projections. Since the dataset contained disease‐related events (e.g., censored status, the death case was identified using time‐to‐event method), Kaplan–Meier (KM) survival curves for overall survival were constructed with a maximum follow‐up of 10 years (since 2009) to estimate overall survival and the associated mortality indicator. A log‐rank test was used to test the difference between subgroups. Relevant commands such as ‘stphplot’ ‘stphtest’ and ‘ estat phtest ’ were used to test the proportionality assumption using Schoenfeld and scaled Schoenfeld residual and the log–log plots during model building and at post estimation [ ]. We performed log–log plots for categorical variables (i.e., age group, sex), and Schoenfeld residual plots for all variables. A p ‐value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Additionally, time‐to‐event analyses were conducted to generate KM curves for each sex, age group and year diagnosed. A Cox proportional hazard model was used to calculate the hazard ratio (HR) for the differences in hazard rate between sex, age group and year of diagnosis. Multivariable analysis stratified by sex and/or age group and interaction terms such as time and the year of diagnosis was employed where appropriate. 3 Results A total of 9002 patients with CLL/SLL and 707 patients with WM were identified in the four cancer registry databases. The populations were predominantly male (CLL/SLL, range 61.04%–64.91%; WM, range 53.85%–70.37%). In total, 2277 patients with CLL/SLL and 192 patients with WM had died by the end of 2018. The most apparent cause of death was not cancer‐related (CLL/SLL, 38.78%; WM, 47.92%), followed by primary cancer (CLL/SLL, 33.64%; WM, 33.33%) and secondary cancer (CLL/SLL, 27.58%; WM, 18.75%) (Table ). 3.1 Incidence Rate and 30‐Year Incidence Trend 3.1.1 CLL/SLL The annual CLL/SLL incidence rate ranged from 659.10–1029.86 (crude) and 600.05–887.92 (ASD) cases per 10 7 person‐years in 2009–2017. The rate slightly decreased in 2018 to 894.20 (crude) and 761.01 (ASD) per 10 7 person‐years (Table ). Incidence rates by sex had a similar temporal trend, but males had

and 192 patients with WM had died by the end of 2018. The most apparent cause of death was not cancer‐related (CLL/SLL, 38.78%; WM, 47.92%), followed by primary cancer (CLL/SLL, 33.64%; WM, 33.33%) and secondary cancer (CLL/SLL, 27.58%; WM, 18.75%) (Table ). 3.1 Incidence Rate and 30‐Year Incidence Trend 3.1.1 CLL/SLL The annual CLL/SLL incidence rate ranged from 659.10–1029.86 (crude) and 600.05–887.92 (ASD) cases per 10 7 person‐years in 2009–2017. The rate slightly decreased in 2018 to 894.20 (crude) and 761.01 (ASD) per 10 7 person‐years (Table ). Incidence rates by sex had a similar temporal trend, but males had a slightly higher annual incidence rate than females (incidence rate ratio, males vs. females, 1.60–1.88). The incidence rate was lowest in the under 40–49 age group and higher in the ≥ 80 age group (Table ). Linear regression analysis suggested that the total CLL/SLL ASD incidence rate is predicted to increase over the next 30 years (Figure ). A coefficient of 30.29 ( p = 0.013), 22.75 ( p = 0.047) and 26.98 ( p = 0.023) was detected for males, females, and all patients with CLL/SLL, respectively, using the 10‐year data (Table ). Joinpoint regression analysis using one segment model showed an average annual percentage change (AAPC) of 3.56%, 4.39% and 3.91% for males, females and total CLL/SLL patients. The magnitude of the change was comparable between linear regression and joinpoint regression results. Although a non‐statistically significant decreased trend between 2009 and 2014 was seen in the joinpoint model with two segments, this model was not selected due to its higher weighted BIC (Table ; Figure ). Using linear regression results, the annual ASD incidence rate was predicted to reach 1351.90 cases per 10 7 person‐years in 2038 (Table ; Figure ). 3.1.2 WM For WM, results showed a stable overall incidence rate between 2009 and 2015, followed by an increasing trend between 2016 and 2018 (Table ; Figure ). While the incidence rate in females fluctuated between 2009 and 2015, the rate increased in 2016 and was highest in 2018 (ASD: 62.80, Crude: 70.28 cases per 10 7 person‐years). Meanwhile, the rate in males was stable between 2009 and 2016 and increased sharply between 2017 and 2018. The incidence rate ratio of WM (males vs. females) ranged from 1.22 to 2.41 for the observed period. The linear regression model predicted a statistically significant ascending trend for the WM ASD‐incidence rate during the 10‐year period (males: coefficient 3.59, p = 0.023; females: 2.66, p = 0.050; total: 3.20, p = 0.009) (Table ; Figure ). Joinpoint regression estimated the AAPC of 4.52%, 3.96% and 4.39% for males, females and total WM with non‐statistically significant evidence to support the decrement between 2009 and 2015 (Table ; Figure ). Similar to CLL/SLL, the past trend was comparable between linear regression results and joinpoint regression results; thus, the ASD incidence rate of WM will reach 130.83 cases per 10 7 person‐years in 2038 (Table ; Figure ). 3.2 Prevalence Rates and the Observed Trend 3.2.1 CLL/SLL For the observed period of 2009–2018, the CLL/SLL 10 years prevalence was 5380.08 per 10 7 persons at the end of 2018. The prevalence was higher in males than in females, with a prevalence ratio of 1.70. During the 10 year observed period, the increasing trend in the prevalence for males vs. females was also determined by linear regression analysis (males, prevalence proportion: coefficient 88.02, p < 0.001 and males, ASD prevalence: 41.92, p = 0.010; females, prevalence proportion: 44.27, p < 0.001 and females, ASD prevalence: 27.50, p = 0.053) (Tables and ). 3.2.2 WM A point prevalence of 412.07 per 10 7 persons was estimated for patients with WM at the end of the observed period (2009–2018). Similar to CLL/SLL, the prevalence was higher in males than in females (ratio, 1.51). Linear regression suggested a coefficient of 10.29 ( p = 0.016) and 4.85 ( p = 0.020) for males by age group specific and by ASD prevalence respectively and a coefficient of 4.03 ( p = 0.106) and 3.52 ( p = 0.055) for females by age group specific and by ASD prevalence respectively, suggesting an increasing trend in the age‐standardised prevalence proportion by sex and age group over 10 years (Tables and ). 3.3 Survival Estimates and Mortality Indicator Due to insufficient follow‐up in the data (median overall survival time was not estimable in the survival analysis) and the median survival time of CLL/SLL being 13.15–13.30 years in the literature [ , ], the annual incidence‐based mortality rate was not calculated. 3.3.1 CLL/SLL The KM analysis estimated that approximately 53% of patients with CLL/SLL were still alive at the end of the 10‐year analysis period (2009–2018), indicating a cumulative mortality rate of 47%. Females had a slightly better survival rate (Figure );
