documents.title: ESMO recommendations use circulating tumor DNA assays

chunks.content: Main Osimertinib is a third-generation, central nervous system (CNS)-active epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)–tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) (EGFR-TKI), with demonstrated efficacy in early and advanced-stage EGFR -mutated (EGFRm) (exon 19 deletion (Ex19del)/L858R) non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) – . Adjuvant osimertinib for a duration of 3 years is recommended for resected EGFRm stage IB–IIIA NSCLC, based on results from the phase 3 ADAURA trial – . In the ADAURA primary analysis, adjuvant osimertinib demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in DFS versus placebo in patients following complete surgical resection of stage IB–IIIA EGFRm NSCLC, with or without previous chemotherapy . DFS benefit was sustained in an updated analysis with a further 2-year follow-up , which translated to a significant improvement in overall survival (OS), with a 5-year OS rate of 88% in the osimertinib group compared with 78% in the placebo group, and an overall hazard ratio (HR) for death of 0.49 (95.03% confidence interval (CI) 0.34–0.70; P < 0.001) . A trend toward an increased DFS event rate was observed after completion of 3 years of osimertinib treatment , suggesting that some patients may benefit from a longer treatment duration with the opportunity to further improve outcomes. However, determining which patients would benefit from a longer treatment duration remains unknown. The standard surveillance paradigm following curative intent therapies includes serial radiographic imaging; however, this detects only macroscopic disease, is confounded by changes in normal tissue after treatment and the optimal scan frequency for surveillance is uncertain – . Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can be detected in liquid biopsies (for example, plasma), providing a minimally invasive diagnostic tool to assess tumor burden and genomic alterations . MRD—the detection of ctDNA after treatment with curative intent—could be a biomarker for early disease recurrence, with the potential to inform treatment and prognosis . Due to low tumor burden, and a concomitant low fraction of ctDNA in patients with early-stage disease, robust detection of ctDNA can be challenging. However, recent advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS) approaches have improved the limit of detection for ctDNA and increased the feasibility of successfully building bespoke tumor-informed MRD assays and applying them in this setting – . A successful technological strategy, generally referred to as tumor-informed MRD testing, leverages the genomic profile from the patient’s tumor to track an individualized set of tumor-specific alterations longitudinally in plasma ctDNA samples , – . Several studies in patients with early-stage NSCLC who have undergone curative intent treatment support the use of tumor-informed MRD assays to predict radiographic clinical recurrence – . Studies in patients with stage I–III NSCLC, such as a prospective study in 261 patients and the LUCID study in 88 patients , showed that MRD detection preceded radiographic progression by a median of 3.4 months and 212.5 days (approximately 7 months), respectively. In a retrospective analysis to track previously identified tumor mutations in posttreatment (radiotherapy, chemotherapy and/or surgery) plasma from 40 patients with stage I–III NSCLC, ctDNA detection preceded radiographic progression in 72% patients by a median 5.2 months . Although studies are limited, these data suggest the potential utility of tumor-informed MRD assays to monitor MRD in early-stage NSCLC. We performed an exploratory analysis to investigate whether plasma-based, tumor-informed MRD analysis could predict disease recurrence during and after adjuvant treatment, in a patient cohort ( n = 220) from ADAURA. We then investigated whether genomic alterations detected in patient tumors before treatment correlate with molecular and clinical outcomes. Here we report a long-term longitudinal MRD analysis from a phase 3 randomized clinical trial in patients with resected EGFRm NSCLC. Results Patient characteristics We performed a retrospective, post hoc exploratory analysis, independent of the statistical analysis plan of the ADAURA study , to investigate whether plasma-based, tumor-informed MRD analysis could predict disease recurrence during and after adjuvant treatment in a patient subset ( n = 220) from the phase 3 trial. Study design details have been published previously , , . Briefly, following complete surgical resection of primary NSCLC, patients received adjuvant chemotherapy (if determined necessary, per physician and patient choice) for up to four cycles. Patients were then randomized 1:1 to receive osimertinib (80 mg once daily (QD)) or placebo for a planned treatment duration of up to 36 months. Plasma samples were collected from day 1 of randomization, and longitudinally during the adjuvant and posttreatment follow-up periods. Baseline computed tomography (CT) scans were performed within 28 days before first dose. Subsequent assessments were performed during the adjuvant treatment and posttreatment follow-up periods (Fig. ). Of 682 patients randomized in ADAURA, 239 (35%) had available matched tumor, germline DNA and plasma samples for development and testing of tumor-specific RaDaR panels at the time of data cut-off (DCO) (Fig. ). Genomic DNA (gDNA) was unavailable for 397 patients due to patients declining germline testing, withdrawing consent

of up to 36 months. Plasma samples were collected from day 1 of randomization, and longitudinally during the adjuvant and posttreatment follow-up periods. Baseline computed tomography (CT) scans were performed within 28 days before first dose. Subsequent assessments were performed during the adjuvant treatment and posttreatment follow-up periods (Fig. ). Of 682 patients randomized in ADAURA, 239 (35%) had available matched tumor, germline DNA and plasma samples for development and testing of tumor-specific RaDaR panels at the time of data cut-off (DCO) (Fig. ). Genomic DNA (gDNA) was unavailable for 397 patients due to patients declining germline testing, withdrawing consent or local restrictions preventing sample collection and tumor tissue was unavailable for 46 patients due to insufficient tissue slides or repatriation. Subsequently, RaDaR panels were successfully designed and validated for 220 (92%) of the 239 patients across both the osimertinib ( n = 112) and placebo ( n = 108) groups and comprised the MRD analysis set. For the remaining 19 patients, whole-exome sequencing (WES) failed for seven patients because of poor DNA yield and/or quality or low sequencing depth, MRD panel design failed for 12 patients because of insufficient tumor-informed mutations detected during WES. An average (range) of 30 (9–47), 32 (8–48) and 32 (9–48) tumor-specific gene variants were included in the panels for patients with stage IB, stage II and stage IIIA disease, respectively (Extended Data Table ). Demographics, disease characteristics and outcomes were generally similar between patients in the MRD analysis set ( n = 220) and overall ADAURA population ( N = 682; Extended Data Table ). However, in the MRD analysis set there were fewer patients with stage IB NSCLC (21%, 47 of 220) compared with the overall ADAURA population (32%, 216 of 682) because of insufficient tumor tissue available to meet the MRD panel requirements. There was also a lower representation of Asian patients in the MRD analysis set (45%, 98 of 220) compared with the overall ADAURA population (64%, 434 of 682) because of local restrictions on the export of human biological material. In the MRD analysis set, the DFS HR was 0.19 (95% CI, 0.12–0.29) and OS HR was 0.42 (95% CI, 0.24–0.74); in the overall ADAURA population, the DFS HR was 0.27 (95% CI, 0.21–0.34) and OS HR was 0.49 (95.03% CI, 0.34–0.70) for osimertinib versus placebo (DCOs were 11 April 2022 and 27 January 2023 for DFS and OS, respectively). MRD status at randomization and MRD clearance RaDaR panels were used to analyze the MRD status of longitudinal samples at randomization and throughout the adjuvant and posttreatment follow-up periods. MRD was considered ‘detected’ at any timepoint when ctDNA was detected for one or more mutations in a patient’s tumor-specific RaDaR panel. Overall, 8% (18 of 220) of patients across both groups had MRD detected at randomization before study treatment (4% (5 of 112) receiving osimertinib compared with 12% (13 of 108) receiving placebo; Fig. ). Of the 18 patients with detected MRD at randomization, none had stage IB, 39% (7 of 18) had stage II, and 61% (11 of 18) had stage IIIA disease (Extended Data Table ). Within the MRD analysis set, 60% (54 of 90) of patients with stage II and 77% (64 of 83) with stage IIIA disease received adjuvant chemotherapy (Fig. ). Among patients with stage II disease, MRD was detected at randomization in fewer patients who received previous chemotherapy, versus those who did not (1% (1 of 90) versus 7% (6 of 90), respectively). In patients with stage IIIA disease, MRD was detected at randomization at similar rates in patients who received previous chemotherapy versus those who did not (8% (7 of 83) versus 5% (4 of 83)), respectively. Although the number of patients with MRD detected at randomization was small, it seemed to be associated with poor outcomes for both the osimertinib and placebo groups, with 17 of 18 patients experiencing a DFS event. The five patients with detected MRD at randomization in the osimertinib group generally had longer DFS compared with the 13 patients in the placebo group (Fig. ). Of the five patients with detected MRD in the osimertinib group, four had recurrence events. Three events were local and/or regional and one was a distant event; two occurred during adjuvant treatment and two after treatment. All 13 patients with MRD detected at randomization in the placebo group had recurrence events (local and/or regional n = 7, distant n = 5, death n = 1). MRD was considered ‘cleared’ if, following the detection of MRD at randomization, subsequent samples within the next two timepoints (24 weeks from randomization) were determined to be MRD undetected. Four of the five patients in the osimertinib group with MRD detected at randomization cleared MRD; the remaining patient did not have samples available for analysis until week 60

was a distant event; two occurred during adjuvant treatment and two after treatment. All 13 patients with MRD detected at randomization in the placebo group had recurrence events (local and/or regional n = 7, distant n = 5, death n = 1). MRD was considered ‘cleared’ if, following the detection of MRD at randomization, subsequent samples within the next two timepoints (24 weeks from randomization) were determined to be MRD undetected. Four of the five patients in the osimertinib group with MRD detected at randomization cleared MRD; the remaining patient did not have samples available for analysis until week 60 of treatment (Fig. ). Of the four patients who cleared MRD detected at randomization, three had undetected MRD until the postadjuvant period after stopping osimertinib (Fig. ) and one had a re-emergence of detected MRD before the end of the planned treatment period (36 months) coinciding with a treatment interruption followed by dose reduction. Of the 13 patients with MRD detected at randomization in the placebo group, none had clearance during treatment or follow-up (Fig. ). Longitudinal MRD analysis of plasma samples MRD events were detected in 31% (68 of 220) of patients across both groups during the analysis period (randomization, on treatment and posttreatment follow-up; Fig. ). In the osimertinib group, 87% (97 of 112) of patients were MRD-free throughout the study compared with 51% (55 of 108) in the placebo group. Of patients with undetected MRD at randomization (osimertinib, 96% (107 of 112); placebo, 88% (95 of 108)), MRD-free status was maintained during the on-treatment and posttreatment follow-up periods in 91% (97 of 107) of patients in the osimertinib group compared with 58% (55 of 95) in the placebo group. Among the 15 patients in the osimertinib group with MRD events, most events occurred after stopping or completing treatment (67%, 10 of 15). Prediction of DFS events with ctDNA-based tumor-informed MRD We evaluated the performance of the RaDaR assay to predict disease recurrence by comparing the occurrence of postrandomization MRD events (molecular recurrence) with DFS events (clinical recurrence or death, whichever occurred first) during the on-treatment and posttreatment follow-up periods. MRD detection using RaDaR had a 65% (95% CI, 55–74) positive percent agreement (PPA; clinical sensitivity) with DFS events and a 95% (95% CI, 91–99) negative percent agreement (NPA; clinical specificity) with DFS-censored patients across groups (Extended Data Table ). The positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV) for MRD were 91% (95% CI, 84–98) and 78% (95% CI, 71–84), respectively. Among the patients who had a DFS event, there were no differences in prevalence of EGFR mutation subtype, race or smoking status according to the MRD status of detected versus not detected (Extended Data Table ). However, numerically, there were more patients with stage IIIA disease, more patients treated with placebo and fewer patients with local and/or regional recurrence or CNS-only recurrence with detected MRD versus not detected (58% (36 of 62) versus 44% (15 of 34); 82% (51 of 62) versus 62% (21 of 34); 50% (29 of 58) versus 74% (23 of 31), respectively). To determine whether longitudinal MRD monitoring could predict a DFS event, a lead-time analysis was performed for the 62 patients across both treatment groups with both a postrandomization DFS event and any detected MRD positive sample through the whole study period. Across both groups, MRD preceded a DFS event by a median of 4.7 (95% CI, 2.2–5.6) months (Fig. ). In addition to tumor-specific mutations, EGFR mutations (Ex19del and L858R) were also included in each RaDaR panel to allow for longitudinal monitoring and correlations with both MRD and DFS events (Extended Data Fig. ). From an analysis set of 206 patients, EGFR mutation detection had 54% PPA and 42% PPA for DFS events and MRD detection, respectively, and a 92% NPA and 100% NPA for DFS-censored patients and MRD-not detected samples, respectively, across groups (Extended Data Table ). Of the 40 patients with detected MRD, detected EGFR mutations and a DFS event, 19 patients had detected MRD ahead of detected EGFR mutations and 19 had detected MRD at the same time as detected EGFR mutations (Extended Data Fig. ). Only two patients had detected EGFR mutations ahead of detected MRD. Detected EGFR mutations preceded a DFS event by a median of 1.0 month (95% CI, 0.0–5.2) across groups but did not precede MRD detection in most patients (lead time of 0.0 months (95% CI, 2.9–0.0 months)). Effect of osimertinib on MRD and clinical disease recurrence To further understand the benefit of osimertinib with respect to molecular or clinical disease recurrence, the combined endpoint of DFS (clinical recurrence or death) or MRD events was assessed from randomization to postrandomization MRD detection, disease recurrence or death (whichever occurred first). Median follow-up time from randomization was 44.2 months (95% CI, 42.4–49.1) and

MRD. Detected EGFR mutations preceded a DFS event by a median of 1.0 month (95% CI, 0.0–5.2) across groups but did not precede MRD detection in most patients (lead time of 0.0 months (95% CI, 2.9–0.0 months)). Effect of osimertinib on MRD and clinical disease recurrence To further understand the benefit of osimertinib with respect to molecular or clinical disease recurrence, the combined endpoint of DFS (clinical recurrence or death) or MRD events was assessed from randomization to postrandomization MRD detection, disease recurrence or death (whichever occurred first). Median follow-up time from randomization was 44.2 months (95% CI, 42.4–49.1) and 19.1 months (95% CI, 11.1–28.3) in the osimertinib and placebo groups, respectively (Fig. ). The DFS and MRD event-free rate at 36 months on treatment was 86% (95% CI, 78–92) versus 36% (95% CI, 27–45) with an overall HR of 0.23 (95% CI, 0.15–0.36) for osimertinib versus placebo. DFS or MRD events were detected at any time postrandomization in 25% (28 of 112) of patients in the osimertinib group compared with 69% (74 of 108) in the placebo group (Fig. ). In the osimertinib group, most (68%, 19 of 28) DFS or MRD events occurred after treatment discontinuation or completion and, of these, 58% (11 of 19) occurred within 12 months of treatment discontinuation or completion. DFS or MRD events, whichever occurred first, were also assessed after patients discontinued or completed osimertinib treatment. In this analysis, there were 28 DFS or MRD events. Patients who experienced a DFS or MRD event ( n = 9) or were censored ( n = 9) before discontinuing osimertinib treatment were included in this analysis to avoid the introduction of survivor bias and had their time to DFS or MRD event in the treatment-free period set to day 1. Median follow-up time after osimertinib discontinuation was 11.7 months (95% CI, 8.3–13.9; Table ). The DFS and MRD event-free rate at 12 and 24 months after osimertinib treatment was 80% (95% CI, 71–87) and 66% (95% CI, 53–77), respectively. Genomic analysis at baseline To determine whether baseline genomic alterations correlated with molecular and clinical outcomes, the baseline tumor WES data used for MRD panel design ( n = 220) were reanalyzed for known oncogenic driver alterations occurring in >1% of samples and compared with MRD and DFS events. Baseline tumor samples were obtained from surgery before use of chemotherapy. Excluding Ex19del and L858R EGFR mutations, TP53 mutations had the highest prevalence, at 45% in the MRD analysis set (Fig. ). The frequencies of other co-occurring alterations associated with cell signaling, cell cycle progression and DNA damage repair were low (<7%). Across both treatment groups, TP53 mutations occurred more frequently in the following: patients with detected MRD at randomization (MRD detected, 72% (13 of 18) versus not detected, 42% (85 of 202)); more advanced disease stage (stage IB, 28% (13 of 47) versus stage II, 46% (41 of 90) versus stage III, 53% (44 of 83)); and receipt of postsurgical adjuvant chemotherapy (yes, 55% (70 of 128) versus no, 30% (28 of 92), Fig. ). However, the benefit of adjuvant osimertinib versus placebo was similar irrespective of TP53 status ( TP53 altered: HR, 0.28 (95% CI, 0.15–0.51); TP53 wild type: HR, 0.17 (95% CI, 0.08–0.34)), seeming to represent a negative prognostic patient subgroup across both groups (Fig. ). Further, a multivariable analysis adjusting for TP53 , disease stage and previous chemotherapy fitted separately for each treatment group, showed that patients with TP53 alterations had a higher risk of DFS or MRD events versus patients with wild-type TP53 (osimertinib: HR, 2.28 (95% CI, 0.96–5.64); placebo: HR, 1.33 (5% CI, 0.82–2.17); Extended Data Fig. ). Discussion The detection of MRD by assaying tumor-derived mutations in ctDNA offers a sensitive tool to identify the risk of disease recurrence after curative intent treatment ahead of radiological evaluation in resected EGFRm NSCLC. If validated for clinical practice, systematic use of MRD monitoring has the potential to personalize postadjuvant patient care and improve outcomes by identifying high-risk patients who could benefit from restarting or intensifying treatment. In the future, with further sensitivity improvements, longitudinal MRD monitoring could also identify patients with low risk of recurrence after adjuvant therapy, potentially sparing them from further treatment and any associated drug toxicities. Therefore, understanding the predictive role and clinical utility of MRD detection is crucial to further improve outcomes for patients undergoing treatment for early and locally advanced NSCLC. As expected, the frequency of MRD detection at randomization was greater among subgroups with more advanced disease: stage IB 0%, stage II 39%, stage III 61%. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of performing an exploratory longitudinal ctDNA-based, tumor-informed MRD analysis in a cohort of patients with resected EGFRm NSCLC from ADAURA. As expected, the frequency of MRD detection at randomization was greater among subgroups with more advanced disease: stage IB 0%, stage II 39%, stage III 61%. Using RaDaR plasma ctDNA-based, tumor-informed MRD panels, we discovered that, for most patients, molecular recurrence based on detected MRD events, preceded clinical recurrence or death, with a median lead time of 4.7 months across both groups in this study. We note that this lead time is potentially related to the specific plasma collection and scan schedule employed in this study. Our results support previous studies showing MRD as a predictor of recurrence in patients with early-stage NSCLC following treatment with curative intent – . In ADAURA, a DFS and MRD event-free status was maintained for most (75%, 84 of 112) patients during adjuvant osimertinib treatment and posttreatment follow-up. Most DFS or MRD events occurred after osimertinib treatment discontinuation or completion (68%, 19 of 28) and within 12 months after osimertinib (58%, 11 of 19). Furthermore, the DFS and MRD event-free rate was high (66%) 24 months after completion or discontinuation of osimertinib treatment; this suggests that osimertinib can reduce or eradicate the micrometastatic component of the disease in some patients, leading to long-term benefit that persists after completion of adjuvant therapy. Longer follow-up is required to adequately assess this hypothesis. We can also hypothesize that, in the ADAURA setting, a subset of patients at risk of recurrence posttreatment completion may benefit from adjuvant treatment beyond 36 months or from treatment intensification via combination strategies. MRD monitoring may provide a powerful tool to personalize the use of postadjuvant treatment, although this requires prospective studies to fully elucidate the risk–benefit of such an approach. In this analysis, only a small proportion (8%) of patients had detected MRD at randomization and this is consistent with a previous study in nonbiomarker-selected patients with early-stage NSCLC . Although patients with detected MRD at randomization are likely to represent a high-risk subset with a poor prognosis, those who received adjuvant osimertinib had a greater rate of MRD clearance and a longer DFS compared with patients who received placebo. The large clinical benefit of adjuvant osimertinib demonstrated in ADAURA, combined with the relatively low rate of MRD detected at randomization samples and frequent occurrence (49%) of MRD in the placebo group, suggest that adjuvant osimertinib should not be limited to patients with detected MRD postoperatively. Additionally, an MRD event-free status was maintained for most patients during osimertinib treatment (87%, 97 of 112), with most MRD events occurring after stopping or completing treatment (67%, 10 of 15). Continued monitoring for detected MRD in the postadjuvant treatment follow-up period may identify a high-risk subset of patients who may benefit from further treatment. Although current MRD technologies are not sensitive enough to determine which patients with EGFRm NSCLC are disease-free postsurgery, continued undetected MRD status may represent a population for whom disease has been eradicated and no further treatment is necessary. Previous studies in patients with resected NSCLC have focused on nonbiomarker-selected patient populations and shown a range of clinical sensitivity and specificity for longitudinal ctDNA detection to recurrence , . The performance of MRD testing in resected EGFRm NSCLC, where tumor mutational burden has been reported to be low , is unknown. Assay sensitivity (65%) and specificity (95%) was similar in the ADAURA trial to the previous LUCID study where RaDaR was also used. However, sensitivity and specificity of MRD assays can differ depending on the assay type, trial design and study population , , , and we anticipate that other MRD assays should yield similar findings. The early clearance of EGFR mutations detected in plasma by droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) has been shown in the advanced setting to correlate with improved outcomes following treatment . The use of droplet digital PCR to detect EGFR mutations could offer a less time-consuming and more cost-effective approach to monitor MRD than the use of tumor-informed panels in late-stage disease. In advanced EGFRm NSCLC, panel-based NGS has been shown to have comparable sensitivity to droplet digital PCR for detection of plasma EGFR Ex19del and L858R mutations . Thus, we customized the RaDaR panels to include EGFR mutations (Ex19del and L858R) to investigate whether detection of these mutations could identify early disease recurrence ahead of MRD detection. more cost-effective approach to monitor MRD than the use of tumor-informed panels in late-stage disease. In advanced EGFRm NSCLC, panel-based NGS has been shown to have comparable sensitivity to droplet digital PCR for detection of plasma EGFR Ex19del and L858R mutations . Thus, we customized the RaDaR panels to include EGFR mutations (Ex19del and L858R) to investigate whether detection of these mutations could identify early disease recurrence ahead of MRD detection. Whereas the detection of EGFR mutations could predict DFS events, EGFR mutation detection had a lower sensitivity and shorter median lead time than tumor-informed panel-based MRD. Among the 40 patients with both detected MRD and EGFR mutations, only two had detected EGFR mutations ahead of detected MRD. Although there will be a trade-off between assay performance and feasibility or cost implications in the real world, these findings reinforce the value of MRD detection using multiple tumor-informed gene variants in the context of resected EGFRm stage IB–IIIA NSCLC. We used the combined MRD or DFS endpoint to assess whether patients with putative de novo EGFR-TKI resistance mutations have worse molecular and clinical outcomes. WES of baseline tumor samples (samples obtained from surgery before use of chemotherapy if given) from patients in the MRD analysis set showed that TP53 mutations were the most common (45%) baseline genetic alteration concomitant with EGFR mutations. Adjuvant osimertinib provided clear benefit with or without co-occurring TP53 alterations. After adjusting for the potentially confounding factors of disease stage and postsurgical chemotherapy in a multivariable analysis, baseline TP53 alterations had a greater association with DFS or MRD events versus patients with wild-type TP53 across both groups. Our data suggest that baseline TP53 mutations may be prognostic within the resected EGFRm NSCLC setting. There is a lack of published data examining the prognostic and predictive value of EGFR/TP53 comutations in patients with resected EGFRm NSCLC, and in the advanced setting the clinical importance of these comutations is unclear . In advanced NSCLC, whereas some studies suggest that patients who harbor EGFR / TP53 comutations have a low response rate and poor prognosis to EGFR-TKI therapy , , others have been unable to demonstrate this – . Recently, patients with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR/TP53 comutations were shown to be more likely to have mixed intrapatient tumor responses (responding and progressing lesions within one patient) to EGFR-TKIs compared with those with an EGFR mutation alone . Further analyses in larger cohorts of patients with early-stage EGFRm NSCLC are warranted to better understand the correlation between TP53 mutations and adjuvant chemotherapy and disease stage, and the prognostic value of TP53 mutations. The baseline rates for putative de novo EGFR-TKI resistance mutations, other than TP53 , were generally low. Key limitations of the MRD analysis were that only a subset of patients from ADAURA were assessed for MRD due to restrictions on sample availability, and the limited clinical sensitivity (65%) of the tissue-informed RaDaR MRD panels. However, there were few technical failures (9%), and the assay successfully detected MRD ahead of DFS for most patients where samples were available. Additionally, scan and plasma sampling schedules differed throughout the study, and scans were also performed less frequently than plasma sampling. The ability to predict disease recurrence using MRD should further improve as more advanced technologies with greater sensitivity are developed. Although MRD monitoring may offer a highly sensitive tool with a lead time between the detection of MRD events and clinical recurrence or death, MRD monitoring may not be amenable to all clinical situations. This is owing to the requirement for sufficient pretreatment primary tumor sample and the time required to build a validated tumor-informed MRD assay. However, given that the ADAURA regimen involves adjuvant osimertinib treatment for up to 36 months, this time provides a sufficient window to develop a robust patient-specific MRD assay for postadjuvant MRD monitoring. The postadjuvant treatment setting therefore represents a clinical scenario where prospective testing would be feasible to validate for future clinical practice. This MRD analysis represents one of the largest patient samples so far analyzed in early-stage resected EGFRm NSCLC, with MRD measured longitudinally across a 3-year adjuvant and posttreatment follow-up period. Unanswered questions and important considerations for future analyses include: whether MRD analyses can be used to determine the optimal duration of adjuvant treatment; what the optimal frequency of MRD sampling is following adjuvant treatment completion; and how MRD detection can inform clinical intervention, including restarting adjuvant treatment or intensifying treatment via combination strategies for patients at high risk of recurrence. Similarly, de-escalation of treatments in lower-risk patients would be important, although our data have not identified any specific factors. Some of these questions should be addressed in the future analyses of the phase 2 TARGET ( NCT05526755 ) trial, a single-arm study of 5 years of adjuvant osimertinib in patients with completely

can be used to determine the optimal duration of adjuvant treatment; what the optimal frequency of MRD sampling is following adjuvant treatment completion; and how MRD detection can inform clinical intervention, including restarting adjuvant treatment or intensifying treatment via combination strategies for patients at high risk of recurrence. Similarly, de-escalation of treatments in lower-risk patients would be important, although our data have not identified any specific factors. Some of these questions should be addressed in the future analyses of the phase 2 TARGET ( NCT05526755 ) trial, a single-arm study of 5 years of adjuvant osimertinib in patients with completely resected EGFRm stage II–IIIB NSCLC . In conclusion, this exploratory analysis of patients from the ADAURA trial suggests that plasma-based, tumor-informed MRD analysis may predict disease recurrence during adjuvant treatment and during posttreatment follow-up. We also show that a DFS and MRD event-free status was maintained for most patients during adjuvant osimertinib treatment and over 24 months posttreatment. These observations suggest that MRD monitoring may inform clinical intervention, including restarting or intensifying treatment. Prospective studies to understand the optimal frequency of MRD monitoring following adjuvant treatment completion and the appropriate clinical interventions following MRD detection are warranted before this can be applied routinely to the real-world clinical setting. Methods Inclusion and ethics The ADAURA protocol and amendments were approved by the relevant ethics committees. The trial was conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Declaration of Helsinki, the Good Clinical Practice guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation, applicable regulatory requirements and the trial sponsor’s (AstraZeneca) policy on bioethics and human samples; the protocol was approved by the relevant institutional review boards or ethics committees associated with each study center. All patients provided written informed consent. ADAURA trial design Full details of the phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled ADAURA trial have been reported previously , , and are available in the study protocol provided with ref. at https://www.nejm.org/ . Briefly, eligible patients were 18 years of age or older (20 years or older in Japan and Taiwan) and had postsurgical stage IB (T2a tumors >3 cm and ≤5 cm in size), II or IIIA NSCLC (classified according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Cancer Staging Manual, 7th edn ), with a centrally confirmed EGFR mutation (Ex19del/L858R) and a World Health Organization performance status of 0 or 1. Following complete surgical resection of primary NSCLC, patients received adjuvant chemotherapy (if determined necessary, per physician and patient choice) for up to four cycles (at physician discretion), no more than 26 weeks postsurgery. Patients were stratified per disease stage (IB, II or IIIA), EGFR mutation type (Ex19del or L858R) and race (Asian or non-Asian), and then randomized 1:1 to receive osimertinib (80 mg QD) or placebo until disease recurrence, meeting a treatment discontinuation criterion or for up to 3 years of treatment. Patients not receiving adjuvant chemotherapy were randomized no more than 10 weeks after surgery. Patient demographics for the overall ADAURA population included biological sex, which was determined based on the assigned definition rather than self-report. A breakdown of biological sex and age is provided for each treatment arm of the overall ADAURA population (Extended Data Table ), the MRD analysis patient set by study group from ADAURA (Extended Data Table ), patients who had detected MRD at randomization (Extended Data Table ) and patients with DFS events by MRD status (Extended Data Table ). Endpoints and assessments The primary endpoint was DFS (per investigator assessment) for patients with stage II or IIIA disease and was defined as the time from the date of randomization until the date of disease recurrence or death from any cause in the absence of disease recurrence. Secondary endpoints included DFS among patients with stage IB–IIIA disease. An exploratory endpoint was to evaluate the feasibility (defined as the success rate for assay creation) of using ctDNA profiling approaches for detection of MRD in early-stage NSCLC patients after completion of surgery (and chemotherapy in eligible patients). Baseline CT or magnetic resonance imaging brain scans were performed within 28 days before dosing of study drug. Subsequent assessments were performed at week 12 and 24, then every 24 weeks during adjuvant treatment (up to 36 months), then every 24 weeks during the posttreatment follow-up period and then every 52 weeks until disease recurrence or death, or study end. Plasma samples were collected from day 1 of randomization, before dosing of study drug (postsurgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, if received). Longitudinal plasma samples were collected every 12 weeks during adjuvant treatment (up to 36 months), then at week 12 and 24 and every 24 weeks during the posttreatment follow-up period (up to 60 months from randomization) and then every 52 weeks until disease recurrence or death, or study end. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue specimens were available from surgical or

24 weeks during the posttreatment follow-up period and then every 52 weeks until disease recurrence or death, or study end. Plasma samples were collected from day 1 of randomization, before dosing of study drug (postsurgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, if received). Longitudinal plasma samples were collected every 12 weeks during adjuvant treatment (up to 36 months), then at week 12 and 24 and every 24 weeks during the posttreatment follow-up period (up to 60 months from randomization) and then every 52 weeks until disease recurrence or death, or study end. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue specimens were available from surgical or diagnostic primary tumor biopsies. Whole blood samples for germline analysis were collected at any time on study. MRD detection RaDaR MRD analysis (NeoGenomics) was performed as outlined in ref. . Briefly, DNA was extracted from matched FFPE tissue sections and buffy coat was derived from the whole blood samples. WES of sheared DNA was performed on tissue DNA. Patient tumor-specific variants were ranked and prioritized for inclusion into custom primer panels containing common population-specific single nucleotide polymorphisms, for internal sample quality control during NGS testing. Apart from tumor-specific variants, sensitizing EGFR mutations (Ex19del and L858R) were included in the RaDaR panels to monitor their dynamics over time. Custom panels were validated by multiplex PCR and library sequencing using the matching tumor and germline DNA from each patient to exclude germline mutations and clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential variants. Cell-free DNA was extracted from longitudinal plasma samples. Amplified libraries were generated using the validated custom panels and high-depth NGS was performed. Sequencing data FASTQ files were demultiplexed using bcl2fastq ; reads were then aligned to the GRCh38/hg38 assembly of the human genome and processed to identify primer pairs, and to count mutant and reference bases. A statistical model was used to assess the significance of the observed counts for each variant and the information was integrated over the entire set of variants from an individual sample to obtain evidence of detected MRD (ctDNA positive) or undetected MRD (ctDNA negative) at the sample level. The model also generated an estimated variant allele frequency for each sample. An ‘MRD detected’ classification was made in alignment with the standard NeoGenomics RaDaR assay algorithm when plasma ctDNA tested positive according to the integrated statistical assessment of mutations in the RaDaR panels. MRD was considered ‘detected’ at any timepoint, when its integrated statistical assessment was above a preset threshold as defined during analytical development . MRD was considered ‘cleared’ if, following the detection of MRD at randomization, subsequent samples within the next two timepoints (24 weeks from randomization) were determined to be MRD undetected. Lead times were defined as the date of the DFS event minus the date of the first postrandomization timepoint with MRD detected. Postrandomization timepoints were used for the lead-time analysis to allow for MRD clearance with osimertinib treatment. Genomic analysis at baseline The genomic data used for pipeline analyses were from WES of FFPE tumor DNA samples described in the above ‘MRD detection’ section. FASTQ files were processed using pipeline software bcbio-nextgen (10.5281/zenodo.3564938). Reads were aligned to the hg38 reference using bwa mem v.0.7.17. All software were run using best-practice parameters established within the bcbio workflow. Variant calling was performed using VarDict v.1.8.2 (ref. ), down to a variant allele frequency of 1% (before filtering and curation) and variant effects were annotated by snpEff v.5.0. Filtering of noncancer variants (common polymorphisms) was performed per VarDict best practice. Copy number analysis for both exon- and whole-gene level was performed using Seq2C ( https://github.com/AstraZeneca-NGS/Seq2C ) for each gene in the panel . The change in the normalized log 2 values was used to determine potential copy number changes. Statistical analysis No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes but our sample sizes are larger than those in refs. , , or similar to those in ref. as reported in relevant previous studies. Baseline demographics and disease characteristics of the MRD analysis set were calculated using the number of patients in each treatment group. DFS for the MRD analysis set was analyzed using a log-rank test stratified by disease stage (AJCC 7th ed., II and IIIA, or IB, II and IIIA), EGFR mutational status (Ex19del/L858R) and race (Asian or non-Asian); the same analysis method that was applied to the primary analysis. DFS events that did not occur within two scheduled visits (plus visit window) of the last evaluable assessment (or randomization) were censored and therefore excluded in the number of events. Patients who had evidence of disease at study entry were censored at day 1. DCO for DFS was 27 January 2023. Due to the low number of events, OS for the MRD analysis set was analyzed using an unstratified log-rank test. DCO for OS was 11 April 2022. This analysis of MRD is

DFS events that did not occur within two scheduled visits (plus visit window) of the last evaluable assessment (or randomization) were censored and therefore excluded in the number of events. Patients who had evidence of disease at study entry were censored at day 1. DCO for DFS was 27 January 2023. Due to the low number of events, OS for the MRD analysis set was analyzed using an unstratified log-rank test. DCO for OS was 11 April 2022. This analysis of MRD is a post hoc exploratory analysis separate from the prespecified primary and secondary endpoints of the ADAURA study. These analyses were not included in the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and therefore P values have not been generated . The Kaplan–Meier approach was used to calculate DFS and MRD event-free rates at 24 and 36 months on treatment for the osimertinib and placebo groups. HR for the combined endpoint of DFS or MRD events in the osimertinib versus placebo group was calculated using an unadjusted Cox proportional hazards model that contained only treatment as a covariate, with the Efron method used to control for ties. An HR of <1 favored osimertinib. Profile-likelihood CIs were also determined. The combined endpoint of DFS (clinical recurrence or death) or MRD events was assessed postrandomization from randomization to postrandomization MRD detection, disease recurrence or death (whichever occurred first). Any patient not known to have had a postrandomization DFS or MRD event was censored at the last follow-up visit when confirmed (date of first postrandomization MRD or DFS event or censoring − date of randomization + 1). The Kaplan–Meier approach was also used to calculate DFS and MRD event-free rates in the posttreatment follow-up period for osimertinib. The 12- and 24-month post-osimertinib discontinuation landmarks were calculated from the time patients discontinued or completed osimertinib treatment. Events in this analysis were DFS or MRD events (whichever occurred first) that occurred after osimertinib discontinuation (time to MRD/DFS − total exposure + 1). Patients who experienced an MRD or DFS event ( n = 9) or were censored ( n = 9) before discontinuing osimertinib treatment, had the time to MRD or DFS event in the treatment-free period set to day 1. SAS v.9.4M7 was used for statistical analysis. Reporting summary Further information on research design is available in the linked to this article. chunks.content: 1 Specificity, Selectivity and Pharmacological Characterization of Acalabrutinib Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) has become a promising target for treating B cell malignancies [ ] and autoimmune diseases [ ]. BTK is a protein kinase belonging to the TEC family, playing a crucial role in B cell receptor (BCR) signaling, which is essential for the activation, proliferation, and survival of B lymphocytes [ , ]. In B cell malignancies, the B cell receptor remains persistently active due to both ligand‐dependent and ligand‐independent processes, leading to constitutive activation of BTK signaling [ ]. Several small‐molecule inhibitors of BTK have revolutionized the outcome of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) patients, highlighting the clinical potential of inhibiting BTK in the treatment of B cell malignancies. Most of the inhibitors developed until now bind covalently to a cysteine residue (Cys481) in the ATP binding pocket of BTK [ , ]. Ibrutinib (PCI‐32765), the first‐in‐class BTK inhibitor (BTKi), which represented an important therapeutic advance for the treatment of CLL [ , ], can induce several adverse effects (AEs) due to its off‐target binding on multiple kinases having a cysteine nucleophile in the same position as Cys481 in BTK: TEC, ITK, BMX, TXK, EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB4, BLK, and JAK3 [ ]. Cardiac events, including atrial fibrillation (AF), hypertension, sepsis, pneumonia, and bleedings, are some of the most common ibrutinib AEs, with sepsis and pneumonia being the most frequently AEs associated with ibrutinib discontinuation [ , , ]. Next‐generation inhibitors with different binding profiles and improved selectivity were developed to decrease the observed ‘off‐target’ effects of first‐generation molecules. Acalabrutinib represents a significant advancement in the treatment of CLL due to its highly selective inhibition of BTK. The molecular mechanism of action of Acalabrutinib involves covalent binding to the Cys481 residue in the BTK active site, resulting in the irreversible inhibition of BTK [ ]. Acalabrutinib inhibits BTK phosphorylation at nanomolar concentrations, thereby potently blocking downstream signaling pathways such as those involving PLCγ2, AKT, and ERK, which are crucial for B cell survival and proliferation. The head‐to‐head comparison of acalabrutinib, ibrutinib and spebrutinib in a competitive binding assay (KINOMEscan at DiscoverX) on a panel of 456 human kinases (395 WT kinases and 61 mutant ones) demonstrated that acalabrutinib is the most selective BTK inhibitor among these compounds, with only 1.5% of the non‐mutant protein kinases inhibited by 65% or more at a concentration of 1 μM [ ]. In line with these results, a TEC phosphorylation assay on human platelets demonstrates that acalabrutinib does not inhibit TEC, with less than 25% of TEC phosphorylation inhibition at a non‐pharmacological concentration exceeding 1000 nM [ ]. Conversely, IC 50 values for acalabrutinib derived from biochemical assays reported TEC inhibition at 37, 93 as well as 126 nM [ , ], highlighting the frequent discrepancies between biochemical assay and cellular test results obtained with small molecules. At variance with acalabrutinib data on TEC inhibition, both biochemical and cellular data of acalabrutinib activity on EGFR [ ] or EGFR/JAK3 kinases demonstrated coherently that acalabrutinib does not inhibit either EGFR or JAK3 kinase activity [ ]. In another study conducted by Kaptein and colleagues, biochemical assays aimed to assess and compare BTK inhibitor potency revealed that ibrutinib and zanubrutinib are the most potent BTK inhibitors, followed by spebrutinib, with acalabrutinib and tirabrutinib showing comparable potency. Importantly, potency differences were largely due to varying inactivation rates, and, in cellular assays using human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (hPBMCs) or whole blood (hWB), those differences were partially lost [ ]. Recently a detailed study aimed to characterize the acalabrutinib major active metabolite, ACP‐5862, to ultimately evaluate its potential contribution to the pharmacological activity during acalabrutinib therapy [ ]. ACP‐5862 showed both half‐life and area under the curve (AUC) approximately twofold higher than acalabrutinib in healthy subjects and cancer patients constituting 35% of the total drug‐related material in plasma [ , ]. In the study, Podoll and colleagues showed that acalabrutinib and ACP‐5862 demonstrated superior relative selectivity profiles when tested in parallel against zanubrutinib and ibrutinib, across a panel of nine kinases (TEC, ITK, BMX, TXK, EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB4, BLK, and JAK3) with a cysteine residue at the same position as Cys481 in BTK. Additionally, a high‐throughput KINOMEscan was performed to assess the kinase selectivity of both ACP‐5862 and its parent compound compared to zanubrutinib and ibrutinib. The results, once again, indicated that acalabrutinib and ACP‐5862 had similar hit rates, which were the lowest among those obtained for the other tested molecules, thus suggesting that ACP‐5862 might enhance the effectiveness of acalabrutinib treatment while preserving the advantages of high BTK selectivity [ ]. In addition to its potent selectivity, acalabrutinib shows improved pharmacologic properties such as excellent plasma exposure, quick oral absorption and short half‐life, allowing a twice‐daily dosing that results in an almost complete and sustained occupancy of

The results, once again, indicated that acalabrutinib and ACP‐5862 had similar hit rates, which were the lowest among those obtained for the other tested molecules, thus suggesting that ACP‐5862 might enhance the effectiveness of acalabrutinib treatment while preserving the advantages of high BTK selectivity [ ]. In addition to its potent selectivity, acalabrutinib shows improved pharmacologic properties such as excellent plasma exposure, quick oral absorption and short half‐life, allowing a twice‐daily dosing that results in an almost complete and sustained occupancy of BTK at 97% and a complete inhibition of BTK phosphorylation at all evaluated time points [ ]. In the same study cohort, composed of patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) CLL, the authors demonstrate that the high level of BTK inhibition in hPBMCs and lymph nodes correlates with significant clinical responses, improvements in hematologic parameters and a lower incidence of AEs typically associated with broader‐spectrum BTK inhibitors [ ]. Interestingly, when acalabrutinib pharmacodynamics (PD) was evaluated in a dose‐escalation study, both BTK occupancy assay and the inhibition of CD69 expression on B cells after ex vivo BCR stimulation reached a plateau, with the BTK median occupancy around 99% at the 75 mg and 100 mg doses [ ]. These data suggest that a dose reduction aimed at managing adverse drug reactions (ADRs) does not affect the therapeutic efficacy of acalabrutinib. The kinase‐binding patterns of BTKis, which involve both on‐target inhibition of BTK and off‐target inhibition of other kinases, are intricately linked to their toxicity. Although acalabrutinib has been demonstrated to be more selective than ibrutinib, some AEs like AF are considered a class adverse effect across BTKis [ , ]. This suggests that AF may result from both on‐ and off‐target effects, with experimental data supporting the involvement of these pathways. Similarly to AF, ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) may also represent an adverse class effect of BTKi therapy. However, the mechanistic explanation for VAs remains hypothetical, and the risks require confirmation through further studies, and no definitive conclusions can be made at this time. In conclusion, while the enhanced selectivity of second‐generation BTKis like acalabrutinib may reduce off‐target toxicities compared to ibrutinib, serious cardiac events such as AF and VAs remain potential class‐wide risks associated with BTKi therapy, highlighting the need for vigilant cardiovascular monitoring. 2 Acalabrutib Safety Profile and Immune System Modulation Available data support the broader immunosuppressive potential of ibrutinib, particularly due to its off‐target effects on T cell‐related pathways. In contrast, acalabrutinib appears safer, with less impact on T cell function, as it demonstrates higher selectivity and minimal off‐target inhibition. In T cell functional assays with Jurkat T cells, ibrutinib inhibited anti‐CD3/CD28–induced IL‐2 production, with an EC50 of 99 nM, demonstrating its broader immune‐suppressive effects, including off‐target activity on T cell kinases. In the same in vitro assay, acalabrutinib showed weak inhibition of the anti‐CD3/CD28–induced IL‐2 production with an EC50 ≥ 10 mM, consistent with its selectivity and minimal effect on T cell kinases like ITK and TXK. Historically, CLL patients have been classified at diagnosis into low‐, intermediate‐, and high‐risk groups based on IGHV mutational status, TP53 aberrations, and CK. This three‐tiered system, while justified by past clinical practice, is not used in the most recent ESMO guidelines [ ]. Instead, ESMO recommends an individualized strategy where therapy is guided by specific molecular features [ , ] ( TP53 disruption, IGHV status, and CK if available) together with patient‐specific factors (fitness, comorbidities, medications, and preferences). Therefore, aligning with ESMO 2024 recommendations, clinical management now prioritizes the combination of individual molecular and patient‐specific features over broad stratification into risk categories [ , ]. A great number of studies have indeed demonstrated that CLL patients harboring TP53 aberrations have an inferior outcome when treated with chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) approaches, while non‐chemotherapeutic tailored treatments targeting BTK have demonstrated significant efficacy in patients with CLL, including those with TP53 aberrations [ , , , , ] (Table ). Currently, acalabrutinib is a second‐generation BTKi with a 6‐year follow‐up phase III trial available. The 6 year follow up of ELEVATE‐TN trial ( NCT02475681 ) was recently published [ ] highlighting the efficacy and safety of acalabrutinib, with or without obinutuzumab, as compared to standard CIT in patients with TN CLL. Previous findings demonstrated consistently longer progression‐free survival (PFS) with acalabrutinib‐based regimens, also in patients with high‐risk disease features. With a median follow‐up of 6 years, updated results from this ongoing study provide further insights into long‐term outcomes. Over a 6‐year follow‐up period, these regimens demonstrated significantly superior PFS compared to the obinutuzumab plus chlorambucil regimen. At a median follow‐up of 74.5 months, PFS was significantly longer for patients in the acalabrutinib‐containing arms, with median PFS not reached (NR) in both arms vs. 27.8 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 22.6–33.2; both p < 0.0001) for chlorambucil‐obinutuzumab. When stratified by IGHV mutation status, the acalabrutinib plus obinutuzumab regimen continued to show superior PFS (HR, 0.08; 95% CI, 0.05–0.12; p < 0.001) as did acalabrutinib monotherapy (HR, 0.12; 95% CI, 0.08–0.18; p < 0.001) in unmutated IGHV patients, compared to the obinutuzumab plus chlorambucil regimen, which had a median PFS of 22.2 months. This could be particularly beneficial in clinical decision‐making as it helps healthcare professionals to consider the risk of AEs when advising patients about their treatment options, even though indirect comparisons could be biased by both observed and unobserved differences between the compared trials and, hence, conclusions should be interpreted cautiously. 6 Mechanisms of Resistance to Acalabrutinib in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CLL</styled-content> Resistance to acalabrutinib can arise through several distinct mechanisms, significantly impacting treatment outcomes in CLL [ , , ]. The most well‐characterized mechanism of resistance to acalabrutinib involves mutations in the BTK gene. Mutations at the cysteine residue at position 481 (C481S) are the most common and represent a key mechanism of resistance across both first‐ and second‐generation BTK inhibitors, including acalabrutinib. This mutation impairs the binding of acalabrutinib to BTK, preventing the drug from exerting its inhibitory effects. As a result, CLL cells with BTK C481S mutations can bypass the blockade of BCR signaling, leading to continued cell survival and proliferation despite treatment. Other BTK mutations, such as L528W and T474I, also contribute to resistance, although these are less frequently observed [ ]. In addition to BTK mutations, CLL cells may develop resistance by upregulating or utilizing alternative signaling pathways that bypass the BCR. These alternative pathways include the activation of Src family kinases (SFKs), phosphoinositide 3‐kinase (PI3K) signaling, and nuclear factor‐kappa B (NF‐κB) signaling. These compensatory mechanisms can maintain B cell survival and function despite the inhibition of BTK. In particular, the upregulation of PI3K/AKT signaling has been implicated in resistance to acalabrutinib and other BTK inhibitors [ , , ]. Furthermore, the CLL microenvironment plays a critical role in the survival and drug resistance of malignant B cells. Interactions between CLL cells, stromal cells, such as nurse‐like cells, and the extracellular matrix can provide protective signals that enable CLL cells to resist drug‐induced apoptosis [ ]. In particular, the presence of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., interleukin‐4, IL‐10, and CXCL12) and the engagement of integrins have been shown to support the survival of CLL cells in the presence of BTK inhibitors [ , , ]. This microenvironmental protection may contribute to the development of resistance to acalabrutinib and other BCR pathway inhibitors. Therefore, the emergence of resistant clones during acalabrutinib treatment can also contribute to therapeutic failure. Clonal evolution, driven by selective pressure from the drug, leads to the expansion of subpopulations of CLL cells that harbor resistance‐associated mutations or alternative survival mechanisms [ ]. This process can result in heterogeneity within the tumor population, complicating treatment strategies and necessitating the use of combination therapies to target multiple pathways simultaneously. 7 Advantages of Fixed‐Duration Treatment With Acalabrutinib in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CLL</styled-content> Fixed‐duration treatment with acalabrutinib in CLL offers several significant advantages, positioning it as an appealing strategy within current therapeutic paradigms aimed at maximizing clinical outcomes while minimizing treatment‐related risks [ , ]. Prolonged administration of BTKi has been associated with cumulative long‐term toxicities such as infections, bleeding events, and cardiovascular complications. Implementing a fixed‐duration regimen allows for planned treatment discontinuation, thereby reducing the risk of these adverse effects. Furthermore, continuous treatment can substantially impact patients' quality of life due to the burden of continuous therapy; a fixed‐duration approach mitigates this impact by enabling patients to resume normal activities following completion of their therapeutic course, fostering a better overall treatment experience. Importantly, clinical studies have indicated that durable responses can be maintained even after cessation of acalabrutinib, with some patients remaining in long‐term remission, thereby supporting the potential for sustained clinical benefit following a fixed course of therapy

Another critical advantage is the potential to prevent the development of drug resistance. Continuous exposure to BTKi increases the risk of emergent resistance mutations in BTK or downstream signaling molecules such as PLCγ2. By limiting treatment duration, the likelihood of resistance evolution may be diminished, thereby preserving the efficacy of acalabrutinib and future therapeutic options. From an economic perspective, while the upfront costs of acalabrutinib are considerable, a fixed‐duration strategy may ultimately lead to lower overall healthcare expenditures by reducing the need for prolonged drug administration, monitoring, and management, a benefit that has already been demonstrated in other oncological settings. Finally, fixed duration acalabrutinib treatment can be effectively integrated with combination regimens, including agents such as venetoclax or immunotherapy approaches, to enhance therapeutic efficacy while limiting treatment exposure. In conclusion, fixed‐duration therapy with acalabrutinib represents a promising and rational strategy in the management of CLL, offering reduced toxicity, improved quality of life, resistance prevention, cost‐effectiveness, and opportunities for personalized and combination‐based treatment optimization. 8 Fixed‐Duration Acalabrutinib Combinations in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">TN CLL</styled-content> Fixed‐duration CIT has shown durable remission in some CLL patients, but continuous treatment with a BTKi (with or without an anti‐CD20 antibody) demonstrates superior efficacy in previously untreated CLL patients. Venetoclax‐obinutuzumab treatment administered intravenously has shown shorter PFS in patients with unmutated IGHV and carries the risk of both tumor lysis syndrome and infusion‐related reactions, necessitating burdensome monitoring, while the ibrutinib‐venetoclax combination raises safety concerns, especially regarding ibrutinib‐related cardiovascular toxic effects in older or comorbid patients. On the other hand, acalabrutinib offers a safer profile than ibrutinib, including reduced cardiovascular AEs [ ]. Numerous preclinical and clinical studies have established that combining BTKi with the BCL‐2 inhibitor venetoclax constitutes a highly promising strategy for the treatment of CLL, particularly in the context of fixed‐duration regimens [ ]. The underlying mechanism driving this synergistic efficacy centers on inhibition of the BCR/BTK signaling axis [ ]. Such inhibition increases the dependence of CLL cells on BCL‐2 for survival, thereby sensitizing them to apoptosis induced by venetoclax [ , ]. Supporting evidence from dynamic BH3 profiling and proteomic analyses reveals that both ibrutinib and acalabrutinib similarly augment CLL cell dependence on BCL‐2 [ ]. Although most experimental and clinical findings have been derived from studies using ibrutinib due to its earlier availability, robust data demonstrate that acalabrutinib produces equivalent biological effects [ ]. Any minor differences in cytotoxicity between agents have not reached statistical significance or may reflect sampling bias [ ]. Importantly, the observed synergy with venetoclax is a true class effect of BTK inhibitors, attributable to their shared on‐target action on the BCR/BTK pathway. Therefore, when selecting a BTKi to combine with venetoclax, broader clinical considerations and individual patient characteristics should guide choice of agent. Collectively, these findings provide a strong rationale for the co‐administration of BTKi and BCL‐2 inhibitors in CLL, and they underscore the class‐wide applicability of this therapeutic strategy for achieving deep and durable remissions. However, the interpretation of these data should take into account that the AMPLIFY trial was run during the COVID‐19 pandemic years. AEs leading to dose reductions, interruptions, or discontinuation were observed across all groups, with neutropenia being the most common reason for dose reduction. Overall, AMPLIFY is the first phase III trial showing that the combination of a second‐generation BTKi with venetoclax significantly improves PFS and provides durable responses with a manageable safety profile in first‐line treatment of CLL. The AMPLIFY trial results show that fixed‐duration acalabrutinib combinations are not only effective but also represent a potentially safer alternative to CIT, venetoclax‐based regimens, and first‐generation BTK inhibitor combinations for TN CLL patients. This improved safety profile may be particularly important for extending fixed‐duration therapy to elderly patients and those with cardiovascular comorbidities, two patient populations who are often at increased risk of treatment‐related toxicities with other regimens. This trial also demonstrates that fixed‐duration acalabrutinib‐venetoclax‐based regimens (with or without obinutuzumab) achieve rates of undetectable MRD (uMRD), as assessed in peripheral blood and bone marrow using both flow cytometry and next‐generation sequencing, that remain constant over time with durability of uMRD responses observed up to 36 months post‐end‐of‐therapy (EOT + 36) [ ]. Notably, these sustained MRD‐negative rates were consistently observed even in subgroups characterized by unmutated IGHV (uIGHV), a population traditionally considered at higher risk for disease progression [ ]. Despite the robust MRD stability data, the clinical utility and prognostic significance of MRD assessment, particularly its depth and kinetic profile, remain incompletely defined in CLL treated with novel fixed‐duration regimens. Current international guidelines do not recommend MRD evaluation as a standard component for routine clinical decision‐making in CLL [ ]. Importantly, the depth of MRD negativity does not invariably correlate with response duration, and its role as a predictive or prognostic biomarker in this context is not yet fully established. To date, MRD status primarily represents a surrogate endpoint for more definitive outcomes, such as PFS and time to next treatment (TTNT). Time‐limited regimens, on the other hand, are increasingly favored to maximize treatment free intervals [ ]. Among these options, the acalabrutinib‐venetoclax combination is particularly attractive for patients prioritizing an all oral therapy with fewer early visits/laboratories when compared to venetoclax–obinutuzumab (Ven O) [ ]. Addition of obinutuzumab to acalabrutinib‐venetoclax can lengthen PFS and increase the percentage of patients with undetectable MRD at end of treatment but should be reserved for selected scenarios such as younger fit patients with high risk features, owing to infusion requirements and added toxicity [ ]. It is also important to note that molecular risk should inform frontline selection: del(17p)/TP53 mutation tilts choice toward a continuous second‐generation cBTKi (acalabrutinib or zanubrutinib), though fixed‐duration regimens remain reasonable in a shared decision making framework given encouraging—yet less mature—data in this subgroup. IGHV status and karyotypic complexity refine prognosis but are not definitive predictive markers to mandate one class over the other in the frontline setting [ , ]. Another pivotal factor to take into account when selecting first‐line treatment is the presence of cardiovascular comorbidities: atrial fibrillation history does not preclude acalabrutinib as AF risk with second‐generation cBTKis is lower than with ibrutinib. Moreover, acalabrutinib's lower hypertension incidence compared to other covalent BTKis is relevant for patients with difficult blood pressure control [ ]. In case the frontline cBTKi is discontinued for intolerance and further therapy is needed, switching to the alternative second‐generation cBTKi may be considered unless the prior toxicity was life or organ threatening; recurrence of the same intolerance event occurs in approximately one quarter of patients, usually at reduced severity [ ]. When further therapy is needed not due to intolerance, but due to the patients relapsing after or being refractory to the frontline therapy, second‐line sequencing is dictated by the previous frontline treatment selection, as summarized in Figure . For patients treated with a continuous cBTKi, Ven‐anti‐CD20 is generally recommended [ ] or, alternatively, a non‐covalent BTKi such as pirtobrutinib could be chosen in order to overcome the most common resistance mutations that might have resulted from long‐term exposure to a cBTKi [ , ]. After fixed duration with Ven O, second‐generation continuous cBTKi therapy (acalabrutinib or zanubrutinib) is recommended for most patients. After BTKi‐venetoclax fixed‐duration combinations, a continuous cBTKi therapy or a Venetoclax‐anti‐CD20 combination is recommended. In the future it might be possible to rechallenge with another BTKi‐venetoclax regimen [ , ]. Moving to third‐line therapy, the generally recommended treatment is a non‐covalent BTKi such as pirtobrutinib after any kind of previous treatment except when pirtobrutinib itself was used as a second‐line option, in which case third‐line therapy should instead be based on a venetoclax‐anti‐CD20 combination (Figure ). Referral for allogeneic transplant can be discussed for patients refractory to at least two prior therapies (including a cBTKi and Ven) who subsequently achieve remission [ ]. Clinical trial participation should be considered at any line when feasible and well aligned with the patient's priorities [ ]. A potentially useful tool in guiding therapy de‐escalation or cessation and informing retreatment strategies is MRD assessment [ ], although MRD correlation with PFS in CLL has been solidly established only in regimens containing an anti‐CD20 monoclonal antibody [ ]. Therefore, a potential strategy other than continuous long‐term therapy and fixed‐duration limited combinations is represented by MRD‐guided therapies. Trials employing MRD‐driven duration, such as FLAIR for ibrutinib‐venetoclax, demonstrate that treatment can be stopped upon achieving sustained uMRD, reducing exposure while maintaining disease control; on the contrary, persistent detectable MRD prompts continued therapy, illustrating an operational framework for MRD adaptive treatment [ , ]. However,

in guiding therapy de‐escalation or cessation and informing retreatment strategies is MRD assessment [ ], although MRD correlation with PFS in CLL has been solidly established only in regimens containing an anti‐CD20 monoclonal antibody [ ]. Therefore, a potential strategy other than continuous long‐term therapy and fixed‐duration limited combinations is represented by MRD‐guided therapies. Trials employing MRD‐driven duration, such as FLAIR for ibrutinib‐venetoclax, demonstrate that treatment can be stopped upon achieving sustained uMRD, reducing exposure while maintaining disease control; on the contrary, persistent detectable MRD prompts continued therapy, illustrating an operational framework for MRD adaptive treatment [ , ]. However, it must be noted that incorporating MRD kinetics assessment into daily clinical practice could currently encounter practical difficulties and be non‐viable by all centers [ ]. What instead should and could easily be incorporated into daily clinical practice is a comprehensive pretreatment work‐up for each individual patient, with the aim to harmonically guide frontline treatment selection and later‐line sequencing. Such assessment should include performance status, comorbidity and medication review (especially anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy), feasibility considerations (visit/laboratory burden), organ function, disease burden/TLS risk, and molecular/cytogenetic profiling (TP53 status, del(17p), IGHV status, karyotypic complexity) in order to improve individualized selection and create a durable sequencing plan [ ]. Shared decision making should be emphasized, as most patients face multiple reasonable options, and therefore their personal preferences should be considered alongside clinical factors [ ]. 10 Conclusion The advent of continuous BTKi therapy has revolutionized the management of CLL, leading to marked improvements in patient outcomes. Presently, according to the most recent ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for CLL [ ], continuous BTKi regimens remain the standard of care for patients at high risk of disease progression. Notably, among the available BTKis, acalabrutinib is specifically recognized as a highly effective and well‐tolerated therapeutic option, with a strong safety profile that makes it suitable for a broad range of patient populations. The introduction of fixed‐duration combination regimens has expanded treatment possibilities, allowing most CLL patients the opportunity to benefit from time‐limited therapy. These fixed‐duration approaches do not just deliver strong efficacy; they also bring significant advantages in terms of safety, improved quality of life through drug‐free intervals, greater cost‐effectiveness, and less reliance on hospital resources. Despite these advantages, currently available fixed‐duration regimens do present some limitations, particularly concerning safety and practical aspects of administration. Given these considerations, the encouraging efficacy and safety findings from the phase III AMPLIFY trial carry important implications for real‐world practice. These results support the use of fixed‐duration regimens on a broader range of patients, which is particularly noteworthy for patients with comorbid cardiovascular conditions, considering that time‐limited acalabrutinib demonstrated a low incidence of AF and hypertension [ , , , ]. The therapeutic landscape for CLL has evolved from an era dominated by continuous therapy to the current availability of both continuous and fixed‐duration regimens. The recent EMA approval of the AMPLIFY regimens underscores this shift, positioning acalabrutinib as a central agent now offering broad flexibility, with both continuous and fixed‐duration approaches available, allowing treatment to be tailored to an individual patient's clinical profile. This flexibility marks an important milestone in optimizing CLL care for diverse patient needs. Author Contributions G.G. and R.D. equally contributed to this paper. chunks.content: Introduction Simulation-based learning plays an important role in clinical pharmacy education because it allows students to practice clinical reasoning and therapeutic decision-making in safe, controlled settings – . Well-designed simulations provide structured scenarios and timely feedback that support cognitive development and progressive skill acquisition – . However, traditional simulation methods are difficult to scale, requiring substantial faculty time, specialized expertise, and institutional resources that limit broad curricular integration , . Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising solution by generating sophisticated, interactive clinical simulations at scale – . Despite their potential, LLMs’ clinical accuracy and educational validity remain uncertain in specialized therapeutic areas , . Most existing evaluations focus on short, discrete knowledge questions rather than extended clinical scenarios that require sustained reasoning, longitudinal decision-making, and contextual adaptation – . This gap is critical because LLMs rely on statistical learning processes that can introduce systematic errors, which may go undetected without rigorous domain-specific testing . One notable error pattern arises from how LLMs process semantically related information. Because these models learn statistical associations from training data, conditions sharing clinical features or terminology may be inappropriately conflated in generated content , . Recent work has shown that word embeddings can misattribute symptoms between distinct diseases when conditions share semantic similarities, with errors stemming from tangential associations rather than direct clinical relevance , . In medical contexts, such conflation can inadvertently merge management strategies for conditions requiring fundamentally different therapeutic approaches, a pattern we refer to as domain entanglement . These errors are particularly concerning in educational settings, as they often appear coherent and authoritative, potentially reinforcing inaccurate or unsafe knowledge among learners who lack sufficient clinical experience to recognize the inaccuracies , . To systematically assess these vulnerabilities, rigorous evaluation requires a strategic selection of test domains that combine authentic educational applications with conditions likely to expose systematic errors , . Hematologic malignancies offer this combination, involving complex, evidence-based treatment algorithms, frequent protocol updates, and challenging clinical decisions that students must master before practice – . Within this domain, acute and chronic myeloid leukemias provide a strategically designed stress test. These conditions share myeloid cell lineage and present with overlapping clinical and laboratory features, creating semantic similarity that may challenge LLMs’ ability to maintain appropriate therapeutic boundaries. However, their management approaches differ fundamentally: AML requires time-sensitive intensive chemotherapy with consolidation decisions guided by molecular features and remission status , while CML requires chronic oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy with ongoing molecular monitoring and specific criteria for adjusting treatment . This pairing enables direct evaluation of whether semantic overlap causes domain entanglement. If models inappropriately recommend CML-specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors for AML patients or apply AML induction regimens to CML cases, it would demonstrate a safety-critical failure mode. Conversely, successful boundary preservation despite semantic similarity would suggest that structured prompting can mitigate this vulnerability. Additionally, the complexity gradient between these conditions (CML following relatively linear therapeutic pathways while AML requires multi-variable conditional reasoning) enables assessment of whether therapeutic complexity independently affects LLM performance, with implications for predicting performance in other therapeutic areas. In this study, we evaluated how well LLMs generate pharmacotherapy simulations requiring accurate reasoning, safe therapeutic recommendations, and sound instructional design. Our primary aims were to (1) characterize LLM performance across instructional design quality, clinical accuracy and safety, and clinical reasoning fidelity, and (2) compare performance between AML and CML to test whether semantic similarity challenges boundary preservation while assessing whether therapeutic complexity independently affects accuracy. Our secondary aims were to (1) compare performance across four major platforms to distinguish general model capabilities from platform-specific characteristics, and (2) examine whether student satisfaction aligns with expert-rated quality to inform oversight requirements for safe educational deployment. Results Session characteristics and inter-rater reliability A total of 103 sessions were evaluated (one student did not complete the study), comprising 50 AML and 53 CML simulations distributed across four platforms: Gemini ( n = 29, 28.2%), GPT-4o ( n = 29, 28.2%), DeepSeek ( n = 23, 22.3%), and Claude ( n = 22, 21.4%). Inter-rater reliability was excellent, with an overall Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.724–0.875), exceeding the prespecified threshold of 0.80. Pairwise agreement varied across rater pairs (Supplementary ), with near-perfect concordance between two reviewers (κ = 0.955) and moderate-to-substantial concordance for pairs involving the educator reviewer (κ = 0.633–0.656) . Full scoring outputs are provided in Supplementary , and complete session transcripts are available in Supplementary . Overall session success rate Of 103 sessions evaluated, 53 (51.5%; 95% CI: 41.7–61.2%) met passing criteria across all three domains simultaneously (Fig. ). Domain-specific success rates were 60/103 (58.3%) for clinical accuracy and safety, 84/103 (81.6%) for clinical reasoning fidelity, and 85/103 (82.5%) for instructional design quality, with clinical accuracy and safety emerging as the limiting domain. Performance by disease type CML sessions
